A table is `<table>` with `<thead>`, one `<tbody>` for each body and `<tfoot>` for its groups. Each group tag stands on its own line and each row is one line: `<tr>`, its cells, `</tr>`. An empty group is not written.

A header cell is `<th>` and a data cell is `<td>`. Explicit `table_cell.scope` writes `scope` with its value; otherwise a head header uses `scope="col"` and another header uses `scope="row"`. In a body with `rowHeadColumns` N, a cell that starts in one of the first N columns is written as a header cell. `headerIds` writes a space-separated `headers` attribute in its listed order, and each id names a header cell.

A cell with a resolved alignment (C2-B-213) carries `style="text-align: VALUE;"`. A resolved vertical alignment adds `vertical-align: VALUE;` after it, one space apart, and stands alone where the cell has no horizontal alignment: `style="vertical-align: top;"`. A cell with no alignment on either axis carries no `style`. An authored `style` keeps its value and takes the declarations after it.

`rowspan` and `colspan` are written only from the counts of the cell and only for a count above 1, so an authored key of either name on a cell is never written: the span marks alone shape the grid, as in 0.1. A cell that a span covers is not written.
The caption of a table is `<caption>`, the first child of `<table>`. The attributes of the table stay on `<table>`.

A table with at least one column that has a `width` writes `<colgroup>` after its caption and before its first group, with one `<col>` per column. A column with a width carries `style="width: P%;"`, where P is the width times 100 written as a decimal number without trailing zeros, so `0.305` gives `30.5%` and `0.25` gives `25%`. A column without a width is a bare `<col>`. A table where no column has a width has no `<colgroup>`.

`aligns`, `valigns`, `widths`, `header-rows`, `footer-rows`, `body-rows`, `body-header-rows` and `body-header-cols` on a table are never written as HTML attributes, whether the table consumed the key or kept it in `attrs` (C2-B-227). `header-cols` on a pipe table or a delimited table is written as an ordinary attribute (C2-B-214).

A cell whose children are not one `cell_paragraph` holds the blocks of an imported or supplied tree (C2-A-091), and each `paragraph` among them is written with `

`. A cell of one paragraph stays on the line of its row: `

c

`. Any other such cell is written as a list item with more blocks is (C2-H-007): a first paragraph on the line of the cell tag, every other block on its own line one level deeper than the row, and the closing cell tag on its own line at the indent of the row, after which the row goes on.

An image paragraph, a code block, a quote or a math block that carries a caption (C2-A-082) is written as `<figure>` around the block and then `<figcaption>` with the caption. The tree has no node for this `<figure>`. With `sourceLines` on it carries the line the block starts on, and the element of the block inside it the line of the block's own opening markup, after its attribute lines.
The `attrs`, `lang` and `dir` of such a block are written on its `

A figure group is `<figure class="carve-figure-group">`. Each panel in it (C2-A-084) is `<figure class="carve-figure-panel">` in place of the `<figure>` of C2-H-062, and the caption of the group is the last child of the group. A table panel is wrapped too: the panel figure holds the `<table>`, which keeps its caption as `<caption>` (C2-H-061) and has no `<figcaption>`.
A caption holds blocks (C2-A-081). A caption with one paragraph, which is every parsed caption, writes that paragraph bare inside `

The caption number mark `#` in a caption is replaced by the number of the caption in its sequence. The sequences, the label word that selects one, and the numbering of equations are as in 0.1. C2-B-207, C2-B-208 and C2-H-149 to C2-H-151 state them. A panel caption takes no number. The number mark of a caption that takes no number, such as the caption of a panel, is written as the character `#`.
With `roundtrip` off the number is plain text. With it on, the number is wrapped in `<span data-carve-caption-number>`.
`caption.short` is not written to HTML (C2-A-175).

Each sequence key (C2-B-208) has its own count, from 1, in the order of C2-H-170. Each caption with a mark takes the next number of the sequence of its key. The label words are not a closed list: `Figure`, `Table`, `Listing` and `Equation` have no special meaning, the block under the caption does not select the sequence, and `Fig.`, `figure` and `Figure` count apart. The number is written in place of the mark as a decimal number, and the rest of the caption is written as it stands. A caption without a mark is written as it stands and takes no number.
The captions and numbered equations of footnote bodies take their numbers after those of the document body, in the order of the footnote numbers. One in an unused footnote definition takes none.

Captions and numbered equations of one key are counted in document order, a node before the nodes inside it, the document body first and then the footnote bodies (C2-H-150): the caption of a table takes its number before an equation in a cell of that table.

In a supplied tree, a display `math` node that carries `numberPrefix` takes the next number of the sequence whose key is its `numberPrefix`, counted together with the captions of that key. The number is written after the math element as ` PREFIX N`. Inline math takes no number. A display math node inside a block or a `figure_group` whose caption has a mark takes no number of its own: the nearest such caption around it owns the number. `numberPrefix` has no source spelling, so a parsed tree holds no numbered equation, and `^ Equation #` numbers a caption.

A comment renders nothing in every form: line, block and braced. The whitespace around a braced comment stays as written. A *comment line* of a paragraph or another leaf, a line that holds nothing but comments of any form and spaces, takes one of the two line breaks around it with it: the break behind it is not written, or the break before it when the content ends with the comment. The test is made in each list of inline children on its own, also in the children of an inline node such as a strong span: a line of that list is what stands between two of its breaks, and the end of the list counts as the end of the content. The tree keeps both breaks.
Frontmatter renders nothing.

A link definition and an abbreviation definition render nothing, except that with `roundtrip` on a run of abbreviation definitions writes a template (C2-H-178). A footnote definition renders only through the footnote section (C2-H-089).

An include directive that was not expanded is an `include` node (C2-A-181). It renders as a paragraph that holds the directive as text, written bare or with `

` as a `paragraph` node at its place would be (C2-H-006, C2-H-007, C2-H-034, C2-H-040): `{{`, a space, the path as C2-H-171 writes it, the section, the options in the order of C2-W-058 and the entries of `invalid` as the tree holds them, each after one space, a space and `}}`. An unexpanded include that has a caption is never written bare: its paragraph and the paragraph of the caption (C2-N-074) each get `

` on lines of their own. It is reported with the code `include-unresolved`. An include is unexpanded when no resolver was given or when its expansion failed (C2-N-061); an expanded include writes its children and nothing else (C2-N-075).

When an unexpanded include is written, a path that holds a space, a tab, `#`, `@`, `}`, `"` or `“` stands in double quotes, with a backslash before each `"` and `\` in it, as the writer writes it (C2-B-202, C2-W-058), so the text reads back as the same directive. An option value that holds a space, a tab, `@` or `}` stands in double quotes, and every other value stands bare. The value is the one the tree holds. An invalid option is written as the source spelled it (C2-A-181), so `@cols:"a,,b"`, which is no list of names (C2-B-205), stays `@cols:"a,,b"`. A `cols` list of names is written as its names joined by commas in one pair of double quotes; the tree keeps no quotes (C2-A-181). The writer does the same (C2-W-058). A value that starts with a double or a single quote is written in double quotes too, since bare it would read as the start of a quoted value (C2-B-204).
The inline nodes map to elements as follows.
A replacement is a `delete` followed by an `insert` (C2-A-097) and renders as `<del>` directly followed by `<ins>`, with no wrapper.
Emphasis and strong nest in the tree order: `<strong><em>` or `<em><strong>`, as written (C2-A-096).

A span with one of the keys `abbr`, `time` or `kbd` is written as the element of that name in place of ``. A value of `abbr` becomes `title` and a value of `time` becomes `datetime`, each only when it is not empty, so `[x]{time}` and `[x]{time=""}` are `x`; a value of `kbd` is dropped. Several keys nest in the fixed order `abbr`, `time`, `kbd` from inside out, and the remaining attributes go on the outermost element. An authored `title` or `datetime` wins over the derived one. The three keys match in lower case only: a key in another case, `KBD` or `Abbr`, is an ordinary attribute, so `[x]{KBD}` is `x` (C2-H-013). As in 0.1 (CARVE-P10-003 to CARVE-P10-007).

The names `samp`, `var`, `cite` and `dfn` are not core. Without their extension, `[x]{samp}` is a span with the attribute `samp=""`. An unqualified inline extension with no renderer is `<span class="ext-NAME">` around its content. The core never turns an extension name into an element name. In 0.2.0 an extension may give qualified `inline_extension` and `block_extension` nodes. A matching trusted renderer writes its returned HTML string unchanged under C2-X-034. An unknown optional extension renders through its fallback, inside an element that carries the node's attributes where it has any (C2-X-035), and is reported with the code `extension-fallback-rendered`.

A math block is a paragraph that holds nothing but one display math span. The fact is set when the paragraph closes (C2-B-158, C2-B-198) and is the mark `role: "math"` (C2-A-184), as for a block image. It is written as `

` around the display form of C2-H-072, and it takes a caption (C2-H-062).
A smart-punctuation node is written as its glyph. With `smartTypography` off it is written as its `source` (C2-A-098).

Three shapes reach the renderer only in a supplied tree (C2-A-175). `small_caps` is `<span class="smallcaps">` around its content. `ruby` is `<ruby>` that holds, for each pair, the base, then `<rp>(</rp>`, `<rt>` around the annotation and `<rp>)</rp>`. A `section` node is `<section>` around its blocks, indented like every container.

A link is `<a href="URL">` around its content, with `title` when it has one. An autolink is a link whose content is its body as written. The destination of an email autolink is `mailto:` followed by the address, and its content is the address.

An image is ``, with `title` when it has a tooltip. `alt` is always written, empty for a decorative image. A supplied image without `src` writes `src=""`. A `longDescription` writes its blocks as visible HTML after the block that contains the image. This keeps block elements outside a paragraph and needs no generated id or reference.

A direct link, a reference link, or an autolink inside link text is unwrapped: its content is written and its anchor is not (C2-A-111). A resolved cross-reference inside link text writes its generated plain text without an anchor. A mention or tag with a `social` URL inside link text writes its inert span instead of an anchor. These rules apply at every depth of the link text. An unresolved reference or cross-reference writes its ordinary text. Raw HTML, trusted symbol values, and extension renderer output remain verbatim; the core does not inspect anchors supplied by those payloads. A core citation group writes text and makes no anchor.
A destination that `urlPolicy` denies is written as the empty string, and the element stays: `<a href="">`. The denial is reported as the render loss `destination-denied`.

A link reference resolves against the link definitions, then against the headings (C2-I-081, C2-I-084). A reference that a heading resolves is `<a href="#ID">` with the id of that heading. The first matching heading in document order wins.

An unresolved full or collapsed reference renders its brackets and label as literal text: `[`, rendered children, `]`, then `[key]` for `refForm: "full"` or `[]` for `refForm: "collapsed"`. An image adds `!` and uses its `alt` as text. No source form is rebuilt for the children. A footnote reference or inline footnote among them keeps its ordinary meaning. A shortcut of parsed source has a matching definition and never reaches this rule (C2-I-072); an unresolved shortcut of a supplied tree (C2-A-213) renders `[`, its rendered children and `]`, with no label after them. The attribute blocks glued to the reference follow its text as one brace block in the fixed order (C2-I-085, C2-H-139), for a render of source and of a supplied tree alike.
An unresolved footnote reference renders as the text `[^key]`, and an unresolved cross-reference as the text `</#key>`.

An attribute block that is attached to an unresolved reference is written after it as text, as one brace block in the fixed order: id, classes, language, keys. A key with an empty value is written as its name alone. A value that holds whitespace, `"`, `'`, a backslash, `|` or `}` stands in double quotes, with a backslash before each `"` and each backslash in it; every other value stands bare.

The attributes of a link definition are merged into every link and image that resolves through it. The classes of the definition come first and the classes of the reference follow. An id and a key of the reference win over those of the definition. The keys of the definition that the reference does not carry come first, in the definition's order, then the keys of the reference in its order: a definition `{j=2 k=1}` and a reference `{m=4 j=3}` give `k="1" m="4" j="3"`.

Footnotes are numbered from 1 in the order of their first reference in the document. A labeled footnote and an inline footnote share the one sequence. A later reference to the same label reuses its number. References in the body of the document are numbered first, in document order; references that stand inside a note are numbered after them, note by note in the order of the notes' numbers.

A footnote reference or inline footnote writes its note mark as `N`. The second and later references to one note have the ids `fnrefN-2`, `fnrefN-3`, and so on, each suffixed when taken (C2-H-202). An id the author wrote on a reference replaces the generated one, and the backlink of the note points to it. When a note mark occurs anywhere in the text of a direct or reference link, including inside an inline descendant, nothing is written at its place. The marks are written directly after the closing `` of the outermost rendered link in source order. The footnote and inline footnote nodes stay at their places in the tree, and the backlinks point to the moved marks. An image's alternative text and every other plain text rendering are unchanged. A cross-reference has generated plain text and no inline children that can hold a note mark. A heading's generated id is on its heading or section element, not on an enclosing anchor, so a link inside a heading follows this rule as elsewhere.

The footnotes are written in one section: `<section role="doc-endnotes" aria-label="LABEL">`, then `<hr>`, then `<ol>` with one `<li id="fnN">` per note in number order, its id suffixed when taken (C2-H-202). LABEL is the `endnotes` string of `labels`.

The ids of C2-H-088 and C2-H-089 take part in the uniqueness of C2-H-024. They are allocated after every other generated id (C2-H-024, C2-H-025, C2-H-156, C2-H-158), reference by reference in the order of C2-H-087: a reference that introduces note N allocates `fnN` and then its own id, and a later reference to note N allocates its own id. An id that is already taken gets the suffix `-2`, then `-3`, until it is free, so a taken `fnref1-2` becomes `fnref1-2-2`. The `href` of the reference and the backlinks of the note use the final id. An id the author wrote on a reference is reserved first like every authored id and is kept. 0.1 left these ids out, so an authored id or a heading slug could duplicate them.
The body of an inline footnote is one paragraph.

The backlinks are appended to the last block of the note that renders something when that block is written as `

`, and otherwise stand in a paragraph of their own. A note with one reference has one backlink, `↩`, where LABEL is the `footnoteBacklink` label (C2-H-125). A note with several has one per reference, each with `K` after the glyph and `LABEL K` as its label, joined by one space.
A footnote definition that no reference uses is not written.
The section stands at the end of the document, after the last block, unless a `footnotes` directive places it (C2-H-158). As in 0.1 (CARVE-P9-073).

With no numbered footnote in the document, no section is written. A note whose every reference is degraded (C2-H-165) or stands in a note that is not written is not written, and with no note left no section is written, as in 0.1.

A cross-reference resolves against the ids of headings, of numbered captions and of the panels of a figure group whose caption is numbered (C2-A-084), under NFC and without case folding (C2-I-097). The id of a numbered caption or of a panel is the `attrs.id` of the block that carries it.

A resolved cross-reference is `<a href="#ID">` around generated text. For a heading the text is the plain text of the heading. For a numbered caption it is the label word and the number, such as `Figure 1`. For a panel it is the label word and the number of its group and the letter of the panel in panel order, `a` to `z`, then `aa`, `ab` and so on, such as `Figure 1a`, as in 0.1. 0.2.0 renders this default text for every cross-reference: a `display` (C2-A-116) that an extension or a supplied tree set is kept in the tree and selects no other text in the core.
An abbreviation node is `<abbr title="EXPANSION">` around the term.

One render has a budget for derived text: `derived_text_bytes` of `data/limits.json`, 1,000,000 bytes, or `derived_text_factor`, 8, times the source length in UTF-8 bytes, whichever is more. The source length is the byte length of the source the renderer parsed; for a supplied tree it is the root's `srcByteLength` (C2-A-010), 0 where that is absent, and, for a tree read from JSON text, never more than the byte length of that text; a call given a tree as a value has no such text, and the cap does not apply. Abbreviation nodes written as `<abbr>` (C2-H-098) and resolved cross-references (C2-H-096) draw on the one budget in the order the renderer writes them. An abbreviation costs the UTF-8 byte length of its expansion as the definition holds it, before escaping; a cross-reference costs the byte length of its generated text as written in HTML, after escaping. A node whose cost is more than what remains draws nothing and is written in its plain form: an abbreviation as its term, with no `<abbr>` and no `title`, and a cross-reference as `<a href="#ID">` around its key. A later node that fits what remains still draws on it. The first node of a render that does not fit reports `derived-text-budget` in the render-loss channel, once per render. The source length is an input of the render beside the tree: tree equality skips `srcByteLength` (C2-A-162), so two equal trees with different lengths can render different HTML where the budget binds. A supplied tree without `srcByteLength` has the fixed budget of 1,000,000 bytes, whatever the length of its JSON text. A host may raise neither number. As in 0.1, which reported nothing.

A mention is `@NAME` and a tag is `#NAME`. When `social` gives a URL for it, the element is `@NAME` or `#NAME`, with no ``, as in 0.1. Where a mention carries `label` (C2-A-101), the label replaces `@NAME`, inside `` in the span and directly inside `` in the link.

A symbol whose name is in the `symbols` table is written as the table's value, verbatim. A symbol with no entry is written as its source, `:NAME:`. A symbol that carries attributes is wrapped in a `<span>` that carries them, around the value or the source.

*Definitions.* Link, footnote and abbreviation definitions stand anywhere at the top level, also after their uses. A streaming renderer buffers every leaf that holds a reference or, for abbreviations, every leaf, until the end of the document, unless the caller supplies the definitions in advance.

*Id collision counter.* The set of authored ids of the whole document is needed before the first generated id is final (C2-H-024). A streaming renderer buffers from the first heading without an authored id to the end of the document, or runs a first pass that collects the authored ids.
*Forward references.* A heading reference, a cross-reference and a caption number in a cross-reference can point at a block further down. They resolve only at the end of the document.

*Footnotes.* The number of a note is known at its first reference (C2-H-087), so a reference outside link text can be written at once when the definitions are known. A reference inside link text waits for the link's closing tag (C2-H-088). The note bodies and their backlinks are buffered to the place of the section, and a `::: footnotes` div above the last reference has to wait for the end.

*Tightness.* Whether a list is loose is known only when the list closes (C2-B-191). A streaming renderer buffers each top-level list as a whole, because the first item's `

` depends on a blank line that may follow the last item but one.

*Captions.* A caption line follows its block (C2-B-146), and it decides whether a `<figure>` wraps the block and whether a table has a `<caption>` as its first child. A streaming renderer holds back each image, table, code block, quote, math block and figure group until the next line is read.
*Sections.* A section closes at the next heading of the same or a lower level number, or at the end. Its opening tag needs only the heading, so sections need a stack and no buffer.
*Description wrapping.* Whether the first paragraph of a description is bare is known only when the description closes (C2-H-040).
*Task lists and table groups.* The `task-list` class and the head and the foot of a table are known when the list or the table closes.
A renderer may buffer more than these clauses require. Its output has to equal the output of a renderer that works from the finished tree. 0.2.0 defines no streaming renderer with weaker guarantees.

With `roundtrip` on, the renderer adds attributes that carry tree facts HTML has no spelling for, and writes the abbreviation definitions as templates (C2-H-178). The option adds the carriers, the carrier element of a raw span (C2-H-051) and the abbreviation templates, and changes no rendered text. It is off by default.
A carrier exists only for a fact the tree holds. A spelling that the sidecar holds has no carrier, and neither has a field that 0.2 deleted.
The carriers of 0.1 (CARVE-P10-015, CARVE-P10-016) and their fate in 0.2:

The reserved names are the 18 names of this table that stay, are new or stay reserved: 15 stay, 2 are new, and `data-carve-src` stays reserved. The set is a list, not a prefix: another `data-carve-` name is an ordinary authored attribute.

An authored attribute with a reserved name is dropped on every element, with `roundtrip` on or off, and reported as the render loss `carrier-attribute-dropped`. The attribute line of a definition inside an abbreviation template (C2-H-179) is text and not an attribute of an element: it keeps every key it holds, a reserved name included.
A presence carrier is written as the bare attribute name, with no value. A reader takes the name as presence and does not compare a value.

The quote form, the form of a hard-break block, the numbering form of an ordered list, continuation rows, the table form, the declared head count of a delimited table and the verbatim text of a reference are sidecar facts (C2-L-016 to C2-L-023, C2-L-057) and have no carrier. Source that is imported back from HTML is written with the defaults of C2-L-030 to C2-L-041.

The HTML importer is part of 0.2.0. It reads the 17 carriers of C2-H-115, the abbreviation template among them, and the reserved name `data-carve-src`, as the section "Import" states (CARVE-P10-017, CARVE-P10-021), and maps every other element and attribute as `import-html.md` states.
`data-carve-tight` is written on every tight list, with no test on its items.

Under `roundtrip` a resolved reference written in the collapsed form carries the presence carrier `data-carve-ref-collapsed` beside `data-carve-ref`. A reference in the full form carries `data-carve-ref` alone. A shortcut reference carries the presence carrier `data-carve-ref-shortcut` beside `data-carve-ref`.

With `roundtrip` on, each maximal run of consecutive `abbreviation_def` nodes among the children of the document is written at the place of the run as one `<template data-carve-abbreviations>`. A node of any other type ends the run, a comment included, so two definitions with a comment between them give two templates. A template stands where the first definition of its run would stand, inside the section that holds that place when `sections` is on (C2-H-026). With `roundtrip` off a definition writes nothing (C2-H-071). A profile does not degrade an `abbreviation_def`, also one outside the profile (C2-H-165): the template is data and no presentation, so it is written under every profile, and the definition is not reported as degraded.

The text of the template is the run as the canonical writer spells it: each definition by C2-W-055, with its attribute line directly above it (C2-W-047), and one blank line between two definitions (C2-W-017). No line ending follows the last line. The text is escaped as text content (C2-H-002) and stands between `<template data-carve-abbreviations>` and `</template>` with nothing else around it. The start tag stands on its own line with the indent of its level (C2-H-005); every later line of the text starts at column 0, as a line break inside inline content does.

Every definition of the run is in the text, in tree order: one that no abbreviation uses and one whose key an earlier definition holds (C2-B-085) are written like every other one. The renderer neither drops nor merges a definition.

A definition that the writer cannot spell is in the text as the writer writes it, and the render reports the writer's loss entry (C2-W-117). An expansion that holds a line break is such a case: it is written with one space in place of each line break (C2-W-055), so the template still reads back as a run of definitions (C2-H-187).

The HTML importer reads an HTML fragment and returns a tree. This section states what it does with the 18 reserved names of C2-H-115, how it rebuilds the definitions that have no carrier, and what does not survive. An element that carries none of them is read as `import-html.md` maps that element (C2-M-007). Where this section says that a carrier is ignored, the importer reads its element in the same way, as if the carrier were not there: the HTML is read as it stands.

A carrier sets only the facts its row of C2-H-186 names. How the importer reads an element that carries no carrier does not depend on carriers elsewhere in the document, except a carrier of an ancestor whose row names that reading, as `data-carve-line-block` does for the lines it holds. So `

a b

` imports to the same tree alone and beside `
    `, and a render with `roundtrip` that holds no carrier imports as every other render does.

The importer parses the HTML by the HTML Standard. The text of a `<template>` is the text of its template contents, which the HTML parser places in the content fragment of the template and not among its child nodes.
A carrier is read only on an element that the importer reads as structure: an element of the kind and at the place the table of C2-H-186 names. On any other element the carrier is ignored.

A carrier whose value is malformed, which contradicts the HTML around it or which contradicts another carrier of its element is ignored. The column "Ignored when" of C2-H-186 lists these cases for each name. Where two carriers contradict each other, both are ignored. A carrier that is ignored sets no tree fact, and the other carriers of its element are read as usual.
An importer never keeps a reserved name as an authored attribute, whether it reads the carrier or ignores it. What a reader does with each name:

A `<template data-carve-abbreviations>` is read only at the top level of the flow: as a child of the fragment, or of a `<section>` that the importer reads as the section of a heading (C2-H-026). Its text is parsed with the Carve block reader as a document of its own, with no second grammar. When that document holds at least one block and every block is an `abbreviation_def`, those nodes are inserted, in their order, among the children of the document at the place of the template, with their attributes and without `pos` (C2-A-159). Otherwise the template gives no definition.

A link definition renders nothing (C2-H-071) and has no carrier, as in 0.1. The importer rebuilds the definitions from the references whose `data-carve-ref` it reads. For each key it makes one `link_reference_definition` whose `href` is the `href` and whose `tooltip` is the `title` of the first `` or `` in document order that carries the key. The rebuilt definitions stand after the last block of the document, in the order in which their keys are first met, and the footnote definitions follow them (C2-H-194). A rebuilt definition has no attributes: the attributes that a definition merged into its references (C2-H-141) are read as attributes of each reference.

Two elements with one key and a different `href` or `title` occur only in HTML that was changed after the render, since every reference of a key resolves to one definition. The first element decides the definition. A later element is still read as a reference with the key, so it resolves through that definition: its own `href` and `title` are not read.

HTML holds no trace of three facts of link definitions, so they do not survive: a definition that no reference uses, a later definition of a key that an earlier one holds (C2-B-085), and the place of a definition among the blocks. In the source, `unused-link-reference-definition` (C2-W-106) reports the first and `duplicate-link-reference-definition` the second.

A footnote definition renders only as a note of the footnote section (C2-H-089), which holds one note per used footnote, in the order of the footnote numbers. The importer reads each note that carries `data-carve-footnote-label` as a `footnote` whose key is the value and whose blocks are the blocks of the note without its backlinks. These definitions follow the rebuilt link definitions, in the order of the notes. A note that carries `data-carve-inline-footnote` gives no definition: its reference reads back as the inline footnote (C2-H-186). The key and the blocks of every used footnote survive, and so does the place of a `footnotes` directive that places the section (C2-H-158). As for link definitions, an unused footnote definition, a later definition of a key and the place of a definition among the blocks do not survive. `unused-footnote-definition` (C2-W-106) and `duplicate-footnote-definition` report the first two in the source.

Round trip is promised only for HTML that the renderer wrote with `roundtrip` on and that was not changed afterwards. For such HTML the importer recovers each fact that a carrier names. It does not recover what has no carrier: the sidecar facts of C2-H-119 and the facts that HTML and the carriers do not hold.

The facts of this table are known not to survive a render with `roundtrip` and an import, in addition to the sidecar facts of C2-H-119 and the definitions of C2-H-193 and C2-H-194. 0.2.0 adds no carrier for them. Each row gives a minimal input, in which `⏎` stands for a line break, and the source that the import gives back as the canonical writer spells it. Rendering that source again gives the same HTML, except for rows 1, 5, 6, 7, 13, 16, 19, 23 and 24.

The list of C2-H-195 is complete as far as known. A tree fact that neither the table of C2-H-186, nor C2-H-119, C2-H-193, C2-H-194 or the table of C2-H-195 names, nor a fact the render does not write (C2-H-188), is expected to survive a render with `roundtrip` and an import of the unchanged HTML. A round trip that loses such a fact is a defect of this specification or of the engine, and the fix is a row in that table or a fix of the engine.

With `rawHtml` on, raw HTML is passed through verbatim (C2-H-053), so a document can hold a template or a carrier that the renderer did not make. The importer cannot tell the two apart and reads them alike. A carrier is data and not a grant: reading one never makes the importer trust the HTML around it, and a renderer applies its options and the URL policy to an imported tree as to any other.
A sanitizer that removes `<template>` elements or `data-` attributes removes the facts they carry. The rest of the HTML still imports: an element whose carrier was removed is read as it stands.

A `<figure>` that holds one block element and then a `<figcaption>`, and that is no figure group, is read as that block with the caption in its `caption` slot when C2-A-082 lets that block carry a caption and it has none yet (any other such figure is a `figure_group`, C2-M-043), and the attributes of the `<figure>` and of the block element merge into the block's `attrs` (C2-M-043). A panel `<figure class="carve-figure-panel">` is read the same way without its class, and a panel that holds a `<table>` gives that table.
Fourteen of the 20 options affect rendering. No option of this section changes the tree, except that `headingIds` controls a resolution result.

`mode` is `interactive`, the default, or `static`. Static output is self-contained: an extension renders through its static path, and a diagram without a build-time renderer falls back to its source as a code block. An unknown value is refused.

Static mode writes core math as interactive mode does: an inline math node and a math block keep the `math` span with the TeX delimiters (C2-H-072, C2-H-077), as in 0.1. Core math has no build-time renderer, so no entry of `renderers` (C2-H-123) applies to it.
`renderers` maps an extension name to a build-time renderer and is read only in static mode.
`symbols` maps a symbol name to its output (C2-H-101). The values are trusted and written verbatim.

`labels` replaces the strings the engine writes itself, such as the label of the footnote section and of a backlink. A label is text and is escaped where it is written. A key left out keeps its English default. The core writes no string of the keys `indexBackref`, `codeGroup` and `tocNav`, which are kept for extensions.

`social` holds the URL templates and the resolvers for mentions and tags (C2-H-100). Without it, both render as inert spans. It has five fields, each optional, and no other: `mentionUrl` and `tagUrl` are strings, `resolveMention` and `resolveTag` are functions of the host, and `context` is a value of the host that the renderer passes on and never reads. A template gives its string with each `{name}` replaced by the name, percent-encoded as UTF-8 with every character encoded except ASCII letters, digits and `-`, `_`, `.`, `!`, `~`, `*`, `'`, `(` and `)`; every other part of the template is written as it is. A placeholder is `{`, one or more ASCII letters, digits or underscores, and `}`. `{name}` is the only one: a template that holds another, such as `{user}` or `{tag}` of 0.1, is refused with an option error before the render starts (U-341). A resolver is called with one object and returns a URL, or nothing. The object has `kind`, the string `mention` or `tag` (not the `kind` of a mention node, C2-A-101), `name`, the name as written without its sigil, and `context`, the value of the field `context` unchanged, absent where `social` has none; as in 0.1, where `context` was the option `socialContext`. A resolver is final, as in 0.1: where `resolveMention` is given, `mentionUrl` is not read, and a mention for which it returns nothing or an empty URL, or for which it throws, is the inert span, as in 0.1, and the error does not leave the render; a tag works the same with its own pair. A template is used only where its pair has no resolver. An empty URL is no URL. The URL is a sink of the URL policy (C2-H-159).

`sourceLines` adds `data-source-line` (C2-H-016). Default off. `sections` turns section wrapping on or off (C2-H-026). Default on. `smartTypography` selects glyph or source for smart punctuation (C2-H-078). Default on. `roundtrip` adds the carriers (C2-H-112). Default off. `rawHtml` passes raw HTML through (C2-H-053). Default off. The HTML importer reads the same option: off, it drops comments and raw elements (C2-M-066).

`urlPolicy` sets which URL schemes pass on `href`, `src` and every other URL sink: a deny list, whose default is the 0.1 list of script schemes and protocol-handler schemes, or an allow list. The option has no off value. The filter also removes blocked attribute names, event handlers among them, and blanks a `style` value that holds a URL function, as in 0.1 (PART 9 section 25). The list of blocked attribute names is `dropped_attributes` in `data/url-policy.json`. C2-H-159 to C2-H-162 state the test and the filter. An object that holds both a deny list and an allow list is refused (C2-H-137); an empty object is the default deny list.

`profile` restricts the features a render accepts: `full`, `article`, `comment` or `minimal`, as in 0.1. C2-H-163 and C2-H-164 state what each one accepts. A construct outside the profile renders in its degraded form and is reported. The report has the code `profile-construct-degraded`.
`strictLosses` turns every render-loss entry into an error (C2-A-172): the render returns no output.

`headingIds` controls generated heading ids (C2-H-022). Its values are `off`, `keep-case`, `lower`, `ascii`, `ascii-lower`, `ascii-strict` and `ascii-strict-lower`, and the default is `keep-case`. With `off` no id is generated, and an authored id is still written.

A render loss is an entry of the diagnostics record with the channel for render losses (C2-A-173). The 0.1 loss codes that apply to HTML stay: `raw-format-dropped`, `destination-denied`, `carrier-attribute-dropped`. The catalog lists every code of the channel (C2-W-113). `destination-denied` has the severity error.

The URL sinks are the `href` of a link and of an autolink, the `src` of an image, each token of an authored attribute of the list `url_list_attributes` (C2-H-161), and a URL that a `social` template gives (C2-H-126). A destination is tested on a copy: first every character of the list `probe_removes` of `data/url-policy.json` is removed from it, anywhere in the value, so `java` U+0001 `script:` tests as `javascript:`. U+FFFD is on the list because a U+0000 of the source is read as U+FFFD (C2-B-218) before the test. When the rest starts with an ASCII letter, then ASCII letters, digits, `+`, `-` and `.`, and then a colon, that run is the scheme, compared without ASCII case. A destination with no scheme, such as a relative path or a fragment, passes under a deny list and under an allow list. A network-path reference such as `//x.org/p` is one: it takes the scheme of the page, as a relative path does. The `default` of `urlPolicy` in `data/options.json` is the default deny list. Only a bounded, percent-encoded `data:image/svg+xml` URL produced by the standard `imgFence` sanitizer and passed directly to its `` source is admitted despite a denied `data` scheme (C2-X-059, C2-X-060); authored `data:` URLs and every other sink keep this test.

Under a deny list a destination fails when its scheme is on the list, and under an allow list when it is not. A failed destination is written as the empty value, `href=""` or `src=""` (under `comment` a link or an autolink has no `<a>`, C2-H-163), and is reported with `destination-denied` once per destination. The link text, the alt text and the visible text of an autolink stay. An authored `href` on a link and an authored `src` on an image are not written: the destination stands, so an attribute block cannot bring back a failed one.

On every element, an extension's included, an attribute whose name is in the list `dropped_attributes` of `data/url-policy.json`, compared without ASCII case, is not written: every name that starts with `on`, `srcdoc` and `formaction`. An authored value is written empty when its text before the first colon, with the characters of `probe_removes` removed and in ASCII lower case, is a scheme of the default deny list, whatever `urlPolicy` holds: `{title="Shell: bash"}` gives `title=""`. A value that holds no colon is not tested. An attribute of the list `url_list_attributes` is split at its separators, and the whole value is written empty when any token fails this test or the policy of C2-H-160, or when the unsplit value fails this test: `ping="java script:x"` gives `ping=""`, and so does an `https` URL in `srcset` under an allow list without `https`. An authored value is one written in an attribute block or copied by an extension onto its element. `id` is not tested, and neither is a value the renderer takes from text: a link title, alt text and the label of a task box stay as written. Three places need a word. Classes are tested one by one: an authored class that fails is left out and the others stay, the element's own classes among them. The `lang` field of a supplied tree is tested like an authored value. The expansion of an abbreviation definition is text and is not tested, while `abbr` and `time` written in an attribute block are authored values and are. The default deny list applies to authored values under every policy by intent: such a value is no URL sink that `urlPolicy` governs (C2-H-159), a script or a later tool may still read it as a URL, and the option has no value that turns the filter off (C2-H-128).

An authored `style` value is written empty when it holds one of the texts of `style_patterns` in `data/url-policy.json`, tested after its CSS escapes are decoded, its whitespace is removed and its ASCII letters are lowered. A backslash and one to six hexadecimal digits decode to that code point and take one whitespace character after them; a backslash and a line break decode to nothing; a backslash and any other character decode to that character. The value that passes is written as the author spelled it.

The bidirectional controls U+202A to U+202E and U+2066 to U+2069 are never written between tags: not in text, not in code, and not in text the renderer makes, as a title paragraph, a label paragraph, the text of a cross-reference (C2-H-096) and a degraded form (C2-H-165). They can make source read in another order than it runs. They stay in the tree and in the canonical form, and an attribute value keeps them; the scheme test removes them from its copy (C2-H-159, `probe_removes`). Raw content that is passed through unescaped is not filtered, and neither is the text of an abbreviation template (C2-H-179), which is data for a reader and not presentation.

A profile decides for each node by its type and its axis, block or inline. A type on the deny list of its axis is outside the profile. Otherwise, when the axis has an allow list, a type is inside exactly when the list names it. Otherwise it is inside. An image paragraph, a code block, a quote or a math block that carries a caption is tested as its `<figure>` (C2-H-062), a type that no allow list names, so under an allow list it is outside and is degraded as a whole. No other rule excludes a type, an unknown one included. The four profiles are the rows of `profiles` in `data/url-policy.json`: `full` accepts everything, `article` everything but raw content, and `comment` and `minimal` the listed types. `comment` writes `rel="nofollow ugc"` on every link. Under `comment` a link or an autolink whose destination fails (C2-H-160) is written as its text with no `<a>`, as in 0.1: a link as the plain text of its children (C2-H-165), an autolink as its visible text. A node that stands deeper than `max_nesting` levels below the document, each block and each inline level counted, is outside the profile like a node of a refused type. An input longer than `max_length` UTF-8 bytes is refused before it is parsed: the render returns an error and no output.

The degraded form of a node outside the profile is its plain text, and no placeholder word stands for it: a node writes the text it holds and, where this clause names one, the mark of its kind, and a node that holds no text and has no such mark writes nothing. An inline node is written as the plain text of its children, and a qualified inline extension as the plain text of its fallback (C2-X-032); an image as `[img: ALT]`, the mark of its kind around its alternative text, so `[img: ]` where that is empty; a no-break space as U+00A0, a hard break and a soft break as one space, a smart punctuation node as its glyph; a footnote reference as `[^` and its key and `]`; a `comment` and a `critic_comment` give no text, so a paragraph that holds only comments still writes nothing (C2-H-019); every other inline node with no children as its plain text by C2-H-143, so a `code`, a `literal_inline` and a `math` node give their value and an autolink its visible text, a `raw_inline` as its value, a resolved `xref` as the text it writes in its link (C2-H-096) and an unresolved one as typed, and a `symbol` as `:name:`, as in 0.1. These inline forms hold for an inline node that is degraded while its block stays, and for every node inside it at any depth. Inside a block that is degraded as a whole, the plain text is that of C2-H-143 for every node except an image, which keeps `[img: ALT]`, and a `raw_inline`, an `xref` and a `symbol`, which give the text of the inline forms, so a node with no children writes the same text at both levels. An include is written as the source text of its directive. A block becomes one paragraph of its plain text behind the mark of its kind: for a heading one `#` for each level and a space (the source may have used `=`), `> ` for a quote, `- ` for each item of a list, `---` for a thematic break, one line per table row with ` | ` between the cells and a hard break between the rows, the value without its final line break for a code or raw block, and the title and the blocks joined by single spaces for a div, an admonition and a directive. A block that carries a caption writes it after its degraded form, as one more paragraph of its plain text, in which `caption_number` gives its number (C2-H-143): `^ Figure #: cap` degrades to `Figure 1: cap`, and a figure group with no block still writes its caption. Any other block that holds blocks is written as those blocks in their degraded forms, in order, and any other leaf block as one paragraph of its plain text: a description list gives one paragraph for each term and the degraded blocks of each description, and a block extension the blocks of its fallback. A node that leaves no text is dropped. A degraded node is reported once (C2-H-129), and the nodes inside it are not reported again.

For `max_nesting` the children of the document stand at level 0, and each block level and each inline level below adds one. A node at a level above the bound is outside the profile; a node at the bound stays, and its children are degraded. A `list_item` counts a level but is never degraded on its own: it keeps its `<li>`, and its blocks are degraded. Degradation comes before C2-H-069: a node at the bound writes its children in their degraded forms, so a soft break beside a comment line among them (C2-H-069) is one space.

A link carries at most one `rel` attribute, and none when neither the author nor the profile gives a word. It stands behind `href` and `title` and before the id and the classes, and holds the authored words in their order and then the words of the profile that are not among them: `{rel=me}` under `comment` gives `rel="me nofollow ugc"`. The authored value passes C2-H-161 first, so a value that test empties gives no authored word. An autolink is a link for the profiles: it is allowed where `link` is and takes the same `rel`. A mention or a tag that `social` gives a URL is a link for the profiles too: where `link` is outside the profile it is written as its inert span (C2-H-100), and elsewhere it takes the same `rel`.
The lists name 0.2 node types. An inline literal counted as code in 0.1, so `literal_inline` stands in the lists that hold `code`.

Resolution does not read `profile`: a reference to a heading resolves as it does without a profile, and the tree does not change (C2-H-121). The render reads it. The one place resolution reads it is the view of an extension node (C2-X-032): a node the profile degrades is resolved in its fallback, and the tree does not change either. A heading outside the profile is degraded (C2-H-165) and writes no element and no id, so a reference link to it is written in its unresolved form (C2-H-085), as if the heading did not exist. A cross-reference outside the profile writes its resolved link text under C2-H-165; one inside the profile follows C2-H-086 when its heading was degraded. A link that is itself outside the profile is degraded and writes the plain text of its children.
These are the 20 options, and there are no others. An application may spell a name by the convention of its language. An option that an engine does not offer is refused, not ignored.
A task box whose item has no plain text in its direct paragraph or heading children writes no `aria-label` attribute on its checkbox.

An `abbr` span with neither an authored `title` nor a nonempty derived abbreviation value writes no `title` attribute. The test is made on the value as written, before the filter of C2-H-161: an authored `abbr` that the filter empties gives `title=""`.

The engine exports the scheme test of C2-H-159 and the default deny list, the `default` of `urlPolicy` in `data/options.json`, as public functions and data for every consumer that writes a URL sink. A consumer applies the same test instead of copying the policy.

In text content and attribute values, the renderer replaces a character that the HTML input stream rejects with U+FFFD. This includes U+0000, C0 controls other than tab, line feed, form feed and carriage return, U+007F, C1 controls, unpaired surrogates and Unicode noncharacters. A surrogate pair that spells a noncharacter is replaced once. Raw HTML and HTML returned by a host extension renderer remain the host's responsibility.
The importer takes a string of HTML and returns a 0.2 document tree, its canonical Carve source and a diagnostics record. The tree is valid by C2-A-188: it passes the schema and the reader's checks.

The input is a document when, after any leading ASCII whitespace and comments, it starts with `<!doctype` or with `<html`, compared without ASCII case. A document is parsed with the HTML Standard's parsing algorithm for documents. Any other input is a fragment and is parsed with the HTML fragment parsing algorithm with a `body` element as the context element.

The importer reads the tree the parser builds, not the input text. So character references are decoded, a carriage return and a CR LF pair are one line feed (C2-H-195 row 1), U+0000 in text is U+FFFD, attribute names are in lower case (C2-H-195 row 13), and the elements the parser opens, closes or moves stand where the parser put them. The importer repeats none of this work and reports none of it.

A document's children are the children of its `<body>`. The `lang` of `<body>`, or else of `<html>`, is the `lang` of the document node, and the same holds for a `dir` read as the attribute row `dir` reads it (C2-M-052). Every other attribute of `<html>` and `<body>` is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`.

`<head>` and everything in it are dropped and reported once with `import-element-dropped`: the title, `<meta>`, `<link>`, `<base>`, and the scripts and styles of the head. The doctype is dropped and reported in the same way.

An input that would give a tree deeper than the nesting limits a reader accepts (C2-A-171, C2-B-190, C2-I-118) is refused. The importer returns no tree, and the command line fails with status 2 and the category `import-input-invalid`, in the form of C2-W-101.

Where an element carries a reserved name of C2-H-115, `html.md` governs what the name sets, when it is ignored (C2-H-185, C2-H-186) and how the definitions are rebuilt (C2-H-191 to C2-H-194). This document governs every element and every attribute that no carrier covers, and the reading of a carrier's element in every respect the carrier's row does not name.

The importer reads every input in the same way. It has no mode for Carve HTML and no mode for foreign HTML, and it never guesses which tool wrote the input. A carrier is read where it stands, an element without one is read by this document, and the two combine in one input element by element (C2-H-197).
A carrier that `html.md` ignores is reported with `import-carrier-ignored`, with the element as the locator. The reserved name is never kept as an attribute (C2-H-186).

The conventions of the Carve renderer that need no carrier are part of the mapping and apply to every input: the section a render opens at a heading (C2-M-026), the footnote section (C2-M-061 to C2-M-064), the classes of the table "Conventions" (C2-M-035), the task box (C2-M-032) and the alignment declarations (C2-M-075). Foreign HTML that uses one of them is read as Carve HTML that uses it.

Each element is read in one of two contexts. The children of the document, of a `
`, `
`, `
  • `, `
    `, `

Among blocks, a run of adjacent text nodes, comments and elements that are no block element of `elements` is one paragraph, as a render writes a bare paragraph. A run that holds only whitespace gives nothing. With the import option `rawHtml` on, a comment in a run that also holds inline content, text that is not whitespace or an element, is a `raw_inline` of that paragraph; a run that holds only comments and whitespace gives one `raw_block` per comment (C2-M-065). A run splits only at a block element.

Inside inline content, an element that `elements` maps to a block is read as a `span` of its inline content, with its attributes, and is reported with `import-element-mapped`. The HTML parser already closes a `

` before a block element, so this happens only inside other inline elements, as in `

x

`.
Text in inline content is kept as it stands, except for the rules of the section "Whitespace". Each line feed in it is a `soft_break`. Adjacent text is joined into one `text` node (C2-A-040).
Text that holds only whitespace between two blocks is not read. Whitespace here is the ASCII whitespace of the HTML Standard: space, tab, line feed, form feed and carriage return.

In inline content, spaces and tabs directly before or after a line feed are removed, and a run of line feeds with only spaces and tabs between them is one `soft_break`. A line feed directly before a `
` is removed: it is layout (C2-H-195 row 5).
At the start and at the end of the inline content of a block, whitespace of every kind is removed, and so is a `soft_break`. A no-break space is no whitespace and stays.

A `
` at the end of the inline content of a block is removed: it renders no line.
The rules C2-M-017 to C2-M-019 change no visible text. Each application is reported with `import-whitespace-normalized`, whose severity is `hint`.
A run of spaces inside a line is kept: a Carve paragraph holds it, and the renderer writes it back as it stands.
The text of `<pre>` is read verbatim, with no rule of this section, and so is the value of a code span, a math node and a raw node.

`

` is a `paragraph`. A paragraph whose only content is one image is an image paragraph, `role: "image"` (C2-H-020); one whose only content is one display `math` node has `role: "math"` (C2-A-184).
`<h1>` to `<h6>` is a `heading` of that level. `<div role="heading" aria-level="N">` with an integer N above 6 is a heading of level N (C2-H-021), and `role` and `aria-level` are not kept.

The `id` of a heading element is its authored `attrs.id`. Without the carrier `data-carve-generated-id` the importer cannot tell a generated id from an authored one, so every id is authored (C2-M-091).

A `<section>` whose first child element is a heading element, with only whitespace before it, is the section a render opens at a heading (C2-H-026), unless it is a footnote section (C2-M-061), which this clause does not read. It gives the heading and then the blocks that follow it in the section; the `<section>` itself gives no node. Its `id` is the heading's id (C2-H-027). Where the heading element carries an `id` of its own that differs, that `id` wins, and the `id` of the `<section>` is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`.
Every other attribute of such a section is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`. A render writes no other attribute on it.
A `<section>` that does not open with a heading is read as a `div` with its attributes, and is reported with `import-element-mapped`.
`<blockquote>` is a `block_quote`. `<hr>` is a `thematic_break`. A `<div>` is a `div`, unless C2-M-024 or the table "Conventions" makes it something else. All three take their attributes.

`<pre>` is a `code_block`. Its value is the text of its `<code>` child when it holds one, and otherwise its own text, in both cases with the markup inside dropped. A value that is not empty and does not end with a line feed gets one (C2-A-045). The first class of `<code>` that starts with `language-` gives `syntax`, the rest of the class. Any other attribute of `<code>` is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`. The `title` of `<pre>` is the title (C2-H-048), and the other attributes of `<pre>` are the block's attributes.

`<ul>` and `<menu>` are a bullet `list` with the marker `-`, and `<ol>` is an ordered `list`. `<li>` is a `list_item`. The `type` of `<ol>` gives the style when it is `a`, `A`, `i` or `I`, and decimal otherwise. Its `start`, read as an HTML integer, gives `start` when it is not 1 and is a start value of the list's style: between 0 and 999999999, and at least 1 on a list of letters or roman numerals (C2-B-045, C2-B-219); another value is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`. `data-delim=")"`, which every render writes (C2-H-031), gives the delimiter `)`; otherwise the delimiter is `.`.

The first `<input type="checkbox">` that is a child of `<li>` is the task box; each further one is dropped and reported with `import-element-dropped`, also with `rawHtml` on. The item has a `task` whose mark is the value of `data-task-state` when that value is the state attribute of a row of `task-states.json`, and otherwise `x` when the box carries `checked` and a space when it does not. A `data-task-state` with another value is ignored and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`. One space directly after the box is removed. `type`, `checked`, `disabled` and `aria-label` of the box are read; any other attribute of it is dropped and reported. The class `task` and the declaration `list-style: none` that a render gives a task item (C2-H-032), and the class `task-list` of its list, are not kept.

A list is loose when an item has a `

` with no attribute as its first child, after whitespace and the task box, since a tight list writes that paragraph bare (C2-H-034). A list is also loose when an item holds more than one block that is no list. Otherwise it is tight. A list with one item is tight even so (C2-B-062).
A child of a list that is no `<li>` is dropped with its content and reported with `import-structure-repaired`. Text that holds only whitespace is not such a child.

`<dl>` is a `definition_list`, `<dt>` a `definition_term` of inline content and `<dd>` a `definition_description` of blocks. A `<div>` child of `<dl>`, which the HTML Standard allows around a group of terms and descriptions, is read as the children it holds. Any other child is dropped with its content and reported with `import-structure-repaired`.

`<table>` is a `table`. `<thead>` is a `table_head`, `<tbody>` a `table_body` and `<tfoot>` a `table_foot`. Rows that are direct children of `<table>` form one `table_body` of their own. The groups take the order of C2-A-086: the first `<thead>` is the first group and the first `<tfoot>` the last wherever they stand, as HTML displays them, and this move is not reported; each further `<thead>` or `<tfoot>` is a `table_body` at its place and is reported with `import-structure-repaired`. `<tr>` is a `table_row`, and `<th>` and `<td>` are a `table_cell` with `header` true and false.

A cell that holds no block element holds one `cell_paragraph` of its inline content. A `soft_break` or `hard_break` in it becomes one space (C2-H-195 row 7) and is reported with `import-whitespace-normalized`. A cell that holds a block element holds those blocks, and one empty `cell_paragraph` when every one of them is dropped (C2-M-069, C2-M-070, C2-A-091).

Where an attribute and a declaration of the same axis both stand, the declaration gives that axis, and the `align` or `valign` attribute is then dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped` (C2-M-075). The values of `scope`, `align` and `valign` compare without ASCII case and are kept in lower case; a value outside the set of its field (C2-A-092) is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`. Any other `<figure>` that holds one block, which C2-A-082 lets carry a caption and which has none yet, and a `<figcaption>` is that block with the caption in its `caption` slot, and with the attributes of the `<figure>` and of the block element as its attributes, merged as consecutive attribute blocks are (C2-A-035), the figure's first: classes add up, and an id, a key, a `lang` or a `dir` of the block element replaces that of the figure, which is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped` (C2-H-199, C2-A-183). A figure with no `<figcaption>` that holds one block which C2-A-082 lets carry a caption is that block, with the attributes merged in the same way. Every other figure is a `figure_group`: one that holds no block or more than one block, one whose block C2-A-082 does not let carry a caption, and one with a `<figcaption>` whose block has a caption already.
These elements and classes are read as the Carve node a render writes them for. A class that a convention reads is not kept in `attrs.classes`.

`<code>` is a `code` node whose value is its text, with the markup inside dropped.

`<math>` is a `math` node when it holds a TeX source: the text of an `<annotation>` whose `encoding` is `application/x-tex`, `text/x-tex` or `LaTeX`, or else its `alttext`. `display="block"` makes it display math. A `<math>` with no TeX source is its text, reported with `import-element-mapped`.

`` with an `href` is a `link` whose `href` is the value and whose `tooltip` is its `title`. `` without an `href` is its content, in a `span` when it has attributes. `` is an `image` with `src`, `alt` (empty when absent) and `tooltip` from `title`; a `longdesc` is its long description, a paragraph with one link to that URL.

A destination is tested with the default deny list of C2-H-159 and C2-H-160. A link whose `href` fails is its content, in a span when it has attributes, and an image whose `src` fails is its alternative text, in a span when it has attributes. A `longdesc` that fails is dropped. Each failure is reported with `import-destination-denied`. The importer applies no other URL policy: a renderer applies its own policy to the tree it is given (C2-H-189).

Each attribute of an element is read by the row of `attributes` that matches its name: a row whose match is `name`, `prefix` or `reserved`, and only when none does, the row `*`. Where the row says `key`, the attribute is a key of `attrs` with its name and its value as they stand, in the order the parser gives.

The attributes that a clause of this document reads for an element, such as `href` on `<a>` or `start` on `<ol>`, are fields of its node and are not kept as keys. A `class` that a convention reads is not kept (C2-M-035).
A name that is no key by C2-I-030, such as `x:y` or `data-ü`, has no spelling in an attribute block. The attribute is dropped and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`.

A `style` is a key with its value as written, except the exact declarations of C2-M-040 and C2-M-075. It is not parsed further, and no other tree fact is taken from it. The renderer tests it when it writes it (C2-H-162).
Every element is read by its row of `elements`. An element with no row is read by the row `*`: an inline `span`. The treatment of a row is one of these:

Every treatment but `map` and `unwrap` is reported: `div` and `span` with `import-element-mapped`, `drop` with `import-element-dropped`, and `raw` as C2-M-066 states. `unwrap` is reported with `import-element-mapped` unless the row says otherwise. An element whose counterpart needs a parent element and that stands outside it, such as an `<li>` outside a list or a `<figcaption>` outside a `<figure>`, is read with the treatment `unwrap`: its children are read in its place. `<details>` is a `div`. Its first `<summary>` child is a paragraph of the summary's inline content, the first block of the div.

A `<section>` with `role="doc-endnotes"`, or whose classes include `footnotes`, is a footnote section. An `<a>` with `role="doc-noteref"` or the attribute `data-footnote-ref` is a `footnote_ref` whose key is that of the note its `href` names, or else its fragment without the prefixes of C2-M-061. A `<sup>` whose only content is such an `<a>`, or whose first class is `footnote-ref` and which holds one, is that reference alone. The `id` a render generates on a reference (C2-H-088) is not kept.

A backlink of a note, an `<a>` with `role="doc-backlink"`, with the attribute `data-footnote-backref` or with the class `footnote-backref`, is dropped without a report, with the spaces before it. A paragraph that held only backlinks is dropped.

The footnote definitions stand after the blocks of the document and after the rebuilt link definitions (C2-H-194), in the order of the notes. A footnote section with a title or a label, or with blocks after it, gives a `footnotes` directive at its place (C2-H-158). Its title and its label are the `admonition-title` and `div-label` paragraphs of C2-M-035 among its children before its first `<ol>`; the generated `id` of the title and the `aria-labelledby` of the section are not kept.

With the import option `rawHtml` on, a comment is a `raw_inline` with the format `html` in inline content and a `raw_block` with the format `html` among blocks. An element of the treatment `raw` is the same, with its outer HTML as serialized by the HTML Standard as the value. A raw block value ends with a line feed (C2-A-045, C2-A-048).

The importer reads the option `rawHtml` of C2-H-137, whose default is off. With it off, every comment, every element of the treatment `raw` and every `data-carve-raw` span (C2-H-186) is dropped with its content and attributes, and each is reported with one `import-element-dropped` entry whose `foreignType` is its tag name or `#comment` (C2-M-081). Such an import loses every comment, every script and style, every embedded object, media element, canvas, image map and form control of `elements`, every `<svg>`, `<noscript>` and `<template>` that is no abbreviation template (C2-H-187), and every `<input>` that is no task box. The tree then holds no raw node, so neither the written source nor a later render with any setting carries raw content of the input. With the option on, the raw nodes of C2-M-065 are kept and are not reported, since each holds its element whole. Whether raw HTML then reaches the output is decided where the tree is rendered: with `rawHtml` off, which is the default, a raw block renders as a code block and a raw span as its escaped text (C2-H-050, C2-H-051), and the profile `article` refuses both (C2-H-129). Raw content in the tree is data and not a grant (C2-H-189).
A reserved name of C2-H-115 is removed from an element before the element is serialized as raw content, as C2-H-186 requires.
The importer returns a tree that the 0.2 reader accepts and that the writer can spell wherever the HTML holds a fact Carve can hold. C2-M-069 to C2-M-074 state how.

A `paragraph`, `heading` or `definition_term` with no content after the rules of this document is dropped. So is an inline node that needs content and has none (C2-W-116), except a `span` with attributes, which Carve spells as `[]{...}`. A drop that loses an attribute is reported with `import-structure-repaired`; one that loses nothing is not reported.
A `list` with no item and a `definition_list` with no entry are dropped and reported with `import-structure-repaired`.
The HTML parser never puts an `<a>` inside an `<a>` (C2-M-003), so the tree holds no link inside a link.

Ids are kept as written, also when two elements carry the same id. The tree then holds a duplicate id, which the reader reports with `duplicate-id` (C2-A-039); the importer adds no report and changes no id.

A tree that holds a fact the writer has no spelling for in that place, such as blocks in a table cell, a row span the source cannot express or a `dir`, is returned as it stands. The writer reports it with `field-unspellable` or `structure-unspellable` (C2-W-117), in the same record.

An `align` attribute of the same element is then dropped, since the declaration wins in a browser, and reported with `import-attribute-dropped`.

An importer reports into the diagnostics record of C2-A-172. Every entry has a code, a severity, a position, a message and a channel (C2-A-173). The codes of the importer are in the render-loss channel, as those of the writer are (C2-W-104), and a code keeps that channel in every tool.

Expansion is part of 0.2.0. Every engine that offers the `includes` option (C2-H-137) expands include directives as this document states, and an engine that does not offer the option refuses it (C2-H-137).

Only an `include` node is expanded, and only a block line makes one (C2-B-156). There is no inline include: `{{ ... }}` inside inline content is text, each of its braces read on its own (inline chapter, braced forms), so a directive in a sentence, in a heading, in a table cell or on a lazy line of a paragraph (C2-B-024) stays text and is never passed to a resolver.

The `includes` option holds a resolver (C2-N-007) and the two limits (C2-N-064, C2-N-065). A library call that gives no resolver expands nothing: every include stays unexpanded and is reported with `include-no-resolver` (C2-N-061).

A command-line tool expands includes by default when it reads its entry document from a file and writes any target other than Carve source. It uses the resolver of C2-N-012 with the containment root set to the directory of the entry file, as a canonical path with every symbolic link resolved. The tool offers a way to turn expansion off and a way to name another root. With the entry read from standard input there is no entry file and so no default root: the tool expands nothing unless the caller names a root. A tool that expands nothing, with expansion turned off or with standard input and no root, has no resolver, and each include is reported with `include-no-resolver` (C2-N-003). With a named root, an include of standard input resolves against that root.

A processor whose output is Carve source does not expand, whether or not a resolver is given: `carve fmt`, a render to the Carve target and every other pipeline whose product is Carve source return the directive as the author wrote it. Such a processor reports no `include-no-resolver` (C2-N-003), since it expands nothing by its own rule. (I15, carried over)

Expansion runs after the top-level document is parsed and before resolution (C2-A-135), as part of the parse that the `includes` option configures. A tree in which expansion ran lists `includeExpansion` in the root `stages` (C2-A-135). Expansion runs whenever the parse has a resolver, also when the document holds no include.

A resolver is a function of the host. It receives the decoded path of the directive (C2-B-202), the section name when there is one, the decoded valid options (C2-A-181), and the id of the including file, which is absent when the directive stands in a top-level document that has no id. It returns either the text of the target and an id for it, or one error cause: `not_found`, `outside_root`, `unreadable` or `non_text`.

The resolver returns the whole target. It may read the section and the options, for example to decide access, but it does not select: the processor applies every selection, transform and mode to the text the resolver returned.

An id is a string that names one target. Two spellings of a path that reach the same target give the same id, so `a/b.crv` and `a/./b.crv` are one id. The cycle check (C2-N-066), `pos.file` (C2-N-019) and the include node's `file` (C2-N-017) all use this id.

A path is resolved relative to the including file, never relative to the root or to the working directory of a process. The one exception: with the entry read from standard input and a named root (C2-N-004), the path base of the entry document is that root, so its includes resolve against the root.

Content is text when it is well-formed UTF-8 and holds no U+0000. A resolver reports any other content as `non_text` and does not replace a byte: the replacement rule for the top-level input does not apply to an included file. A leading U+FEFF of a returned text is not content.

The resolver of a command-line tool reads files. It resolves the path against the directory of the including file, takes the canonical form of the result with every symbolic link resolved, and returns `outside_root` unless that form lies inside the canonical root. A `..` segment is allowed when the canonical result stays inside the root, and an absolute path is allowed only when it canonicalizes inside the root. A path that starts with a URI scheme, letters and `:` before any `/`, gives `outside_root`: the resolver fetches nothing remote.

The containment test comes before any test of existence. For a target that does not exist, the resolver canonicalizes the longest prefix that exists and appends the rest normalized; a result outside the root is `outside_root` whether or not the target exists, so the cause never reveals the existence of a file outside the root. Inside the root, a missing target is `not_found` and a file that cannot be read is `unreadable`. The file the resolver reads is the file it tested: no change of the file system between the test and the read, such as a symbolic link turned to a directory outside the root, makes it read a file outside the root, so a resolver that tests a path and then opens that path again does not meet this clause. A resolver meets it by testing what it opened: it opens the file, then compares the identity of the open handle, its device and file number, with that of the canonical path it tested inside the root, or it opens each segment of the path from a handle of the root without following a link out of it. A host whose platform offers neither does not give the resolver of C2-N-012 a file system that untrusted documents or other processes can change during the expansion: it serves the files from a store that does not change between the test and the read, such as a snapshot or a set of files read into memory before the expansion, or from a directory that the platform confines, such as a preopened directory of WASI.

One expansion has one root. A nested include resolves its path against its own including file (C2-N-010) and is still tested against the root of the top-level document; the root is not re-based per file. A configured root is an absolute path, and a root that is not absolute is refused: expansion then stays off, as with no resolver.

An included file is parsed as a document of its own, with the parse options of the top-level document. It has its own contents and its own depth counts: the block limit (C2-B-190) and the inline limit (C2-I-118) count within that file. A construct that is open at the end of the file, a fence, a list, a div, a quote or a comment block, ends there, as at the end of any document. Nothing of the including file is read by that parse, and nothing in the included file captures a line of the including file.

The blocks of that document, after selection (C2-N-027 to C2-N-052), become the `children` of the include node. The include node stays where the directive stood. There is no splice of source text, so a directive cannot complete or interrupt a construct of the including file. The root of the expanded tree declares each extension that the parse of an included file declared, a name once (C2-A-017, C2-X-002); that parse has the extensions of the top-level document (C2-N-015), so the declarations agree.

An include node carries `file`, the id the resolver returned, whenever the resolver returned a text for it, and `children` exactly when it was expanded. An unexpanded include has no `children`; an include of an empty file, or of a selection that holds no block, has an empty `children` list. A node that has `children` also has `file`. Both fields are resolution results (C2-A-133): tree equality skips them.

Expansion is recursive: the includes in an included file are expanded the same way, each relative to its own including file. Directives are expanded in tree order, a node before the nodes inside it, so the resolver is called and the size cap is charged (C2-N-065) in that order.

Positions are local to their own file. Every positioned node that an included file produced carries `pos.file`, the id of that file (C2-A-142), and lines, columns and offsets counted in that file. The include node itself is positioned in the file that holds the directive (C2-A-182). No position is mapped into the offsets of an including file.

A selection by lines or by region (C2-N-034 to C2-N-041) is parsed as a document of its own too, and its positions keep the coordinates of the file: the first selected line is the line it is in the file, not line 1. Frontmatter belongs to the file, so a selection opens frontmatter (C2-B-161) only when it starts at line 1 of the file; in a selection that starts later, a `---` line and the lines after it are ordinary content. Its children are the blocks of the selected lines and then, as under a section (C2-N-031), in source order, every definition of the file that the selection did not take: each link reference, footnote, abbreviation and citation definition of the file parsed whole whose first line is not selected. Its references therefore resolve against the definitions of their whole file (C2-N-054).

In Carve mode the frontmatter of an included file is that file's frontmatter: when the selection takes it, which a selection by lines or region does only from line 1 of the file (C2-N-020), it is the first child of the include node, it renders nothing (C2-H-070), and it is not the metadata of the top-level document. With `code` the frontmatter lines are content of the payload (C2-N-042).
