A directive may stand wherever a block line stands: as the only block of a list item, a description or a quote, or among other blocks. The include is then a child of that container, and its children are blocks of that container for rendering (C2-N-075). The spacing of the list is decided in the including file (C2-B-062): blank lines inside the included file do not make the list loose.

An included file is parsed with the abbreviation definitions of its own source, and for every term that those do not define, with the abbreviation definitions of the file that includes it, then of the file that includes that one, out to the top-level document. A term its own file defines takes its own expansion (C2-I-098, C2-N-055).

A directive uses at most one selection. Which options exclude each other and which need a context are the rows of `conflicts` in `data/includes.json`: two selections exclude each other, a section excludes `code`, and `rows` and `cols` need a code include whose language is `csv` or `tsv` and whose attributes carry the `table` flag. A directive that breaks a row is not expanded, and `include-selection-conflict` reports it.

An include that holds an invalid option (C2-B-206) is not expanded, and `include-option-invalid` reports it: an invalid option never silently drops out of a selection, so `{{ a.crv @lines:5-2 }}` does not read the whole file. (I7, carried over)
Without a selection the include takes the whole file. Without `code` the selected source is read as Carve.

A section `#name` is matched against the included file's own parse, before the includes of that file are expanded and before its ids meet those of any other file (C2-N-057). It is matched the way a cross-reference matches an id (C2-H-095), exactly and with case: `#intro` does not match a heading whose id is `Intro`.

The first of two steps that matches wins. First, a heading whose id is the name, authored or generated in that parse, selects its section: the heading and the blocks after it in the same block sequence, up to the next heading of the same or a lower level number or the end of that sequence. A heading inside a container is bounded by that container. Second, a block with the authored id `name` selects that block alone, with its own attributes. Within a step the first match in document order wins, a container before the blocks inside it. (I1a, carried over)

A block in the sense of C2-N-028 is a node in a block list of the file's body at any depth that is not a definition, a comment, frontmatter or an include, whose own id is no target (C2-N-072). An id carried only by something else, an inline node, a list item, a table row or cell, a term, a footnote or a block inside a footnote, selects nothing.
A section that selects nothing leaves the include unexpanded, and `include-section` reports it. The file stays a resolved dependency: the node keeps `file`.

Under a section the children are the selected blocks and then, in source order, every definition of the file that the selection did not take: link reference, footnote, abbreviation and citation definitions. The references of the selected blocks therefore resolve against the definitions of their whole file (C2-N-053). A definition renders nothing on its own, and a footnote that nothing references is not written (C2-H-092).

An included heading's id in the merged tree is decided by the merged tree (C2-N-057), so a heading selected by its generated id may carry another generated id after expansion. The section name decides only what is selected.
`shift` composes with a section (C2-N-048). Everything else that holds for a whole file holds for a section: its positions are those of the file, and its nested includes expand after selection.

`lines` selects physical lines of the file, counted from 1, both ends included. Lines are split as the block chapter splits them, a final line ending begins no further line, and a leading U+FEFF is not content, so an empty file and a file holding only U+FEFF have no lines. (I1, carried over)

A range that starts past the last line leaves the include unexpanded, and `include-lines-out-of-range` reports it; the node keeps `file`. A range that starts on or before the last line and ends past it selects through the last line.
The selected lines are parsed as a document (C2-N-020). A slice that cuts a fence, a list or a div ends that construct at the end of the slice.

`region` selects the physical lines strictly between the opening and the closing marker of the named region; the two marker lines are not selected, and marker lines of other regions between them stay selected source. An empty region selects an empty source. Markers are found by physical line before anything else reads the file, except the record parse of a table include (C2-N-046). (I1b, carried over)

An include that reads Carve recognizes only the line-comment markers of C2-B-217: `%% #region name` and `%% #endregion` with an optional name. A bare `#region` line, a `// #region` line and a braced comment are text in that mode, so a region they mark is not found.

A code include recognizes these markers, each alone on its line after optional spaces and tabs: `#region name`, `// #region name`, `-- #region name`, `/* #region name */`, `<!-- #region name -->` and `%% #region name`, and the same forms with `#endregion` and an optional name. A block comment's closer ends the same line.

In both modes the keywords are case-sensitive; a `%` run of three or more opens a comment block and is no marker; a keyword run on by an ASCII letter, digit or `_` is no marker, and run on by any other character is a malformed marker; spaces and tabs may stand between the comment opener and the keyword and between the name and a closer; and a leading U+FEFF does not hide a marker on line 1.

An opener names its region and a closer may omit the name. Distinct names may nest, a named closer matches the innermost open region, and one name opens at most once in a file. A malformed, unmatched, mismatched, unclosed or repeated marker, an opener without a name, and a name the file does not open leave the include unexpanded, and `include-region-invalid` reports it; the node keeps `file`.

With `code` the include has one child: the node that a fenced code block would give whose attribute line is the attribute line of the include, whose language is the value of `code`, and whose content is the selected source. A bare `code` gives no language; none is inferred from the file name. The payload is not read as Carve: no construct is recognized in it, and a directive in it is text that is never expanded. (I1c, carried over)

The payload holds one line per selected line, each ended by one line feed, as an authored fence's content is: a CRLF becomes a line feed, a lone CR stays as content of its line (C2-B-010), a last line without a line ending gains one, a selected blank last line keeps its line feed, and an empty selection gives the value `""`. A leading U+FEFF of the file is not payload; a U+FEFF that opens a later line is.

The child's `pos` is in the included file. It starts at column 1 of the first selected line, after a leading U+FEFF on line 1, and ends directly after the last character of the last selected line, without its line ending. An empty selection has a zero-width span at the start of the file, after a leading U+FEFF, or at column 1 of the closing marker line of an empty region. A table made from the payload (C2-N-045) has the same span, and its cells keep their positions in the file.

With the `table` flag in the include's attributes and the language `csv` or `tsv`, the child is the delimited table such a fence gives (C2-B-180), with bad quoting reported as on an authored fence (C2-B-181). `rows` selects records and `cols` projects columns (C2-N-046, C2-N-047).

`rows` counts the parsed records of the whole file from 1, header records included, after the leading U+FEFF is removed. A quoted field that holds line breaks is one record. A whole physical line that is a well-formed marker of C2-N-039 is no record under any selection or none: it is no row, no cell, and does not count toward `rows` or `header-rows`. A marker is recognized only outside a quoted field, here and for `region`: inside a quoted field the line is data of that field. The first `header-rows` records of the file, one by default, form the head, and the last `footer-rows` records of the file, none by default, form the foot. Both are written under any selection, and a selection chooses only body records, so a head or foot record inside the range is not repeated. A `lines` selection chooses, whole, the records of the whole file whose first line lies in the range, also one that ends past the range, so a quoted field is never cut. The two counts are taken on the records of the whole file as C2-B-221 takes them on the rows of a table: the head takes its records first, and a `footer-rows` count larger than the records below the head takes them all. A `rows` range that starts past the last record leaves the include unexpanded with `include-rows-out-of-range`, and an end past the last record is clipped. (I1d, carried over)

`cols` with a list of names takes the columns whose head names match exactly, in the order given, so it may reorder them. The names are matched against the head of the whole file (C2-N-046) under any selection: a `lines` or `region` selection chooses records and never makes a new head. A requested name that the first head record lacks or holds twice leaves the include unexpanded with `include-cols-invalid`, and a name requested twice with `include-cols-duplicate`; an empty or a repeated head name that no request names is not tested. `cols` with a range selects columns by number and is valid only with `header-rows=0`; on another table, or past the last column, it gives `include-cols-invalid`. `cols` combines with any one selection or none. (I1d, carried over)

`shift` with a number N adds N to the level of every heading among the children of the include, at every depth, headings of nested includes included. A level that would fall below 1 or rise above 6 is set to 1 or 6, the heading is kept, and `include-heading-clamp` reports it. A shift changes no text and no id: an authored id stays, and a generated id is computed from the unchanged text (C2-N-057), so a cross-reference into a shifted heading still resolves. Section numbering counts the new levels. (I8, carried over)

`shift:auto` computes N as (C + 1) - T. C is the level of the nearest heading before the include in document order that stands in the include's own block container or in a container around it, where an expanded include counts as no container; a heading inside a sibling container that closed before the include does not count, and with no such heading C is 0. T is the lowest heading level among the children after selection and after the includes inside them are expanded. With no heading among the children, `auto` changes nothing and reports nothing. (I8, carried over)

Shifts are applied once the tree is expanded, include by include in tree order, an include before the includes inside it. Each include reads the levels as the shifts before it left them, so a nested `auto` places its headings relative to the assembled document and is not shifted twice.
`shift` on a code include has no effect and reports nothing, since its child holds no heading.
The children of an include hold no node of the including file, and an include's selection, transform and mode act only on its own children.

The file of a node is the file whose parse produced it: the top-level document, or the included file of the nearest expanded include around the node. The including file of an include is the file of the include node.

A link reference is looked up in the link definitions of its own file first, which for a selection are those of the whole file (C2-N-020, C2-N-031), then in those of the including file, then in those of each file further out, up to the top-level document, and only then in the headings of the whole tree (C2-A-109, C2-H-083). The first file that defines the key decides. A definition never reaches inward: a reference in an including file does not see a definition of the file it includes.

A footnote reference and an abbreviation look up their definition the same way: their own file first, then outward to the top-level document. Two files may each define a footnote with one key; they are two notes, and each reference reaches the note of the nearest file that defines the key. (Changed from 0.1, which renamed the second label: I5.)
Footnotes are numbered once, over the expanded tree, by the order of their first reference (C2-H-087), and the footnote section collects the notes of every file.

Ids run over the expanded tree by the existing rules: the authored ids of every file are reserved in document order, then generated heading ids follow in document order with the suffixes of C2-H-024. Nothing is renamed: an authored id keeps its spelling in every file, and no rename is reported. A generated id that the merged tree suffixes is a generated id like any other (C2-A-134).

An authored id that stands in two files is a duplicate id like one that stands twice in one file: `duplicate-id` reports the later occurrence (C2-A-039), both elements are written with it, and a cross-reference `</#id>`, a link to `#id` and a link reference that resolves to a heading reach the first occurrence in document order, also when they stand in the file that holds the later one.
Caption numbers and equation numbers are counted once, over the expanded tree, in the order of C2-H-170.
Within one file a second definition of a key is a duplicate (C2-B-085). A key that two files each define once is no duplicate and reports nothing.

Every failure leaves the include unexpanded and reports one code, the code of its cause, at the include node in the parse channel with severity warning. The causes, their codes and the order in which they are tested are the rows of `causes` in `data/includes.json`; the first cause that applies is reported and no later one is tested. No failure removes the directive, and no failure is silent: past the cap `include_diagnostics` of `data/limits.json`, 100 entries, a failure is counted and not listed (C2-T-024).

The causes that are tested before the resolver is called, `no_resolver`, `option_invalid`, `conflict`, `depth` and `size_spent`, never call it, and the node has no `file`. A cause the resolver returns leaves the node without `file`. A cause tested after the resolver returned a text, `cycle`, `size_exceeded` and every selection cause, leaves `file` on the node: the file was read.
A failure in an included file is reported at the include node in that file. The range of a finding is counted in the file of the node its path names (C2-A-173, C2-N-053).

The top-level document stands at depth 0, and a file included from a file at depth D stands at depth D + 1. A directive whose file would stand deeper than the limit `include_depth` of `data/limits.json`, 16, is not resolved and reports `include-depth`. A host may lower the limit and may not raise it.

The size cap `include_bytes` of `data/limits.json`, 8388608, bounds the sum of the UTF-8 byte lengths of every text the resolver returns in one expansion, the same file counted each time it is read. A text that would carry the sum past the cap is refused with `include-budget` (`size_exceeded`) and does not count toward the sum, and once the sum has reached the cap every later include is refused with `include-budget` before its resolver is called (`size_spent`). A host may lower the cap and may not raise it.

A cycle is an include whose returned id is the id of the top-level document or the `file` of an include around it. It is refused with `include-cycle`, so a file that includes itself, directly or through other files, is read once on that chain.

The two limits also bound the work: each directive is at least seven bytes of source, so the number of resolver calls is at most the length of the top-level input and of the returned texts divided by seven. There is no separate bound on resolver calls.
A message names the path as the directive wrote it and the cause. It never repeats an error text or a path that the resolver produced, so an absolute path of the host does not reach the output.

Included content gets the same treatment as the including document: one `urlPolicy`, one `rawHtml` setting, one `profile` and every sanitizing rule of the HTML document apply to the whole expanded tree. No option is relaxed or tightened for content because it was included.
An unexpanded include renders as C2-H-133 states, the directive as text in a paragraph, and the render reports `include-unresolved` in the render-loss channel, whatever the cause.

The attribute line above a directive attaches to the include node (C2-B-095), and the writer writes it back (C2-N-080). With `code` it acts through the child, which carries the same attributes (C2-N-042), and the `table` flag selects the delimited table (C2-N-045).

A caption line directly below a code include attaches to the include (C2-B-147). When the include is expanded, its child carries the same caption, and the child is captioned as an authored code block or table is (C2-H-062). The copy in the child has no `pos`: its characters are in the including file, and a node under the children of an include is positioned in the included file (C2-A-142). The caption of the include keeps its position. A caption below an include without `code` is text, and `unattached-caption` reports it (C2-B-149).

An expanded include renders its children and nothing else: no element, no attribute and no `data-source-line` of its own. Every HTML rule that reads the blocks of a container or of the document reads the children of an expanded include in its place, recursively: section wrapping (C2-H-026), the one-line forms of an item and a quote (C2-H-006, C2-H-007), the bare first paragraph of a description (C2-H-040) and the placement of the footnote section (C2-H-158).
With `sourceLines` on, an element rendered from an included node carries the line it starts on in its own file (C2-H-016, C2-N-019). The line is not mapped into the including file.

A profile tests an include like any block (C2-H-163). `full` and `article` accept it. Under `comment` and `minimal`, whose allow lists do not name `include`, the include is outside the profile, expanded or not, and is written in its degraded form, the source text of its directive (C2-H-165); its children are not written, and `profile-construct-degraded` reports it once.
An unexpanded include is a render loss (C2-N-070), so with `strictLosses` on a render of a tree that holds one returns no output (C2-H-130). An expanded include is no loss.

With `roundtrip` on, an expanded include still writes only its children, so an import of that HTML gives the included blocks in place of the directive. The render reports this as the render loss `include-expanded-roundtrip`, once for each expanded include that no expanded include holds. The abbreviation template of C2-H-178 covers the children of the document only; the definitions of an included file get no template.

A Carve writer writes an include as its directive (C2-W-058), with its attribute line above it and its caption below it. It never writes the children and never writes `file`, and it reports no loss for either: both are resolution results (C2-N-017). (I12, carried over)
Because tree equality skips `children` and `file`, `parse(fmt(x)) == parse(x)` holds for a document with includes whether or not either side was expanded (C2-W-002).

The source-layout record covers the nodes of the top-level document. The nodes in the children of an include have no entries, and the include node has its own entry like any block, `optionSpelling` included (C2-L-055).

The dependencies of a document are the include nodes of its tree, in tree order. Each names its path as written, its including file (C2-N-053), and whether it was read: a node with `file` was read, a node without `file` was not. With no resolver, every directive is a dependency that was not read.

A host that watches files for changes watches the distinct `file` values of the tree, and for each node without `file` the place its path would name relative to its including file. A host that wants a set rather than a list removes repeats by id.

A linter expands includes when its caller gives a resolver or a root, by the rules of this document and with the same limits. Without one it reads no include target, and each include reports `include-no-resolver` as in any parse. (I16, carried over)

The top-level document is linted as it is. Every Carve include that the expansion accepted is linted with every rule and with the options of the top-level document, over the source the expansion parsed: the whole file, the line range or the region. For a section the whole file is linted, and only the findings from the first line of the selected heading or block through the last line of the last selected block are kept. A rule that reads the payload of a block also runs on a code include's child.

A finding in included content names its file by id, with a line and a column counted in that file, and its tree path, which leads through the includes that reached it. A finding is reported once for each distinct file, line, column and rule; where one position is reached more than once, the first reach in document order supplies the path. `shift` does not make a range distinct. Lint control comments count the lines of their own file (C2-B-216).
On a delimited table include, `lines` is valid and counts physical lines, and lint adds the hint `include-lines-table-rows-hint`, which suggests `rows`.
Parsing, AST JSON, CLI JSON and rendering are the same with and without a sidecar. An AST reader does not accept a sidecar as a tree.
A sidecar belongs to the one tree it was returned with. Its paths do not hold after that tree is edited.
A sidecar does not survive a write: the written source is a new input with a layout of its own.
The tree wins. A writer ignores a sidecar fact that contradicts the tree, such as a `sourceFormat` on a table that a delimited table cannot hold.
The sidecar is an object with six required fields and no others:
A reader refuses a sidecar version it does not implement.

A reader also refuses a record that breaks C2-L-011, C2-L-012, C2-L-020, C2-L-027 or C2-L-056, judging a fact only on an entry whose node type defines it. The first-fragment wrap of C2-L-048 meets C2-L-020. A writer ignores an entry whose path names no node of the tree, and a fact that is not defined for the type of the node its entry names (C2-L-006).
A node entry has `path`, `startByte` and `endByte`, and may have any of the facts below. It has no other fields.
`path` is an RFC 6901 JSON Pointer into the tree. The empty string is the root, and `/children/2/children/0` is the first child of the third block. This is how every sidecar fact refers to its node.

Entries stand in document order, a node before the nodes inside it, which compares each index of a `path` as a number: `/children/2` stands before `/children/10`. The slots of one node are visited in the order `title`, `children`, `caption`, and its other slots after them in the order of `data/node-slots.json`, the named slots of an extension node in the order of its declaration (C2-X-020). The nodes in a `fallback` have no entry. No two entries have the same path.

`startByte` and `endByte` are a range in bytes of the original input, start inclusive and end exclusive: its UTF-8 bytes, or under `"base64"` the bytes as given (C2-L-056). For a node that has `pos` they equal `pos.startOffset` and `pos.endOffset` (C2-A-141): a byte-order mark and every CR are counted as they stand. A range never exceeds the byte length of the input. An offset into a node value, as in `wraps` (C2-L-020), counts the UTF-8 bytes of that value.

`encoding` is `"base64"` exactly when the input was given as bytes that are not well-formed UTF-8 (C2-B-218), and `"utf-8"` for every other input. Under `"base64"`, `source` holds those bytes in the base64 alphabet of RFC 4648, section 4, with padding, and the ranges count them as they stand, so they still equal `pos`. A string input with an unpaired surrogate is no byte input: it keeps `"utf-8"`, and its `source` holds U+FFFD in place of the surrogate, whose three bytes are the ones C2-B-218 counts. For the bytes `61 FF 62` the sidecar has `"encoding": "base64"` and `"source": "Yf9i"`, and the entry of the paragraph spans bytes 0 to 3.

A producer does not invent a range. A node whose source is not one contiguous range, such as a cell joined from continuation rows, has an entry whose range runs from the start of its first piece to the end of its last. Such a node has no `pos` (C2-A-156), so this range is not a position.

Source and ranges are the minimum. A fact other than the required facts of C2-L-047, C2-L-052, C2-L-054 and C2-L-059 is optional. An absent optional fact means unknown: a producer omits what it did not measure, and a consumer does not read an absent fact as a value.
A writer that finds no fact uses the default of the section "Defaults". That is a rule about writing, not a reading of the document: the default is never reported as what the author wrote.

`bare` says whether an ordered list was numbered with the bare dot or with written numbers. A list that mixes both (C2-B-043) records the form of its first marker, and the formatter writes the whole list in that form. The tree holds only the start value (C2-A-056).
`fenced` says which of the two quote forms the author wrote. Both give the same `block_quote`.
`hardBreakOpener` says which of the two forms of a hard-break block the author wrote. Both give the same `div` (C2-A-068).
`continuationLines` on a row entry is the number of continuation rows below that row, the ones with only empty fragments included.

`wraps` on a cell entry is a list of objects, sorted by `line`. Each has `line`, the number of the continuation row counted from 1; `path`, the pointer of the text node among the children of the cell's paragraph that holds the space joining that row's fragment (C2-B-184); and `offset`, the UTF-8 byte offset behind that space in the node's value, where the fragment starts. A wrap falls between two fragments, so it never lies inside another node (C2-L-048). The one exception is the wrap of the row where the first fragment that is not empty stands, for a cell whose fragments before it are empty: no space joins that fragment, and its wrap has `path`, the pointer of the first inline node of the cell's paragraph, of any type, and `offset` 0 (C2-L-048). A continuation row whose fragment of the cell is empty adds nothing and has no wrap for that cell (C2-B-184). A wrap in a cell that spans rows also has `row`, the number of rows below the cell's own row.
`rawRef` is the only place that holds a reference label as typed. The tree holds the folded `key` and the `refForm` (C2-A-105).

`sourceFormat` says how a table was written. The tree is the same for a pipe table and a delimited table with the same cells in the same groups (C2-A-088): blocks Examples 267 and 268 give equal trees.

`headerRows` on the entry of a delimited table is the effective count of a valid `header-rows` attribute the source gave (C2-B-209, C2-B-221), 0 included. A table without the attribute, and a pipe table, on which the attribute has no effect (C2-B-186), have no such fact. The groups of the tree hold the partition; the fact records only that the count was written. A `headerRows` that differs from the number of head rows of the tree contradicts the tree, and the writer ignores it (C2-L-006).
`markerRaw` is the exact source text of the marker that opened the node. For a heading it tells `#` from `=`, and for a fence `openerRaw` gives the length of the run.

`continuationStyle` has one value, chosen in this order: `lazy` when a paragraph line stands left of the content column, else `indent` when a later line reaches the content column, else `marker_line` when all content is on the marker line, else `none`.
`blankLinesBefore` and `blankLinesAfter` are the authored counts, not a normalized 0 or 1.
`openerRaw` and `closerRaw` come as a pair. An unclosed block has `closerRaw` present and empty. `openerRaw` is never empty.

`continuationStyle` has no value for a list continuation marker and `attachment` has none for a block attached by one, since 0.2 has no such marker. No fact records a leading or a trailing pipe, since a row always starts and ends with a pipe (C2-B-166).
A fact that the schema declares and this document does not define is a defect.

An include entry may carry `optionSpelling`, a closed object keyed by the option names of `data/include-options.json`; each value is the exact quoted or bare source spelling of that option value. The tree keeps the decoded typed value (C2-A-181), and the formatter uses this fact only when it decodes to the same value.

A decimal ordered list whose delimiter is the period is written with the bare dot on every item, the first included. A list that does not start at 1 carries its start value in a `start` attribute on the attribute line above it (C2-B-045): a number on the first marker would be read back as the numbered form. The writer clause names the exceptions (C2-W-044).

Every other ordered list is written with its numbers, letters or numerals in sequence from the start value: a list whose `marker.style` is not `1`, and a list with the `)` delimiter, since a bare `)` is not a marker (C2-B-036). A first marker that could read as another style is written as C2-W-045 says.
A bullet list is written with the character in `marker.char`. A writer writes `-` only where the tree says `-`, and does not change the character to separate two lists.
A quote is written with `>` lines.

A div with the class `hardbreaks` is written with the hard-break opener when every line break inside it is a `hard_break` and `hardbreaks` is the last of its classes, and in the class form otherwise. The opener adds the class last (C2-A-068), so the opener form on any other div would change the order of its classes.
A table row is written on one line, with no continuation rows.
A table is written as a pipe table. A table with no rows is written as a delimited table, because a pipe table needs a row.

A code block is written with the shortest run of at least three backticks that is longer than every bare backtick run on a line of its `value`, at any indent (C2-W-038). A fenced container is written with a colon run of the smallest length of at least three that is longer than the runs of the divs inside it (C2-W-039).
A heading is written with `=`.
A thematic break is written as `***`.

A reference is written from the tree: its text, then `[key]` for the form `full` or `[]` for the form `collapsed`. The form `shortcut` writes only its text in brackets, with no label tail. C2-W-075 spells a key that starts with a caret or an at-sign.

The remaining layout is the canonical layout of the Writer document: one blank line between blocks where the tree's `spacing` does not say otherwise, content indented to the content column, a bare `---` for YAML frontmatter, double quotes for a title.
Where 0.2 has two equal forms, the formatter keeps the form the sidecar records: ordered numbering, the quote form, the hard-break form, the table form, a declared head count and continuation rows.
`markerColumn` on the entry of a `comment` that came from a comment-only line inside a quote is the column of the quote mark on that line. No writer rule reads it.

The writer reads nine facts: `bare`, `fenced`, `hardBreakOpener`, `wraps`, `continuationLines`, `sourceFormat`, `headerRows`, `rawRef` and `optionSpelling` (C2-W-083, C2-W-084). The measured facts of the section "Measured facts carried over" have no reader in the 0.2 documents. They are for editors and other tools that need the layout as typed.

Every node in a list of blocks of the top-level document (C2-A-051), outside a caption and a table cell, and every `list_item`, `definition_term`, `definition_description` and `caption` has an entry with `blankLinesBefore` and `blankLinesAfter`, 0 included, since an absent fact means unknown. Table groups, rows and cells, the blocks inside a cell, the lines of a line block and the blocks inside a caption have no such facts, and the blocks of a `fallback` have no entry (C2-L-011). The blocks in the children of an expanded include have no entries (C2-N-082). An inline node has an entry only when it has a fact. The examples of this document show only the entries and facts under discussion.

The `wraps` of a cell are sorted by `line`, and those of one line by `row`; a cell that spans rows has `row` on every wrap, 0 for its own row. A cell whose content starts in a continuation row has no joining space: its wrap for that row names its first inline node with `offset` 0.

`rawRef` starts at the opening bracket, without the `!` of an image, and ends at the bracket that closes the reference, without an attribute block. In the full and collapsed forms this is the label's closing bracket; in the shortcut form it is the text pair's closing bracket. It is read without the prefixes of the lines it crosses, and the pieces are joined by a line feed.

`markerRaw` of a definition is its label with the colon, as `[^n]:`, `[r]:` and `*[A]:`, and its `metadataSeparatorRaw` is the colon with the spaces behind it, so the colon is in both. For a `definition_term`, `markerRaw` is `::` and the separator is the run of spaces between the mark and the term text.

A task box and the attribute blocks glued to a marker are not content of the item: `contentColumn` of `- [x] a` is the column of `a`. This is a fact of the layout record only: the marker tests of the block chapter read the text behind the marker before the box is taken out (C2-B-229).

`continuationStyle` stands on every `list_item`, `definition_description` and `footnote`, with `marker_line` when the node has no later line. `lazy` is a later line of a paragraph inside the node, at any depth, that stands left of the content column; `indent` is a later line at or right of it. A parse never gives `none`, which occurs only in a supplied record, as for `attachment` (C2-L-054).

A line is blank inside a quote when it carries exactly the marks of the open quotes and nothing else. Blank lines behind the last content of a quote that still carry its mark are counted as `blankLinesAfter` of the last block of the quote; a blank line without the mark is outside the quote and counts for the blocks around the quote.

A `figure_group` and a delimited table have no `openerRaw` and no `closerRaw`. A parse gives every `caption` the `attachment` `preceding`; `none` occurs only in a supplied record. A comment whose line lacks the mark of its quote has no `markerColumn`. `lineEndings` reports what the source holds, a lone CR included, although a lone CR ends no line (C2-B-010).

A comparison of a parse with layout against stated facts, as a test makes, holds these facts required: `source`, `lineEndings`, `bom` and the ranges of each entry; `blankLinesBefore` and `blankLinesAfter` where C2-L-047 gives them; `continuationStyle` where C2-L-052 gives it; and the `attachment` of a `caption` (C2-L-054). A required fact the producer omits fails the comparison. Every other fact is optional (C2-L-014): a stated optional fact is compared where the producer records it, and its absence passes.

The role of a line depends only on that line, the stack of open blocks and five facts the scanner keeps about the lines directly above. The stack of open blocks is the open containers and, innermost, the open leaf with what its opener set: the kind of the leaf, the first line and the line count of a text leaf (C2-B-017, C2-B-157), the marker column of a heading (C2-B-154), the closer and the opener column of a fence (C2-B-109, C2-B-110), and the rows and head of a table (C2-B-178, C2-B-187). The five facts are: whether the line is line 1 of the document (C2-B-161), the pending attribute lines (C2-B-090), the number of blank lines directly above (C2-B-052), the block that closed directly above, for a caption (C2-B-146), and the blank lines held back at the end of an opaque body (C2-B-113). A pending attribute line waits for the next line (C2-B-092); no other block fact waits for a later line.
Columns count code points from 0, starting after the quote marks of the open quotes: column 0 of quoted content is the column directly behind the innermost quote mark and its one space.
A leading tab advances the column to the next multiple of 4, for counting only: the bytes are kept as written, also in code.
Tab stops count from the start of the line, not from a container's content column.
Indent stripping removes whole characters, so a tab that straddles the strip column is kept.
Prefixes are read outside-in, in the order the containers were opened: for a quote inside a list item the quote mark sits past the item's marker.

A blank line belongs to no container: the next line that is not blank decides which containers stay open, so an indented line belongs to its item after any number of blank lines. A quote is the exception: a blank line without its mark ends it at once (C2-B-032).

A U+0000 in the source is read as U+FFFD, in text, in code and in every other value, so a tree from a parse never holds U+0000 (C2-A-044). Offsets count the bytes of the source as it stands. An unpaired surrogate in the string a host passes is read as U+FFFD in the same way and counts three bytes. A source given as bytes is decoded as UTF-8 by the WHATWG decoder: each maximal subpart of an ill-formed sequence is read as one U+FFFD, and offsets still count the source bytes, so the U+FFFD spans the bytes it replaces, and a layout sidecar keeps such a source as bytes (C2-L-056). The bytes `61 FF 62` give the paragraph `a`, U+FFFD, `b`, whose characters span offsets 0 to 1, 1 to 2 and 2 to 3; the bytes `61 E2 82 62` give `a`, one U+FFFD over offsets 1 to 3, and `b`. A source is never refused for its encoding.
A line ends at LF, a CR directly before that LF is not part of the line, and a lone CR is not a line end.
A line that opens no other block opens a paragraph.
An open paragraph takes every line that is not blank, whatever its indent or prefix, and such a line is a *lazy line*.
A paragraph closes at a blank line, at an interrupter or with its container.
Interrupter (a): a fence line, which is a run of three or more backticks, colons or percent signs that opens or closes a fence, a div or a comment block (C2-B-108).

Interrupter (b): a list marker with content at an open list's column continues that list when its marker matches under C2-B-049. A marker left of every open list continues the outermost open list when its marker matches under C2-B-049 and the container that holds that list owns the line (C2-B-025); otherwise it closes the open lists and opens a new one, whatever its value, in the innermost container that owns the line (C2-B-228). A marker indented past an item's, description's or footnote body's marker, and not between the columns of two open lists (C2-B-055), opens a nested list without a blank line only when it is a bullet, a bare dot or an ordered marker of value 1. Below `- We moved in`, ` 2024. It was good` is a lazy line. A nested list starting at another number stands after a blank line, directly on the marker line, or between the columns of two open lists (C2-B-055).
Interrupter (c): a description mark or a term mark with content at an open description list's column, or a definition line at column 0 while a definition is open.

Interrupter (d): a caption line (C2-B-146), only when the paragraph so far is exactly one block image line (C2-B-197) or one display math line (C2-B-198). A caret line that the container of the paragraph does not own is no caption line and is a lazy line, in an item as in a quote (C2-B-018): below `- ![](a.png)`, a line `^ cap` at column 0 is text of the item's paragraph.
Interrupter (e): a table row (C2-B-166).

Interrupter (f): a thematic break (C2-B-159). A line of three or more stars and nothing else has no reading as prose. Like a fence line it interrupts wherever it stands: at an open list's column it closes the list, and indented past a marker it stays in that item.
Interrupters (b) and (c) count only on a line that carries the quote mark of every quote the list or the definition sits in, and a quote inside the item does not count.

A list marker line without the quote mark, while the paragraph sits in a quote inside an item, closes that quote: at the list's column it is a sibling item, and indented past the item's marker it opens a nested list in the item.

Every line that is not one of the six interrupters and not a region marker line (C2-B-137) is a lazy line of an open paragraph. These lines are no interrupters and so are lazy lines: a heading, a quote, an attribute line, a definition, an include directive, a `%%` comment other than a region marker (C2-B-137), and a list marker that interrupter (b) does not take (C2-B-015). An open stanza of a line block takes lazy lines as an open paragraph does, as in 0.1, except a heading, a quote, an attribute line and a definition, which end the stanza: `- ::: |`, ` a`, `b` is one stanza of two lines in the item. A lazy include directive or list marker is a line of text of the stanza (C2-B-123). A lazy `%%` line, one that the container of the line block does not own, is a comment-only line (C2-B-137) and no line of the stanza: its comment is an inline child at the end of the `line` above it, and the stanza goes on below it. A `%%` line that the container owns is a line of the body and is text (C2-B-135).

With no paragraph open, a line belongs to the innermost open item, description or footnote body whose marker it is indented past, measured from that item's own marker column, also when the item joined its list at another column (C2-B-054, C2-B-055), and to a quote when it carries the quote mark.
A container that does not own the line closes, with every container inside it.
The content of an item, a description or a footnote body is stripped by at most its content column.
The first line of a nested block sets that block's base column.
The content of a fence is stripped by at most the indent of its opener. Where the opener stands left of the content column of its item, the body is stripped by at most the opener's column.

A marker left of the list's column, directly after item text, is a sibling item (C2-B-015, C2-B-054), so markers that are right-aligned, as ` 9.` above `10.`, form one list. The list's column is then the column of that sibling's marker: after ` - a` and `- b`, the line ` 2. c` stands past the column of the list and is a lazy line of `b`. `ordered-marker-right-aligned` reports an ordered marker of such a sibling that ends where the list's markers end, `uneven-list-indent` reports the other uneven columns (C2-B-054), and the formatter writes all markers at one column.

An interrupter closes the open paragraph, and the line is then read as a line with no paragraph open: C2-B-025 decides which containers own it, and an item, a description or a footnote body whose marker it is not indented past closes with every block inside it (C2-B-026). The lists inside a closed body are closed with it, so a list marker continues only a list whose container owns the line (C2-B-015, C2-B-054). This holds for every interrupter and every container whose body is its marker line and the lines indented past its marker. A line that is no interrupter stays a lazy line of the paragraph at any column (C2-B-012).
The quote mark is `>` followed by a space or by the end of the line, so `>a` is text.
A quote owns a line only when the line carries its mark or is a lazy line, so a blank line without the mark ends the quote, and two quotes separated by a blank line are two quotes.
Every marker needs one space and at least one further character on its line, so a bare marker and a marker without its space are text.
A bullet marker is `-` or `*`.
The bullet character is part of the list's kind, so an item with the other character starts another list (C2-B-049).

An ordered marker is a number of one to nine digits, one ASCII letter, or a roman numeral of two to nine letters, followed by `.` or `)`, or the bare dot `.`, so a bare `)` is never a marker, and a run of ten or more digits or letters is text. A roman numeral is written in one letter case and in its standard form, from 1 to 3999: thousands as up to three `m`, then each lower place as `cm`, `cd` or an optional `d` and up to three `c`, and likewise with `x`, `l`, `c` and with `i`, `v`, `x`. Two or more letters that do not form such a numeral, as in `civil.` or `iiii.`, are text. The 0.1 engine took any run of these letters.
The kind of an ordered list is its numbering style and its delimiter.
In a roman list a single roman letter is a sibling.
In an alphabetic list every single letter is a sibling, `i` included.
The list starts at the value of its first marker.

The first marker fixes the style without reading a later line: digits and the bare dot are decimal, two or more roman letters are roman, a single `i` or `I` is roman, and every other single letter is alphabetic. Later markers are tested in the open list's style (C2-B-038, C2-B-039); a marker that does not match it starts another list (C2-B-049).

The bare dot numbers automatically: it takes the next number, so digits with a dot and the bare dot are siblings in one list. A bare dot is no marker when the text behind its required space starts with another dot and a space, so `. . . and then silence` is a paragraph. A task box behind the space is read only after this test (C2-B-229).

A later marker that does not match the open list's style splits an ordered list: `i.` then `j.` gives a roman list of one item and an alphabetic list, and `v.` then `vi.` gives an alphabetic list of one item and a roman list, also with a lazy line of the first item between them (C2-B-024). `ordered-list-kind-split` reports a split after a one-letter first marker that is one of the seven roman letters `i`, `v`, `x`, `l`, `c`, `d` and `m` in either case, when the next list has the other letter style in the same case and begins with fewer than three blank lines between them. Three or more blank lines end the list on purpose (C2-B-052) and are not reported.
A `start` value of more than nine digits is no start value, as a marker of more than nine digits is no marker (C2-B-036): the list keeps the start of its first marker and `start` stays a key.

The `start` attribute on the attribute line of an ordered list sets the number of its first item. It is read into the start value of the list and is not kept as a key, so a list written with the attribute and a list whose first marker carries the number give the same tree. Where both are written, the attribute decides. The value is an unsigned decimal integer; on a list of letters or roman numerals it is at least 1. Any other value is no start value and stays an ordinary key.

A task box is `[`, one of the nine characters space, `x`, `X`, `_`, `/`, `!`, `-`, `>` and `?`, and `]`, directly after the required space of a bullet or ordered marker and followed by one space and at least one further character.
The box character `X` is read as `x`.

A marker line is read in three steps. First the marker is tested on the text behind its required space, a task box included, as the bare dot is (C2-B-043). Then a task box is read directly after that space (C2-B-046). Then the content starts behind the box and its space. In `. [x] . x` the text behind the first dot is `[x] . x`, which does not start with a dot, so the dot is a marker, the item has a box, and its content `. x` is a nested ordered list (C2-B-058).

A list marker at an open list's column is a sibling when it matches the list in bullet character, or in ordered style and delimiter. A task box is a fact of its item and not of the list: items with and without a box are siblings in one list. In 0.1 a boxed item and a plain item never shared a list.
A list marker at an open list's column that does not match closes that list and opens a new one.
One or two blank lines do not end a bullet list, an ordered list or a description list.
Three or more blank lines before a marker at the list's column end the list, and that marker starts a new one.

Two lists of the same kind in one container, with nothing between them but fewer than three blank lines and comment-only lines (C2-B-137), are one list. Any other block between them keeps them apart, a `%%%` block at column 0 among them, which sits at top level (C2-B-014, C2-B-228).

Adjacency holds at any column for bullet and ordered lists: with no paragraph open, a marker left of every open list continues the list above it when it matches the outermost open list in kind (C2-B-049) and the container that holds that list owns the line (C2-B-025), and `uneven-list-indent` reports it, except the right-aligned ordered marker that C2-B-030 leaves to `ordered-marker-right-aligned`. A description list has no kind and no adjacency across columns: a term mark or a description mark at another column than the open description list starts a new list.
An item may start with any block: the block opener stands directly after the marker, on the marker line.
A marker line that holds another marker with content has a nested list as the item's first block.
A line that starts with `+` is text unless it is a table continuation row (C2-B-175).
An ordered nested list may start at any number.
A marker line whose second marker has no content holds that marker as text: `- -` is an item with the text `-`.
A list is loose only when a blank line stands between two of its items, so a list with one item is tight.
A blank line counts for the list whose sibling follows it.
There is no `{loose}` attribute: the key `loose` on a list has no effect on tightness, and `deprecated-loose-attribute` reports it.
A term line (`::`) and a description line (`:`) at the list's column form a description list.
An entry with terms only is valid.
A term is one inline leaf: its text starts at the content column of its mark, so spaces and tabs behind the mark's one space are not part of it, and continues like paragraph text.
A fence line or a table row directly below term text is an interrupter, and because a term owns no lines, it closes the description list, whatever its indent.
A term owns no lines: after a blank line, a line that is not a description line or a term line at the list's column closes the list, whatever its indent.
A description may start with any block on its marker line.
A description with one visible block has a bare paragraph. A comment and a definition are not visible blocks (C2-H-040).
A description line with no term above it is text.
A term takes no block opener: a quote mark or a list marker after the term mark is term text.
The further blocks of a description are indented past its mark.

In a description with several blocks every paragraph gets `

`.

Below description text a fence line or a table row is an interrupter as in any paragraph: at the list's column it closes the list (C2-B-026), and indented past the description mark it stays in the description.
A nested description list starts on a description's marker line, or after a blank line, indented past the mark.
One or two blank lines between a term and its description, between two descriptions or between two entries do not end the list (C2-B-051) and do not change what it renders.
A definition stands at column 0 outside every container, so a definition-shaped line inside a container is text, and `definition-in-container` reports it.

A footnote definition is `[^label]:`, a space and content on the same line. The label follows the rules of a footnote reference label (C2-I-087): it may hold spaces, and it holds no unescaped bracket.

A link definition is one line: `[label]:`, one or more spaces, a destination and an optional title, so a label and a colon followed by nothing or only spaces is text. The destination and the title are those of an inline link tail (C2-I-067, C2-I-068), except that the destination holds at least one character: a run without whitespace, then optionally exactly one space and a title in double or in single quotes, then optionally exactly one space and one valid attribute block (C2-I-028), then only spaces and tabs. So `[a]: /u 'T'` has a title, `[a]: /u {.c}` carries the class `c` (C2-B-106), in `[a]: /u"T"` and in `[a]: "T"` the quotes are part of the destination, and `[a]: /u "T"` with two spaces is text. The label does not start with `^`: that shape is tested first and is a footnote definition (C2-B-082).

An abbreviation definition is one line: `*[label]:` with a label of one or more ASCII letters and digits, a space, and a plain-text expansion that is not empty. Exactly one space separates the colon from the expansion: every character after it belongs to the expansion, a leading space or tab included, except the spaces and tabs at the end of the line.

For a duplicate label the first definition wins, and `duplicate-footnote-definition`, `duplicate-link-reference-definition` or `duplicate-abbreviation-definition` reports the later one. The range of a `duplicate-footnote-definition` finding is the definition marker `[^label]:` of the later definition, without its content or lazy lines (C2-W-138).

The body of a footnote definition is the content on its marker line and the blocks indented past its marker. The marker line may start with any block, as the marker line of an item does (C2-B-057): `[^n]: > q` holds a quote.
References resolve after block parsing, so a reference may stand before its definition.

Anything but spaces and tabs after the URL, the title or the attribute block of a link definition makes the line text, and so does a brace block that is no valid attribute block. A brace block glued to the URL is part of it: `[a]: /u{.c}` has the destination `/u{.c}`.

An attribute line is one or more glued brace blocks `{...}`, alone on its line, each a valid attribute block (C2-I-028 to C2-I-034). A line of braces that is no valid block, such as a braced inline form alone on its line, is text.
An attribute line applies to the block that starts on the next line and is owned by the same container, with no column test.
An attribute line is held pending until the next line: a block takes it, and otherwise it becomes a closed paragraph before the next line is classified.
Glued brace blocks merge into one.
Every block takes an attribute line, a definition and a `%%%` comment block included.

An attribute line is a line like any other for ownership, so one that its container does not own closes that container (C2-B-026). It is neither a blank line nor a comment-only line, so two lists with an attribute line between them are not one list (C2-B-053).
The order inside a brace block is fixed in the tree and the output: the id, then the classes, then the language, then the keys, classes and keys each as written.
A brace block on a marker line closes on that line.
The attributes of an item or a cell abut the marker, as in `-{.i} b`.
Consecutive attribute lines merge into one.
When a brace block or a merged run of them holds several ids, the last id written wins.
An attribute block glued to a div name, a code fence language or a raw fence format does not stop the block from opening, and `fence-opener-fallback` reports it with severity error.

The attributes of a link definition, from its attribute line and from the block at the end of its line, merged in that order as glued blocks are (C2-B-093), are merged into every link and image that uses it, and the link's own values win.
Consecutive attribute lines that no block takes, because a blank line or the end of their container follows, become one closed paragraph that holds every one of those lines as text.
A brace block with no content, alone on a line, is text and not an attribute line.
A description mark and a term mark take no abutting brace block: `:{.c}` and `::{.c}` are not marks, so the line is text.

A run of three or more backticks opens a code fence; a run of tildes opens nothing and is text, where 0.1 and Markdown read it as a second fence character. A code block that holds a backtick fence takes a longer run (C2-B-110). Further, a run of three or more colons opens or closes a div, and a run of three or more percent signs opens a comment block. Text behind the percent run on the opener line, without the spaces and tabs before it, is the first line of the comment's value, as in 0.1.

The closer of a code fence or a div has the opener's character and at least its length, on a line owned by the same container, with no further column test. A comment block closes at a bare run of `%` of at least the opener's length (C2-B-110) on any line, whatever its indent and also where the line lacks the marks of the quotes around the block, and that line closes no container, as in 0.1. A line with a quote mark that the block's container does not have is no closer.
The closer of a code fence and of a comment block is a bare run: a run followed by other text is content of the body.

An unclosed code fence, div or comment block ends with its container and never turns back into text, and `unclosed-code-fence`, `unclosed-container-fence` or `unclosed-comment-fence` reports it with severity error.
The body of a code fence is code and the body of a comment block is hidden: neither is read for blocks or inline content.
Blank lines at the end of an unclosed code fence, comment block or line block are not part of its body, so a trailing blank line never changes the tree.
The body of a div is read as blocks.
A code fence whose info string is `=` directly followed by a format name is a raw block: its body goes to an output of that format as written and is not code.

The value of a code block is its body lines, with one line feed after each line, including the last line when the end of input closes an unclosed fence. Trailing blank lines of an unclosed fence remain excluded under C2-B-113.
`comment-fence-closer-with-text` reports a percent run followed by other text in the body of a comment block.

After the run, a code fence opener holds an optional language word, an optional quoted title and an optional label in brackets, in that order. A label in brackets, here and on a div opener (C2-B-119), is the text between `[` and the first `]` behind it (`bracket_label` in `data/line-shapes.json`), so it holds no `]`, and it holds no line break, since an opener is one line.

After the run, a div opener holds an optional name or sigil, an optional quoted title and an optional label in brackets, in that order. A name stands after one or more spaces behind the run, like a sigil (C2-B-196): a name glued to the run, as in `:::note`, makes the line text. A title or a label may stand with no name before it, after one or more spaces behind the run as a name does: `::: "T"` opens a div with a title, and `:::[x]` is text. Behind those spaces a sigil starts a sigil div also when further words are glued to it, and C2-B-122 reports the words: `::: >a` opens a quote fence. When neither a name, a sigil, a title nor a label starts there, the line still opens an anonymous div, and C2-B-122 reports what follows the spaces: `::: *` and `::: {.x}` open a div with no name. Such a line never closes a div (C2-B-125).

The quoted title of a code fence renders like a `title` attribute, which is also accepted on an attribute line. In the tree they are two things, the `title` field and a key (C2-A-032), and where both are written the key wins in HTML (C2-H-048). The quoted title of a div, an admonition or a directive is the `title` field of that node and renders as its title paragraph (C2-H-042). Its value, the text between the quotes, is an inline content of one line, read once the opener is split into its parts, so a `%%` after whitespace in it starts a line comment that ends at the closing quote (C2-I-023).

The label in brackets is metadata for a group extension, such as the tab label of a code group. On a code fence it renders nothing in the core; on a div, an admonition and a directive the core writes it as a label paragraph (C2-H-154). It is a string in the tree (C2-A-187).

An unquoted title or further words in the info string do not stop the block from opening, and `fence-title-syntax` reports them. A raw fence (C2-B-116) and a sigil div (C2-B-196) take no title and no label: what follows the format or the sigil is further words in this sense, is not kept in the tree, and is reported. The 0.1 engine read such a line as text. A second space behind the backtick run leaves the opener with no language (the empty option of `code_fence_opener` in `data/line-shapes.json`), so what follows is further words: ```` ``` b ```` opens a code block with no language and `b` is reported.

A language word, a div name and a raw format name are each the longest run of their characters (refs `language_word`, `div_name` and `raw_format` in `data/line-shapes.json`). A raw format name starts with an ASCII letter and goes on with ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`. The first character behind the run that is not one of them ends the run; it is part of no name. Where it is not a space, a valid attribute block there is an attribute block (C2-B-105), and any other character, a brace block that is no valid attribute block included (C2-I-028 to C2-I-034), starts further words (C2-B-122). So `::: glossary>` opens the directive `glossary`, ```` ```js} ```` opens a code block with the language `js`, and ```` ```=html~ ```` opens a raw block with the format `html`, and `fence-title-syntax` reports `>`, `}` and `~`. Likewise `::: e{_a} y` opens the div `e`, and `fence-title-syntax`, not `fence-opener-fallback`, reports `{_a} y`.

The body of a line block is one leaf that recognizes only prefixes, the closer and a comment block (C2-B-108): every other line is a line of text. A comment block there is hidden (C2-B-112), adds no line and ends no stanza, as in 0.1.
A hard-break block and a quote fence are containers, and their bodies are read as blocks.
A bare colon run closes the innermost open div it is long enough for, and otherwise opens an anonymous div.
A colon run followed by a name or a sigil always opens a div, at any length.

The name of a div decides what it is: `note`, `tip`, `warning`, `danger`, `info`, `success`, `example` and `quote` give an admonition, `figure` with no title and no label gives a figure group, and with one of them a plain div with the class `figure`, `bibliography`, `footnotes`, `glossary`, `index`, `references` and `toc` give a directive, and every other name gives a plain div with that name as a class, and names are compared as written. Figure groups do not nest: anywhere inside a figure group, also in a quote, a list item or any other container of its body, `figure` with no title and no label gives a plain div with the class `figure` too, and `figure-group-nested` reports it (as in 0.1).
The classes of a div stand in one order: the name of a plain div first, then the classes of its attribute line as written, then the class of a sigil opener, `line-block` or `hardbreaks`, last.
A line of a line block keeps the spaces that lead it after the strip (C2-B-027) as content.
A blank line in a line block ends a stanza, and the next line starts a new one.

A stray `:::` at column 0 below an item with an unclosed div closes the item (C2-B-026) and opens an anonymous div at top level (C2-B-125), and `unclosed-container-fence` reports it with severity error.
A sigil stands after one or more spaces behind the colon run: without the space the line is not a sigil div opener and is text.
The line form is `%%` at the start of a line or after whitespace, it runs to the end of the line, and elsewhere `%%` is text.

After a list marker, a quote mark, a description mark, a term mark or a heading marker, a comment counts as content: the block opens, or stays open, and holds the comment as a comment node and no paragraph, on the first line of a quote as on a later one.

The comment of a comment-only line, and a comment that stands alone after a marker or a quote mark, is a child of the open leaf when one is open, and otherwise a comment node of the innermost open container, whatever the line's indent. Inside the leaf it stands in the innermost inline node open at its place, and no inline atom spans the line: for an atom that opens before it, such as a code span, a math span, a braced comment or an editorial comment, the content ends at the line, so an opener whose closer stands only on or after it is text (C2-I-017, C2-I-043).

A paragraph that holds one or more comments and nothing else but the breaks between them counts as content of its container and renders nothing: no empty paragraph element is written. So does a paragraph whose content holds only comments once the breaks that C2-H-069 does not write are left out.
Block rules classify lines first, so a braced comment that would span an interrupter line is left unclosed and stays text, and `unclosed-braced-comment` reports it.
A marker followed by a comment is the only spelling of an empty item, description, term or heading: there is no sentinel for an empty body.

The lint control comments and the region markers of an include are line comments that a tool reads, and their shapes, and the block boundary a region marker makes (C2-B-137), keep their 0.1 definitions. C2-B-215 to C2-B-217 state them.

A lint control comment is a line comment whose `%%` is followed by exactly one space and then by one of the keywords `carve-lint-disable-line`, `carve-lint-disable-next-line`, `carve-lint-disable` and `carve-lint-enable`. The keyword ends the comment, or is followed by spaces or commas and a list of rule ids separated by spaces or commas. No id means every rule. A keyword with another character glued to it, and a `%%` followed by two spaces, give no control comment. A control comment may stand on a comment-only line or behind content. It is a comment like any other: it renders nothing and changes no block. Text of this shape in a code span, a code block, raw content, a braced comment or a comment block controls nothing.

`carve-lint-disable-line` suppresses the named rules for the findings reported on its own line, and `carve-lint-disable-next-line` for those on the next line, also where that line belongs to another container. `carve-lint-disable` suppresses them from its own line to the end of the document, and `carve-lint-enable` lifts that from its own line. For each rule, the last of these two that names it, or names no rule, decides. An enable does not lift a line scope. A finding counts at the line it reports. In an included file the line scopes count the lines of that file, and a document scope ends with the file.

A region marker of an include is a line that holds, after optional spaces and tabs, a line comment whose content is `#region` and a name, or `#endregion` and an optional name, and after that only spaces and tabs. Spaces and tabs may stand between `%%` and the keyword and between the keyword and the name. The name is an ASCII letter or `_`, then ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`. The keywords are case-sensitive. A keyword run on by a letter, a digit or `_`, as in `#regional`, makes no marker; run on by any other character, as in `#region-x`, it makes a malformed marker, which an expansion reports. A `%%%` run opens a comment block and is never a marker. A marker renders nothing; what a region selects is the expansion's job.

A caption line is `^`, one or more spaces and content, directly below its block with no blank line and owned by the same container as that block, with no column test. The caption text starts at the first character behind those spaces that is not a space or a tab, and a continuation line of a caption loses its indent like every line of a content (C2-I-002).

A caption attaches to one of six blocks: an image, a table, a code block, a quote, a math block or a figure group. A code include, an include whose valid options hold `code`, takes a caption too, which its expansion gives to the block it becomes (C2-N-073).
A caption is paragraph-like: its text takes lazy lines and ends as a paragraph does, so a second caption line directly below a caption continues the first.
After a blank line or below any other block a caption line is text, and `unattached-caption` reports it.

The mark is the first `#` in the top-level inline content of a caption that is followed by whitespace, `:`, `.`, the end of the caption or a character that cannot start a tag name (C2-I-092). A `#` before a tag-name character is a tag or text, so `#1` is text. `\#` is a literal `#`. A `#` inside inline markup, such as emphasis, a link or a span, is no mark. Every `#` after the mark is text.

The label of a caption with a mark is its inline content before the mark, without trailing whitespace. Its sequence key is the plain text of the label, computed as for a heading (C2-H-143), except that a symbol gives the text the caption writes for it (C2-H-101). So `*Figure* #` and `Figure #` have the key `Figure`, a comment in the label changes no key, and `^ #` has the empty key. Keys are compared exactly, case included.
A heading is one to six `=`, one space and at least one further character that is not a space or a tab, so seven or more markers or a bare marker run are text.
`#` is accepted in place of `=`.
Everything after that space is inline content: trailing marker characters and a brace block are heading text.

A heading holds its marker line and every line directly below it that is indented past the column of its marker, each joined by a soft break, or by a hard break where the line above ends in a backslash (C2-I-102). A continuation line is a lazy line of the heading as of a paragraph (C2-B-012), so it ends where a paragraph ends (C2-B-013): at a blank line, at a region marker line (C2-B-137) and at every interrupter (C2-B-014 to C2-B-020, C2-B-200), which are a fence line, a table row and a thematic break anywhere, and inside an item a list marker that is indented past the item's marker. Ownership comes first, as for every line (C2-B-025, C2-B-026), and the column is counted behind the marks of the open quotes (C2-B-003): a line that lacks the mark of an open quote closes that quote, so below `> > # H` the line `> cont` is a paragraph of the outer quote. A line that is not indented past the marker starts a new block; a comment-only line is no such line (C2-B-137), so its comment is a child of the heading (C2-B-138) and an indented line below it still continues the heading. So text directly below a heading is a paragraph and two headings need no blank line between them. In 0.1 a heading was one line and an indented line below it was a paragraph.
`=` and `#` may mix in one document, and `heading-marker-mixed` reports it.

An include directive, `{{ ... }}` alone on its line, is a block of one line and not an interrupter, and the shape of the directive is carried over from 0.1. C2-B-201 to C2-B-206 state it, and the Includes document (`includes.md`) states its expansion.

A block image stays a paragraph while its lines are read, and the paragraph is promoted when it closes as exactly one block image line (C2-B-197). A comment-only line is not a line of the paragraph (C2-B-137, C2-B-138), so comment-only lines below that line leave it one line, for a block image as for a math block (C2-B-158).
A paragraph that closes as exactly one display math line (C2-B-198) is a math block, a fact set at close like the promotion of a block image.

A block image line is decided by its shape and not by inline parsing: the line consists of exactly one image form, `![alt](destination)`, `![alt][label]` or the collapsed `![alt][]`, optional attribute blocks glued to it (C2-I-039), and trailing spaces or tabs. The label, which in the collapsed form is the alt text, must be a label under C2-I-079, so `![ ][]` is no such line. An image whose form runs over a line ending is not such a line.

A display math line is decided by its shape and not by inline parsing: the line consists of exactly one display math span, `$$` glued to a code span, optional attribute blocks glued to it, and trailing spaces or tabs. A span that closes on a later line is not such a line.

An include directive is `{{`, one or more spaces, a path, an optional section, zero or more options, one or more spaces and `}}`, with only spaces and tabs after it on the line. Spaces before the section and before each option are optional: `{{ a.crv#s@shift:1 }}` is a directive. A tab is not such a space, so `{{` followed by a tab is text. The closing `}}` is the first one outside a quoted path and a quoted value, so a quoted run may hold `}}`.

A path is bare or quoted. A bare path is one or more characters, none of them a space, `#`, `@`, `}`, `"` or `“` (U+201C), so a bare path ends at the section or at the first option. A double-quoted path is `"`, one or more characters and `"`: a backslash takes the next character with it, and an unescaped `"` and a line end do not occur. Its value is read like a quoted attribute value (C2-I-033): a backslash before an ASCII punctuation character is dropped, and a backslash before any other character stays, so `"a\.crv"` names `a.crv` and `"notes\new.crv"` names `notes\new.crv`. A path in curly quotes, `“`, one or more characters other than `”` and `”`, is read as written, with no escape. An empty path in any form makes the line text (`empty-include-path`).

A section is `#` and a name: an ASCII letter, digit or `_`, then ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`. A directive holds at most one section. The section names a heading or a block of the included file by its id; selecting it is the expansion's job (C2-N-027 to C2-N-031).

An option is `@`, a key and, optionally, `:` and a value. The key is an ASCII letter or `_`, then ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`. An unquoted value is one or more characters that are not `@`, `}`, a space, a tab or a line end, so an unquoted value ends at the next option: `@shift:1@lines:1-8` is two options. A value that starts with `"` or `'` is a quoted value as in C2-I-033, and may hold `@`, spaces and `}}`. Outside `cols`, quoting a value only delimits it: `@lines:"1-2"` is `@lines:1-2`.

The six keys and the shape of each value are listed in `data/include-options.json`. `lines` and `rows` take a range `N-M`: two decimal numbers without a leading zero, the first at least 1 and not greater than the second. `region` takes an ASCII letter or `_`, then ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`. `cols` takes a range or a double-quoted list of column names separated by commas, in which each name is not empty and a backslash takes the next character. `shift` takes `auto` or a decimal integer of one to nine digits with an optional `+` or `-`, as a list marker has at most nine digits (C2-B-219); a longer number is outside the shape. `code` stands alone or takes a language: one or more ASCII letters, digits and `-`, `_`, `+`, `#`, `.`, `/`.

The basic shape of a directive is `{{`, a path, at most one section, any number of options of the form `@key` or `@key:value`, and `}}`, alone on its line, as C2-B-201 to C2-B-204 spell them. Every line of the basic shape is an include directive: the keys and the value shapes of C2-B-205 do not change the block. An option is invalid when its key is not one of the six, when its value is outside the shape of its key, when it has no value and `data/include-options.json` needs one, or when its key stood earlier in the directive. An invalid option has no effect on the tree: the node keeps it as written (C2-A-181), `include-option-invalid` reports it, and the expansion leaves an include that holds one unexpanded (C2-N-025). Whether two selection options may stand together, and every other rule about the content an include brings in, belong to the expansion (C2-N-024).
A thematic break is a line that holds three or more `*` and nothing else but trailing spaces and tabs, at any indent.

A run of hyphens or underscores and the spaced forms are not thematic breaks: they are text, or nested markers for `- - -` (C2-B-058), and `thematic-break-spelling` or `deprecated-spaced-thematic-break` reports them.
Line 1 opens frontmatter when it is exactly three hyphens at column 0, optionally followed by a format name, glued or after one space, and then by trailing spaces and tabs.
The closer is a line that is exactly `---` plus trailing spaces and tabs.
An unclosed frontmatter block runs to the end of the document, and `unclosed-frontmatter` reports it with severity error.

The format name is one word of one or more ASCII letters and digits, in any case and in any order: `toml`, `JSON`, `Yaml` and `1` are format names, and `x-y`, `x_y` and `é` are none. It stands glued to the hyphens, as in `---toml`, or after one space, as in `--- toml`, like the language of a code fence (C2-B-117); the glued form is canonical. Any word of that shape is a format name; `yaml`, `toml` and `json` are the usual ones, and the parser does not read the body for any of them. The word is the only thing on the line: a second word, another character or two spaces leave the line text. The name is kept as written, so `---JSON` has the format `JSON`, which is not `json`. Without a name the format is YAML, for which the bare opener is the canonical form. As in 0.1.

Only a byte-order mark may come before the opener, and a longer run of hyphens on line 1 is text. A byte-order mark at the start of the source is not content: it is skipped before line 1 is read, whatever line 1 holds, and offsets count its bytes (C2-A-141). It is no code point of line 1, so the first character behind it has the column it would have without the mark.

A table row is a line that starts with a pipe after the prefixes and ends with a pipe, after which only a row attribute, a line comment and trailing spaces and tabs may follow (C2-B-167), with at least two pipes, so a pipe alone on a line is text. The closing pipe is a separator under C2-B-169: a line whose last pipe is escaped or stands inside a code span is not a row. The closing pipe is the last pipe of the line, not counting a pipe inside a quoted value (C2-I-033) of a brace block that follows a pipe as a row attribute does (C2-B-167), as in 0.1, and also where a line comment stands before it: `| a | b | %% note | x` does not end with a pipe and is text (C2-B-168). The 0.1 engine read an escaped last pipe as the closer. A row of hyphens and colons, the separator row of a Markdown table, is an ordinary body row: it marks no head and sets no alignment (C2-A-095).

After its closing pipe a row may carry a row attribute, which is a brace block glued to that pipe or one space after it, and a trailing line comment. The comment stands after whitespace, as C2-B-133 requires: `| a |%% x` and `||%%` do not end with a pipe and are text (C2-B-168). The comment stands in the tree as a comment-only line directly below the row would (C2-A-086).
A line that starts with a pipe and does not end as C2-B-166 says is text: the table ends there, the next row starts a new table, and `table-shaped-paragraph` reports the line.
Cells are split before their content is read: a pipe is not a separator when it is escaped or when it stands between a backtick run and its matching closing run on the same line.
