Every cell is a separate inline content, and so is every fragment of a continuation row (C2-B-184). An inline construct never crosses a cell boundary or a row, so a backtick run whose closing run is not in its cell or fragment is text (C2-I-017).

An escaped pipe is a literal pipe in cell text before inline parsing, including a link destination, an image destination, an image label and a reference label. The list is complete: in a code span `\|` stays two characters, and in other cell text it is an ordinary escape. The key of a reference label in a cell holds `|`; outside a cell it holds `\|` (C2-I-079).
A table ends at the first line that is neither a row nor a continuation row.

A cell prefix is the optional header cell mark `|=`, then an optional run of glued brace blocks, merged into one (C2-B-093). The `=` is the header cell mark only where a space, a tab, `{`, one of the alignment marks `<`, `>`, `?` and `~`, or the end of the cell follows it; otherwise it is the first character of the cell's text. So `|= a|`, `|={.c}a|`, `|=|` and `|=< a|` are header cells, the last one holding `< a` since a mark outside a brace block is text (C2-B-182), while `|=a|`, `|==a|` and `|=SUM(A1)|` are data cells whose text starts with `=`. Spaces and tabs at the start and at the end of a cell are padding and not content.

A cell that holds only a span mark, `<` or `^`, joins the cell to its left or the cell above when that cell stands in the same group of the table (C2-B-174). A `<` in the first column, a `<` whose left cell is covered by a row span from above, a `^` in the first row of its group and a `^` below a cell that spans more than one column join nothing (C2-B-173): in `|a|<|` above `|^|b|`, the `^` is the text of its cell.

A span mark that joins nothing is an ordinary cell that holds the mark as text, and `table-span-marker-blocked` reports it. Its prefix applies as on any cell (C2-B-171): `|= ^ |` in the first row is a header cell that holds `^`.

The head, each body and the foot are the groups of a table, and no span crosses from one into another. For the head test (C2-B-178) a `<` with a cell to its left and a `^` below a cell of one column are part of that cell and add no cell to their row, but such a mark with the header mark counts as a header cell; any other span mark counts as the cell it is. So `|= H | < |` is a head row, and below `|= H |` the row `| ^ |` has no header cell and is none. The prefix of a mark that joins is kept for nothing else, and `table-span-marker-attribute` reports a brace block in it, and a header mark on it that does not make its row a head row, as on `|= ^ |` below `| a |`.

A continuation row starts with `+` and ends with a pipe and trailing spaces and tabs, directly below a row or a continuation row. A comment-only line between them does not break the adjacency (C2-B-137).

A fragment past the last column forms a new cell, and each column it skips an empty cell. Such a cell is a header cell when every other cell of its row is one, where a `<` mark counts as the cell it extends and a `^` mark as a data cell. As in 0.1.
The head of a table is its leading rows that have a header cell and no other cell (C2-B-174). Where the source declares no grouping, the rest of the rows form one body.
`header-rows` sets the number of head rows of a delimited table. C2-B-209 and C2-B-210 state its default and its value.
A delimited table, a `csv` or `tsv` fence that the `table` attribute marks, is always a table, and `delimited-table-malformed` reports an unclosed quote as C2-B-181 states, with severity error.

An unclosed quote in a delimited table runs to the end of the fence body, and `delimited-table-malformed` reports it with severity error: its cell holds everything after the quote character, line breaks and separators included, without the final line ending.

In the brace block of a cell prefix the alignment marks come first: a horizontal mark, `<` left, `>` right or `~` center, and directly after it an optional vertical mark, `^` top, `~` middle or `v` bottom. In place of the horizontal mark, `?` sets no horizontal alignment; it stands only before a vertical mark, so `{?v}` sets the vertical axis alone. A vertical mark with no horizontal mark or `?` before it is no mark: `{^}` is no attribute block, and `{v}` holds the bare key `v`. A `?` with no vertical mark after it is no mark either, so `{?}` is no attribute block. The marks are not a part of the attribute grammar (C2-I-029): they are read before the parts, only in a cell prefix, and a block that holds nothing but the marks, as in `|={>} x |` and `|={>^} x |`, is valid there. A part may follow the marks directly, with no space between: `|{>.c} a |` is right with the class `c`, and `|{>^.c} a |` right and top with the class `c`. The marks stand only at the start of the first block of the run of glued blocks (C2-B-171, C2-B-093); every later block is read by the attribute grammar alone, and the first one that is no valid attribute block ends the run, so it and what follows are the cell's text. So `|{>}{^} a |` is right with the text `{^} a`, and `|{.a}{>} a |` has the class `a` and the text `{>} a`. The character directly after the horizontal mark or `?` is the vertical mark whenever it is one of the three, so `{>v}` is right and bottom, `{>vx}` is right and bottom with the bare key `x`, and `{~~}` is center and middle (as in 0.1). A bare key that starts with `v` stands after a space behind the marks: `{> vx}` is right with the bare key `vx`.
Spans resolve backward only: a span mark never joins a cell to its right or below.

Each fragment of a continuation row joins the cell of its column in the row above, and an empty fragment adds nothing. Each fragment is an inline content by itself (C2-B-223), so every inline form opens and closes inside one physical row, and an opener whose closer is not in its own fragment is text, as at the end of a cell. The cell holds the nodes of its fragments in order, with one space of text between two fragments: `` `a `` continued by `` b` `` is the text `` `a b` ``. Span marks are read from the first line of the row; a fragment whose column holds a span mark joins the cell that covers that column once spans are resolved, and under a span mark that joins nothing it joins the cell that holds the mark (C2-B-173).
A fragment of a continuation row reads no cell prefix, no span mark and no row attribute.
On a pipe table `header-rows` has no effect on the head, and `deprecated-table-attribute` reports it.

`footer-rows` makes the last rows of a table its footer, counted among the rows below the head only: a head row is never a footer row, and a count larger than the rows below the head takes them all. In 0.1 a lone header row became the footer. `header-cols` has no effect in 0.2.0, `aligns`, `valigns` and `widths` keep their 0.1 definition except that a list with an invalid entry now has no effect at all, and `body-rows`, `body-header-rows` and `body-header-cols` keep their 0.1 definitions, applied to the rows below the 0.2 head. C2-B-210 to C2-B-214, C2-B-227 and C2-B-230 state them.
A list-table is a div named `list-table` whose body is a list of rows: a later extension defines it, it gives the same table as a pipe table, and this chapter does not restate it.

The head of a delimited table is its first row unless `header-rows` gives a count (C2-B-210). A count N makes the first N rows the head, and 0 gives a table with no head. A count larger than the number of rows is the number of rows, so every row is in the head, and `table-row-count-clamped` reports the count.

The tree holds the effective partition of C2-B-209 in its groups and no count (C2-A-088). The sidecar records the effective count as `headerRows` (C2-L-057), and the writer writes that count (C2-W-066): `header-rows=5` on a table of two rows gives the tree of `header-rows=2`, a head of both rows and no body. `footer-rows` counts on a delimited table as on a pipe table, from the last row upward and only below the head (C2-B-187), so where the two counts together exceed the rows the head takes its rows first: `header-rows=2 footer-rows=2` on three rows gives a head of two rows and a footer of one.

The value of `header-rows` and of `footer-rows` is a count: one or more decimal digits. An empty value counts as 1. A count is valid only in this form. Any other value is invalid, and the attribute then has no effect: the table keeps the partition it has without the attribute. A valid count takes effect also where it equals the default or selects no row.

`aligns` is a list of entries separated by commas. The entry at position N sets the horizontal alignment of column N, and spaces around an entry are ignored. An entry is `left`, `right` or `center` and sets `align` of that `table_column`. The whole value is checked before any entry is applied: every entry, one past the last column included, must have this form, and an empty or malformed entry makes the whole value invalid, so that it sets no column. Entries past the last column set nothing. Fewer entries than columns are valid: the remaining columns stay unset, and `table-column-arity` reports it. `valigns` is the same list for the vertical axis: an entry is `top`, `middle` or `bottom` and sets `valign` of that `table_column`.

`widths` is a list of entries separated by commas, by position like `aligns`, and its whole value is checked in the same way before any entry is applied (C2-B-211). An entry is a decimal number greater than 0 and at most 100. It is a percentage of the table width, and sets `width` of that `table_column` to the number divided by 100: `25` gives `0.25`. An empty entry or any other entry makes the whole value invalid, so that it sets no column. Entries past the last column set nothing, and fewer entries are valid. The widths need not total 100; `table-width-total` reports a total above 100.

A decimal number in a `widths` entry is one or more ASCII digits, optionally followed by a dot and one or more ASCII digits. `30.5` and `5` are entries; `.5`, `5.`, `1e1` and `+5` are not, and such an entry makes the value invalid (C2-B-212).

The alignment of a cell is resolved for each axis on its own. The cell's own mark for that axis (C2-B-182) wins. Then comes the mark for that axis of the last header cell in the head that starts in the cell's column and carries a mark for that axis, then the entry of that column in `aligns` for the horizontal axis and in `valigns` for the vertical axis. Otherwise the cell has no alignment on that axis. A mark on any other cell applies to that cell only, and a header cell that spans several columns gives its marks only to the column it starts in. Where a head mark and an `aligns` or `valigns` entry set the same axis of a column, `table-column-overlap` reports it.
`header-cols` has no effect on a pipe table or a delimited table: there it is an ordinary key.

A table reads `aligns`, `valigns`, `widths`, `header-rows`, `footer-rows`, `body-rows`, `body-header-rows` and `body-header-cols` from its `attrs`. A key whose value is valid and that applies to the table form is removed from `attrs` once its effect is recorded in the tree, in the groups or in the column fields (C2-A-088, C2-A-089). A valid count that the table clamps (C2-B-187, C2-B-209) is consumed too. A key whose value is invalid (C2-B-210 to C2-B-212, C2-B-230), and `header-rows` on a pipe table (C2-B-186), has no effect and stays in `attrs`. Lint reports a kept invalid value as `table-attribute-invalid`; `deprecated-table-attribute` reports `header-rows` on a pipe table.

`body-rows` splits the rows between the head and the foot into bodies, one `table_body` each in source order. Its value is a list of entries separated by commas, spaces around an entry ignored, one entry per body giving its data rows. An entry of `body-rows` and of `body-header-rows` is one or more decimal digits; unlike a count (C2-B-210) it has no empty form. `0` is an empty body, and an empty value gives no body. `body-header-rows`, one entry per body, puts that many rows before the data rows of its body, and every cell of such a row is a header cell. `body-header-cols`, one entry per body, sets `rowHeadColumns` of its body (C2-A-088), and an empty entry sets none; the cells of those columns stay data cells in the tree and are written as header cells (C2-H-056). `body-rows` can stand alone. The two header lists need `body-rows` and exactly one entry per body, and the header and data rows of the bodies must be exactly the rows between the head and the foot; where a value breaks one of these rules, none of the three keys has an effect. The head stays that of C2-B-178 or C2-B-209, so a pipe table writes its head with header marks, not `header-rows` (C2-B-186).

The body of a delimited table is read as records, in the manner of RFC 4180. The separator is a comma for `csv` and a tab for `tsv`. The language word is matched as written, so a `CSV` fence is a code block that keeps its attribute. A line ending ends a row, except inside quotes. A cell that starts with `"` is quoted up to the next `"` that is not doubled: a doubled `""` stands for one `"`, and separators and line endings inside are part of the cell; what stands between the closing quote and the next separator or line ending is added to the cell as written. A `"` anywhere else is an ordinary character. Cells are not trimmed. A cell is plain text: no inline form is read in it, and its `cell_paragraph` holds one `text` node (C2-A-215), or none for an empty cell. A separator always starts another cell, so a row that ends in one has an empty last cell. An empty line is a row of one empty cell, except that one empty line at the end of the body is dropped. An empty body has no rows.
Whether a line is an opener is decided on that line alone and never by whether a closer follows, so a construct with a closer of its own always opens (C2-B-111).

Block nesting stops at depth 200: each open quote, list, item, description list, description, footnote body and div counts one, and while 200 are open an opener of one more is text. Inline nodes do not count; inline content has its own limit (C2-I-118). A marker that opens two containers at once, a list and its item or a description list and its first description, is tested as one: when both do not fit, the whole marker is text and neither opens.

Five facts are set on a node when its block closes and are not roles of a line: the promotion of a block image (C2-B-157), a math block (C2-B-158), the attachment of a caption (C2-B-147), the tightness of a list (C2-B-062) and the footer rows of a table (C2-B-187).

Inline content is parsed one content at a time, after the block pass has settled every line of the document: no block decision depends on inline content, and every definition and heading is known when the first content is read.

A content is the list of its source spans in order, one per line, without the prefixes of its containers, without markers and without indent. Spaces and tabs at the end of a line of the content are not part of it, on the last line as on the others; a space that a backslash escapes is not such a space (C2-I-011). They are removed before any inline form is read, so the rule holds inside a code span, a math span, a literal span, a raw span and a comment as in text. The test is lexical: a space behind an odd run of backslashes is kept, also inside a form that reads no escapes (C2-I-013). A tab behind a backslash is removed like any other tab at the end of a line. In a table cell the padding before the closing pipe is removed first, so a backslash that stands before that padding ends the cell and is a hard break (C2-I-102). A no-break space at the end of a cell therefore has no spelling (C2-W-117).
Two neighboring spans are joined by one line break.
The content is read in one left-to-right scan with four steps in a fixed order of precedence: atoms, the bracket stack, the delimiter stack, attachment.

At each position the scan tries the atoms first. An atom that matches is taken whole: no bracket, delimiter or other atom opens, closes or is matched inside it, and of two atoms the one that starts first wins.

An opening bracket is pushed on the bracket stack. A closing bracket pairs with the nearest open one, and what is glued to the closing bracket decides the construct. Where no glued tail forms another construct, C2-I-072 tests the pair for a defined shortcut. A pair that forms no construct is plain text: its content is read as inline content all the same, and it bounds nothing. A closing bracket with no open bracket is text.
A bracket construct is settled before delimiters pair: a delimiter inside its content pairs only inside it, and a delimiter outside it pairs only outside it.
Emphasis, strong and the braced forms pair on one delimiter stack (C2-I-051, C2-I-059).
Attachment comes last: an attribute block attaches only to a host that has already formed.

Every general category and every character property that a clause of the 0.2 documents names is that of Unicode 18.0.0, whatever Unicode version the host runtime has. `data/unicode-categories.json` lists the code points of the categories L, M, N and Cf of that version, generated from its `UnicodeData.txt`; a code point that Unicode 18.0.0 leaves unassigned is in none of them. The display width of the writer reads the same version (C2-W-119).
A backslash before an ASCII punctuation character makes that character literal text: it opens, closes and starts nothing.

A backslash before a space is a no-break space, except at the end of a line, where the two are a hard break (C2-I-102). In every test of the character before or after a position it counts as whitespace, as U+00A0 does: in `a\ "b"` the first quote opens (C2-I-104), and `*\ a*` holds no strong.
A backslash before any other character is a literal backslash, except at the end of a line, where it is a hard break (C2-I-102).

Escapes are not read inside a code span, an autolink, a cross-reference, a comment or an editorial comment. A link destination reads only the escaped parenthesis and the escaped backslash. A link title and a quoted attribute value read escapes.
A run of one or more backticks opens a code span. The opener is the whole run.

The span closes at the next backtick run of exactly the opener's length. Everything between is code: no escape and no other form is read there, and a line break is content. The spaces and tabs at the end of each line are removed before the span is read (C2-I-002): `` `a ``, two spaces, a line break and `` b` `` give the value `a`, a line feed and `b`.
When the content of a closed span starts and ends with a space and holds a character that is not a space, one space is removed from each end. Content of spaces only is kept as it is.

A backtick run with no closing run of its length later in the same content opens nothing (C2-I-119): the run is text, and so is a `!`, `$` or `$$` glued before it. The scan goes on behind the run, so a shorter or longer run after it may open a span. This holds for a code span, a literal-text span and a math span alike, and in a table cell as anywhere: the cell `` | x `a | `` holds the text `` x `a ``. For this test a comment-only line ends the content (C2-B-138).

A `!` glued before the opening run makes a literal-text span: its content is written as escaped text with no code element. With an attribute block it is written as a span element that carries the attributes.
A `$` glued before a code span makes inline math, and `$$` makes display math. The content is the span's verbatim text. A `$` with no backtick run after it is text.

A closed plain code span with `{=name}` glued to it, `name` a raw format name (C2-B-225), is raw inline; the marker is tried together with the attribute block, before the highlight opener. The content is written unescaped to the output format of that name and dropped for every other format. Anywhere else, after a literal-text span or a math span too, `{=` is read as a braced opener (C2-I-043).

`%%` at the start of a line of the content or after whitespace starts a line comment. It runs to the end of that line and renders nothing, and the spaces before it are dropped with it. Elsewhere `%%` is text, also directly after the opener of a bracket or a braced form: the start of their content is neither a line start nor whitespace.

A line comment takes the rest of its line, every closer on it included. A form that is open at the comment stays open: a matching closer on a later line of the same paragraph closes it, and an opener that never closes is text.
`{%` opens a braced comment that closes at the first `%}` in the content. It may cross line breaks, it does not nest, and it renders nothing.
A valid attribute block is `{`, optional spaces, one or more parts separated by spaces, optional spaces and `}`, all on one line.
A part is `#name` for the id, `.name` for a class, `:tag` for the language, `key=value`, or a bare `key`, which is a key with an empty value.

A name is one or more ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`. A key is an ASCII letter or `_`, then letters, digits, `_` and `-`. A language tag is empty or runs of letters and digits joined by single hyphens.
An unquoted value is one or more characters without a space, a tab, a quote, a backslash, a pipe and a closing brace.

A quoted value stands in `"` or `'`. In it a backslash escapes as in text (C2-I-010, C2-I-012): before an ASCII punctuation character it is dropped and the character is literal, and before any other character it stays. A closing brace is allowed, and the value may be empty.
One part that fits no shape makes the whole run no attribute block. Its opening brace is then read by the next rule of C2-I-043.
A valid attribute block is one atom wherever it stands. One that attaches to nothing is printed as written: nothing inside it is transformed, smart quotes included.

A valid attribute block attaches when it is glued to the end of a formed host, and is literal text otherwise. The hosts are: a span, a link, an image, an autolink, a reference, a code span without a raw marker (C2-I-021), a literal-text span, a math span, a footnote reference, an inline footnote, a symbol, an inline extension, and every closed emphasis, strong or braced span.
Glued attribute blocks after one host merge, in the order written: classes add up, a later id or key replaces an earlier one of the same name, and a later language part replaces an earlier one.

A key named `id` or `class`, in any ASCII letter case, folds into the id or into the classes when the block is parsed, and of several ids the last one wins (C2-B-104). The value of a `class` key is split at runs of spaces and tabs, each piece is one class at the place of the key, and an empty value adds none.

At an opening brace the scan takes the first of these that matches. One: a valid attribute block. Two: `{%`, a braced comment, when `%}` follows in the content. Three: `{#`, an editorial comment, when `#}` follows in the content with at least one character between. Four: `{` followed by one of `*`, `/`, `_`, `~`, `=`, `+`, `-`, `^` or `,`, a braced opener on the delimiter stack.
`/` is the emphasis delimiter and `*` is the strong delimiter. No other character is a bare delimiter: a bare `_`, `~`, `=`, `^` or `,` is text.
A delimiter can open when the character before it is not a word character and the character after it is not whitespace. A bare underscore is ordinary punctuation for this test and for C2-I-048.
A delimiter can close when the character before it is not whitespace and the character after it is not a word character.

A delimiter that can close, with an open entry of its kind on the stack, closes the nearest such entry. Every entry above it is removed, and its characters are text. Otherwise, a delimiter that can open is pushed, also while an entry of its kind is open, so a kind nests in itself. Otherwise it is text.
There is no combined token for strong emphasis. Each order of the two delimiters is plain nesting, in the order written.
A braced opener is `{` and a mark, and a braced closer is the mark and `}`. Each is one token and has no condition on the characters around it.
A braced opener only opens, and a braced closer only closes.

A mark followed by `}` is a braced closer only while a braced opener of that mark is open. Otherwise the mark is read by the bare rules (C2-I-051), where a slash or a star can close a bare span, and the brace is text. Of a run of marks before `}` only the last is the closer and the marks before it are text; with no braced opener of that mark open, the whole run is text.
A braced closer pairs with the nearest open braced opener of its mark. A braced token never pairs with a bare delimiter.
Bare and braced entries share the one delimiter stack, and the first pair closed wins: when a pair closes, every entry opened after its opener is removed, bare or braced, and is text (C2-I-051).
A braced opener that finds no closer, or that is removed, is text (C2-I-119), and its mark is not read again as a bare delimiter: `{*a* b` stays text.
A replacement is a deletion with an insertion glued to it. It is two nodes. There is no arrow form: `~>` is text, and the braced tilde is always strike.

`{#` opens an editorial comment that closes at the first `#}` in the content. Its content is literal: no escape and no form is read in it, and it holds at least one character. It is an atom. The first `#}` decides: where it stands directly behind `{#`, there is no comment and the opener is text.
A bracket pair with a valid attribute block glued to it is a span. Its content is inline content, and the block and every block glued behind it attach to it (C2-I-039, C2-I-040).
A bracket pair with a link tail glued to it is an inline link. The tail is `(`, a destination, an optional title and `)`.

A destination is a run of characters without whitespace, in which parentheses are balanced or escaped. It may be empty. Whitespace is a space, a tab or a line break here as everywhere (Preliminaries), so a no-break space, U+00A0 or U+202F, before or inside the destination is part of it, where 0.1 ended the destination at any Unicode whitespace.

A title follows the destination after exactly one space. It stands in double quotes, which is the canonical form, or in single quotes, which the formatter rewrites. A backslash escapes the quote in it, and spaces may follow it.

The link tail is an atom and stands on one line. It is read only glued to the closing bracket of a pair: with no open bracket, no destination is read. A tail with a space in the destination, a broken title or a line break is no tail: the bracket pair is text and the parenthesis is text.
Link text is inline content and may cross line breaks.

A bracket pair with `[label]` glued to it is a full reference. With `[]` glued to it, it is a collapsed reference, whose label is the source of its own text. A pair without another bracket construct glued to it is a shortcut reference when the folded source of its text is a key of a link definition in the document. A shortcut has no separate label. Without a matching definition the brackets are text, and no reference node forms. A collapsed reference whose own text folds to an empty key (C2-I-079) is no reference: its brackets are text.

`<`, a URL or an email address, and `>` form an autolink. A URL is a scheme (a letter, then letters, digits, `+`, `-` and `.`), a colon and one or more URL characters. An email address is a local part, an at-sign, a domain, a dot and letters. The visible text is the body as written. It is an atom. C2-I-122 to C2-I-124 state the characters.

A `!` glued before a bracket pair that forms an inline link or a reference makes an image. Its alt text is the source of the bracket content, not parsed, except that a backslash before an ASCII punctuation character is removed (C2-I-010). Before any other bracket pair the `!` is text.

A URL character is an ASCII letter or digit, one of `-`, `.`, `_`, `~`, `:`, `/`, `?`, `#`, `[`, `]`, `@`, `!`, `$`, `&`, `'`, `(`, `)`, `*`, `+`, `,`, `;`, `=` and `%`, or a character outside ASCII that does not have the Unicode property White_Space, is not a control character (general category Cc) and is not a format character (Cf), all of the version C2-I-127 pins. Every other ASCII character is no URL character, among them a space, `"`, `\`, a backtick, `{`, `}`, `|`, `^`, `<` and `>`. The scheme holds ASCII characters only, so `<1a:x>` is no autolink.

The local part and the domain of an email address are each one or more ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `-`, `_` and `+`. The domain is followed by a dot and one or more ASCII letters, which end the address. So `<a@b>` and `<a@b.c1>` are no autolinks, and an address with a character outside ASCII is none either.

The body of an autolink is everything between `<` and the next `>`. The autolink forms only when the whole body is one URL or one email address; otherwise `<`, the body and `>` are text, read as any other inline content. The destination of a URL autolink is its body, and that of an email autolink is `mailto:` followed by its body. An attribute block glued to the `>` attaches to the autolink (C2-I-036).
A full or collapsed reference is a node whether or not its label resolves. The inline scan reads the definition keys to decide whether a shortcut forms. Resolution reads the definition values later.

A reference label is the run of characters up to the next `]` that no backslash escapes. It is taken whole: no atom, bracket, delimiter or sigil form is read in it, a code span included, and its source is its key (C2-I-079). The line comment of C2-I-077 is the one exception. The heading lookup reads the stored key once more, and that reading makes no node (C2-I-084).

The lookup key of a label is its source text with every run of spaces, tabs and one line break folded to one space and with the ends trimmed. Case matters, and a backslash stays in the key, also one that escapes a bracket. Reference labels, footnote labels and definition labels share this rule. A label whose key is empty after folding, one that holds only spaces, tabs or a line break, is no label: the brackets are text.
A label may wrap: a line break with the whitespace around it folds to one space. A blank line ends the content and the label with it. A definition line stays on one line.

The stored key of a full or collapsed link reference is looked up first in the link definitions, where it matches a key that is the same string. Only where no definition matches is it looked up in the headings (C2-I-084). A shortcut forms and resolves only from a definition: a heading alone never forms a shortcut reference.

The attributes of a link definition merge into every reference that resolves to it: the classes of the definition and of the reference add up, the definition's first, and the reference's own id and keys win over the definition's.

The heading lookup reads the stored key as inline content of its own, in which no reference is resolved, and takes its plain text by C2-H-143. It takes the plain text of each heading the same way, folds both by C2-I-079 and normalizes both to NFC, as a cross-reference is matched (C2-I-097). The target is the first heading in document order that has an id and whose folded plain text equals that of the key. The match is case-sensitive. A key whose folded plain text is empty matches no heading, also none whose plain text is empty, so `[:smile:][]` below `# :smile:` stays text, as in 0.1. The reference links to that heading's authored or generated id; an explicit id is a destination, not a key the lookup matches. An opener left unclosed in the key is text under the fallback rule (C2-I-119), so the lookup never fails because of markup in the key. No source text is read: a tree resolves the same with and without its source, and the formatter cannot change which heading a key finds. The `key` and the carrier `data-carve-ref` keep the folded label as written (C2-A-104, C2-H-114). A heading that has no id, which is one without an authored id while `headingIds` is `off` (C2-H-022), is no target: the lookup passes over it, and a reference that finds no other heading is unresolved.

An unresolved reference renders its brackets and its label as literal text and its children as HTML: an opening bracket, the rendered children, a closing bracket, then the label in brackets, or an empty bracket pair for the collapsed form. No part of the children is respelled as source. The label is written from the key, so a label that wrapped has one space where the line break was. The attribute blocks glued to it are merged (C2-I-039) and written behind it as text, as one block in the fixed order (C2-H-139), so the HTML is a function of the tree: `[x][no]{.c}{#i}` gives `

[x][no]{#i .c}

`. 0.1 wrote the blocks as typed (U-371). Lint reports a full or collapsed reference that resolves to nothing with `unresolved-reference-link`.
A footnote reference and an inline footnote inside an unresolved reference are ordinary footnotes: each takes its number and makes its note.

An inline footnote, inline extension, footnote reference, citation form, sigil form, task box in marker position and every other bracket construct of this chapter keep their own reading over a shortcut.

`[^`, a label and `]` form a footnote reference. The label is one or more characters up to the next `]`, its key follows C2-I-079, and it may wrap (C2-I-080). The label follows C2-I-076 and C2-I-077. A footnote reference takes no link tail and no reference label: `(` or `[` directly behind it starts ordinary text or the next construct, so `[^n](/u)` is a footnote reference and the text `(/u)`. Where the label is none (C2-I-079), the `[` is text and opens no bracket pair, so a link tail behind it forms nothing.

A footnote reference with no definition renders its brackets, the caret and its label as literal text (C2-I-085). The attribute blocks glued to it follow as C2-I-085 says, in the fixed order: `[^x]{.c}{#i}` gives `

[^x]{#i .c}

`, where 0.1 wrote them as typed (U-207). Lint reports the reference with `unresolved-footnote`.

`^[` opens an inline footnote that closes at its matching bracket on the bracket stack. Its content is inline content, in which `[^` opens no footnote reference and `^[` no inline footnote, at any depth: in both the caret is text and the bracket an ordinary bracket, so `[^1]` and `^[b]` there are text and `[^1](u)` is a link. Unclosed, the two characters are text.
A sigil starts a form only at the start of the content or after a character outside the Unicode letter-or-number class.
The name is ASCII and is the longest run that fits its shape. A sigil with no such name is text, and so is whatever follows a name.

The name of a mention or a tag is one or more runs of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, joined by single dots, and holds at least one letter. It does not end with a dot or a hyphen: a trailing one is text behind the name.
A symbol is `:`, a name and `:`. The name is a letter, a digit, `+` or `-`, then letters, digits, `_`, `+` and `-`. It does not end with a hyphen.

An inline extension is `:`, a name, `[`, content and the matching `]`. The name is a letter or `_`, then letters, digits, `_` and `-`, and the bracket is glued to it. The content is inline content. Unclosed, the form is text.
A mention, a tag and a symbol are atoms. An inline extension is a bracket construct.
`</#`, an id and `>` form a cross-reference. The id is one or more characters without `>`, a space and a line break. It is an atom.

The id is matched exactly, without case folding, once it and the ids it is matched against are normalized to NFC, so a precomposed and a decomposed character match and `ﬁ` and `fi` do not. An unresolved cross-reference is written as the characters typed.
Each occurrence of a defined term in the ordinary text of the inline flow, at any depth of markup, is an abbreviation node that carries the expansion.

A term matches only as a whole word: the character on each side is absent or is not a word character. An element edge is no boundary of its own. An atom is a boundary, and so are the edges of an inline footnote; a braced comment is transparent (C2-I-026), so in `HTML{%x%}s` the term does not match.

Citations are a Tier 2 extension and have no core form. In the core, a bracket pair whose content starts with an at-sign and a key, and that no link tail and no reference label follows, forms no construct, even when a link definition matches its folded content. The brackets are text and the key is read as a mention (C2-I-078, C2-I-090). With a tail or a label the pair is a link like any other (C2-I-066), so `[@a](/u)` is a link whose text holds a mention.

A backslash at the end of a line is a hard break, also where the space behind it that C2-I-002 keeps ends the line. So is a backslash at the end of the content, which includes the end of a table cell.
Every other line break inside a content is a soft break. The spaces and tabs before it and after it are dropped, so trailing spaces on a line never make a hard break.

A straight quote, `"` or `'`, is read from its two neighbors alone, as C2-I-117 defines them: the characters of the same text on each side of it. A mark of a delimiter, a bracket that belongs to a construct and an atom are no neighbors, and a braced comment is transparent (C2-I-026). A no-break space and a hard break are whitespace (C2-I-011, C2-I-102). A quote opens when the neighbor before it is whitespace or opening punctuation, or when it has none because the quote stands at the start of the content or directly behind an opening mark or bracket. Otherwise it closes, also directly behind a closing mark, a closing bracket or an atom. Opening punctuation is one of `(`, `[`, `{`, `=`, `:`, `“` and `‘`, or a straight quote that opens. No quote looks past its neighbors and none depends on another quote that is not its neighbor: quotes do not pair, so an opening quote without a closing quote stays an opening quote.

A run of two or more hyphens becomes dashes: a length divisible by three gives em dashes, otherwise a length divisible by two gives en dashes, otherwise one em dash followed by the rest under the same rule. The rule has no exception for the place of the run: `run --verbose` holds an en dash, and a command-line flag in prose is written in a code span or with an escape, `-\-verbose`. In 0.1 a run after whitespace and before a letter stayed as typed, and `{--}` spelled the en dash there; both are gone, and `{--}` is now an opening brace, an en dash and a closing brace.
Three dots become an ellipsis.

Six runs become arrows: `-->`, `<--`, `<-->`, `==>`, `<==` and `<=>`. The longest match is taken, among these runs and the runs of C2-I-117 together, so `<=>` is the arrow and not `<=` followed by `>`. The single forms `->`, `<-` and `=>` are text. Only replaced runs take part in the match: `->`, `<-` and `=>` take no characters, so `->=` holds the text `-` and the sign for `>=`.

`!=`, `<=` and `>=` become the comparison signs, `+-` becomes the plus-minus sign and `(tm)` the trademark sign. `+-` needs its exact run, as an arrow of hyphens does (C2-I-116): next to another `+` or `-` it is text, so `C++-style` stays as typed. `(c)` and `(r)` are text. For this test and for the exact run of an arrow of hyphens (C2-I-116), the neighbors are the characters of the same text on each side of the run: the mark of a delimiter, opening or closing, is never a neighbor, and a braced comment between two characters is transparent (C2-I-026). So `{++-+}` inserts a plus-minus sign.

Inline nesting stops at depth 200 in each inline content, whatever the blocks around it: the count starts at zero where the content starts (C2-I-120), and no block counts (C2-B-190). The depth of an opener is the number of entries open on the bracket stack and the delimiter stack together when the opener is read. Every opening bracket, `^[`, extension bracket and delimiter opener that was pushed and is not yet closed or removed counts one, whether or not it later forms a construct. An opener read while 200 entries are open is text: it is not pushed and takes part in no pairing, and the scan goes on behind it. The limit counts openers only: a delimiter that can close is tested as a closer first (C2-I-051), also while 200 entries are open, and closes as it would below the limit, inside its bracket (C2-I-007); only a delimiter that closes nothing and can open is an opener the limit makes text. A later closer pairs as if that opener were not there, so a closing bracket pairs with the nearest pushed bracket or is text when there is none, and no closing bracket carries an attribute block onto a construct that never formed. Nothing read after the opener changes the decision.

A form with a closer opens only when its closer is found in the same content. A failed opener is literal text, and the scan goes on directly behind it. An opening brace that fails as an attribute block is first tried as the later braced forms (C2-I-043) and is text only when it opens none of them.
No inline form crosses the end of its content: a table cell and each fragment of a continuation row (C2-B-184), a heading, a term, a caption and a paragraph each end every form that is open in them.

A display math span is `$$`, a backtick run, the content and a closing backtick run of the opener's length (C2-I-019, C2-I-015). A line consists of exactly one display math span when it starts with `$$` and the opening run, the closing run stands on the same line, and nothing follows it but attribute blocks glued to it and trailing whitespace.

Every engine offers the calls of the section "Library" and the program of the section "Commands". A port spells a call, a result field and an error by the convention of its language, as it spells an option (C2-H-137).
The program is `carve`. An engine that installs it beside a 0.1 program may give it another name: the reference engine names it `carve2` on `next2`.

Outside this specification are the Markdown, GFM and Djot importers of the reference engine (`--from markdown`, `gfm` and `djot`), its `upgrade` command, which is part of the JavaScript engine only and is described in `UPGRADING.md` ("Running the rewrite tool"), and its scanner and event helpers. An engine may offer further commands, flags, flag values and calls; none of them takes a name of `data/cli.json` with another meaning.

`data/cli.json` holds the commands, flags, failure categories, calls and entry fields of this document. A row is normative together with the clauses it cites; where a row and its clause disagree, the clause wins.

An engine offers the calls of this table. Each reads the options of `data/options.json` whose `read_by` names a stage the call runs and refuses the others (C2-H-137). `decodeTree` and `validateTree` read `extensions` as the registered standard extensions for their tree reader checks (C2-X-038).
A call refuses with the typed error of its row in the table of C2-T-040, and with no other error; the command line turns that error into the category of the row.
A command line is `carve [COMMAND] [FLAG...] [FILE...]`, and its commands are the rows of this table. With no command it is `render`.

A flag is `--name value` or `--name=value`. A switch is `--name` and takes no value; `--no-name` turns it off. `--` ends the flags, and every argument after it is a file. A flag that the table of its command does not list is refused with the category `usage`.
A flag given twice takes its last value, except `--allow-loss`, which collects every value.

A flag that sets an option is named by the option in lower case with hyphens, so `urlPolicy` is `--url-policy`: a `boolean` option is a switch, an `enum` option takes one of its values, and a `list`, `map` or `structure` option takes JSON text. The one option set otherwise is `includes`, which `--includes` and `--include-root` set (C2-T-018). `extensions` and `renderers` take host code, which JSON text cannot name, so they have no flag: they are options of the library calls only (C2-T-005). A value the option refuses is refused with the category `usage`. An option that the table of a command lists no flag for, or whose flag is not given, has its default; for `includes` C2-T-018 says what holds.
A file is a path, or `-` for standard input. A command with no file reads standard input. The files are read in order, and the outputs of the files follow each other on standard output.

Carve source is read as bytes and is never refused for its encoding (C2-B-218). A tree in JSON is read as strict UTF-8, and a file that is not is refused with the category `input-unreadable`. HTML is read as UTF-8.
A line or a report names a file by its path as given and standard input as `<stdin>` (C2-W-100).

Standard output carries the product of the command and nothing else. The product of `lint` and `diagnostics` is their entries, as lines or as a report, and that of `fmt --check` and `fmt --diff` the report of C2-W-100; every other line of a diagnostic, a note or a failure goes to standard error.

A report flag takes a path, or `-` for standard error. The report is one JSON document for the whole run, followed by a line feed. After repeated instances of one flag have been reduced by C2-T-009, the collision and order rules of this clause apply. Two report flags of one run whose paths resolve to the same absolute path, against the working directory and with `.` and `..` segments removed, are refused with the category `usage` before any input is read. Two report flags with `-` are not refused: both reports go to standard error at the end of the run, in the order of the flags on the command line.
`--write` replaces each file whose output differs from it and leaves the others untouched. With standard input among the files it is refused with the category `usage`.
A failure of status 2 stops the run at its file; what earlier files wrote stays written. Otherwise the status of a run is the highest status of its files.

`render`, `ast`, `lint` and `diagnostics` expand includes as C2-N-004 and C2-N-085 state, through the resolver of C2-N-012. `--no-includes` turns expansion off and `--include-root` names the root. `fmt`, `import` and `migrate-ast` expand nothing (C2-N-005), and neither does a command that reads a tree with `--from-ast`.

A diagnostic line is `FILE:LINE:COLUMN: SEVERITY CODE MESSAGE`, and an entry with no range is written `FILE: SEVERITY CODE MESSAGE`. FILE is the `file` of the entry where it has one (C2-N-063) and the input otherwise. LINE counts line feeds from 1, and COLUMN counts the code points of that line from 1, both at the start of the range.

An entry of the record (C2-A-173) is a JSON object with the fields of this table. The library gives every field but `line` and `column`; the command line adds those two where the entry has a range. The `message` is the text of the engine, for which the catalog row gives the reference wording (C2-W-106); a comparison of two reports does not compare it. A conformance case that states `messageWhen` compares the selected catalog condition separately, as C2-W-106 defines it.

A diagnostics report is `{"files": [...]}` with one object per file in order: `file`, the name of C2-T-013; `diagnostics`, the retained entries in the order of the record; and `suppressed`, the number of entries of that file a cap held back (C2-T-024, C2-T-029). `diagnostics --json`, `lint --json` and `--report-losses` write it.

An include report is `{"files": [...]}` with one object per file in order: `file`, and `dependencies`, the dependencies of its tree (C2-N-083), each an object of `path`, `from` (the including file, absent for the top-level document), `file` (absent where the include was not read) and `read`. A host that watches files reads it as C2-N-084 says. `--report-includes` writes it.
Reports are compared as JSON values: the order of the members of an object is no contract, and the order of a list is.

An expansion retains at most `include_diagnostics` of `data/limits.json`, 100, entries whose code is the code of a cause in `data/includes.json`, the first in the order the failures occur. The result of a call that returns a record gives the number of the others as `suppressedDiagnostics`, 0 where there are none, and the command line counts them in `suppressed` (C2-T-021). An include whose entry is held back stays unexpanded as C2-N-061 says.

A loss is a render-loss entry of a file whose code is not on the allow list. `render` writes each retained loss as a line on standard error, and no entry of the parse or the lint channel, which `diagnostics` and `lint` write (C2-T-031, C2-T-032).

With `--strict-losses` and a loss, `render` writes no HTML for that file and the file ends with status 1 and the category `render-loss` (C2-H-130). The command applies the allow list before `strictLosses`, so an allowed code alone never fails a file.

`--allow-loss` takes a code of the render-loss channel of `data/lint-rules.json`; any other value is refused with the category `usage`. An allowed code is neither written on standard error nor in the report.
`--report-losses` writes the losses of the run, and without a loss it writes the report with empty lists.

`--max-render-losses` takes a count, a decimal integer of at least 0, and its default is 100. Each file retains its first losses up to that count; the others are counted in `suppressed` and written on no line.

`fmt` refuses `--write` with `--check` or with `--diff`, `--check` with `--diff`, and `--normalize` with `--from-ast`, with the category `usage`. Without one of `--check`, `--diff` and `--write` it writes the output on standard output. A writer loss of C2-W-134 ends the file with status 1 and the category `writer-refused`.

`lint` writes the entries that the call `lint` returns, as lines or as a report, and ends a file with status 1 when an entry has the severity `warning` or `error`; a run of hints alone ends with 0. The call `lint` returns the record of its run (C2-W-103): the entries of its parse in the parse channel and its findings in the lint channel (C2-W-113), as 0.1 lint reported an unclosed fence. A rule that is off by default, as each `djot-` rule is, is turned on by its id in `--rules`.
`diagnostics` writes the entries of the parse channel and ends with status 0 whatever they report.
`import` without `--from` is refused with the category `usage`. The value `html` reads the input as C2-M-001 states; the reference engine also takes `markdown`, `gfm` and `djot` (C2-T-003).

`import` applies C2-T-025 to C2-T-029 to the entries of the importer (C2-M-080) and of the writer: with `--strict-losses` a loss of either fails the file with the category `render-loss` and writes no source. Without it, a writer loss of C2-W-134 fails the file with the category `writer-refused`.

An HTML input the importer refuses ends the run with status 2 and the category `import-input-invalid` (C2-M-006). A tree of the importer that fails the reader checks (C2-A-188) is a defect of the importer, and the file ends with status 1 and the category `import-tree-invalid`.

`migrate-ast` writes the migrated tree, as an envelope when the input was one (C2-A-012), and writes each entry of the migration record as a line on standard error (C2-A-180). It ends with status 0, and with status 2 and the category `ast-json-invalid` for an input it cannot read as a tree.
A run ends with status 0 when every file did what was asked and nothing it gates on was found.
A run ends with status 1 and no category when `fmt --check` or `fmt --diff` finds a file that would change (C2-W-100), or `lint` finds an entry of severity `warning` or `error` (C2-T-031).
Every failure with a category in C2-T-040 writes as its first line on standard error `carve[CATEGORY]:` and a message (C2-W-101).
The failure categories, their status and the library error each comes from are the rows of this table.
The writer takes a tree and, optionally, the sidecar that was returned with that tree (C2-L-004). It returns Carve source. `carve fmt` parses its input with the sidecar and writes the result.

For every document `x` that the writer does not refuse (C2-W-016, C2-W-133), `parse(fmt(x)) == parse(x)` under the tree equality of the AST document (C2-A-161, C2-A-162). For a supplied tree `t`, `parse(write(t)) == t` holds when the writer reports no loss (C2-W-011). Root `metadata.fields` with a frontmatter node is an exception: the writer preserves that raw node and does not report `fields`, although a new parse omits them. The source form of an extension that a writer without the extension writes is the other exception (C2-X-023). This is a gate on every pull request.
For every document `x`, `fmt(fmt(x)) == fmt(x)`, byte for byte. This is a gate on every pull request.

A `format` or `write` call that returns only source throws `CarveWriteError` if the diagnostic writer reports `field-unspellable`, `structure-unspellable` or `writer-refused`. The error carries those diagnostics. `formatWithDiagnostics` and `writeWithDiagnostics` return the nearest source and the report. A nearest source that may change on another pass is never returned by a call that cannot carry its loss report.

Equal trees render equal HTML under the same render options and the same source length (C2-H-201), so `fmt` never changes the rendered output, except where it changes the length of the source and the derived-text budget of C2-H-201 binds. The HTML check is a consequence of C2-W-002 and is weaker: a writer that keeps the HTML and changes the tree fails.

The gates outrank every per-construct clause below. Where the spelling a clause names would not parse back to the tree it was written from, the writer takes the smallest departure that restores the tree, and another spelling of the same construct is preferred over a different construct. Such a deviation is conformant.
The test is made on the emitted bytes of the whole output. A construct is not tested alone, because an opener depends on the lines before it.
The writer does not replace one construct by another that renders alike. It does not drop content, move content or re-wrap prose: a soft break stays where the tree has it.
A backslash escape is not a node (C2-A-041), so an escape that the writer adds or removes never changes the tree.
The writer keeps what the tree holds (C2-W-002), takes from the sidecar the author's form where 0.2 has two equal forms (C2-W-083), and writes the one canonical form everywhere else.

This document defines the output. How a writer finds it, by trial and reparse or by an exact test, is its own choice and has no effect on the bytes. Its work on one text grows at most linearly with the length of the text: the procedure of C2-W-088 run as stated, one parse of the whole text for each escape, does not meet this bound on a text that needs many escapes, such as `\[x]` written N times under a definition of `x`. The bound holds with the refusal of C2-W-133: a writer that decides what it can from tables and parses again for the rest (C2-W-089) counts the characters those parses read against its repair limit, and refuses a group that exceeds it. A limit linear in the group, such as the floor of C2-W-133, keeps the work linear, and a refused group is outside byte conformance (C2-W-133).

A Carve writer reports every supplied node or field that source cannot spell with `structure-unspellable` or `field-unspellable`, naming its JSON path (C2-A-175). This includes `scope`, `headerIds`, `longDescription`, `decorative`, `xref.display` and root `metadata.fields`. A parse of Carve source produces none of them. Frontmatter is raw source text and is never parsed into `fields`. When a document has a frontmatter node, the writer writes that node unchanged and reports no separate loss for `fields`; otherwise it reports `metadata.fields` under this rule.

The table of C2-A-175 is not the whole list. For every node, field and value of a supplied tree that no clause of this document writes in a form that reads back to the same value, the writer writes the nearest form it can spell, or leaves the node or field out, and reports the loss: `field-unspellable` for a field, `structure-unspellable` for a node. No such loss is silent. Among these are: a frontmatter value that holds a line of three hyphens, and a frontmatter format that does not have the shape of a format name (C2-B-164); `spacing: "loose"` on a list of one item; a caption with more than one block; a class that holds a space, a tab or a line break; a definition key that holds a closing bracket with no backslash before it, or that folds to nothing; an abbreviation definition whose key is not one or more ASCII letters and digits, or whose expansion is empty, ends with a space or a tab, or holds a line break (C2-B-084, C2-W-055); a line comment whose value holds a line break or ends with a space or a tab; a `non_breaking_space` node at the end of a table cell (C2-I-002); a code span, a literal-text span or a math span whose value starts with a line break and ends with a backtick (C2-W-077); a paragraph, a list or a description list with no children; a `figure_group` anywhere inside another `figure_group`, which reads back as a div (C2-B-127); `directive.tocTarget`; an `autolink` whose `text` is no email address or whose `href` is not `mailto:` followed by that `text`; an `abbreviation` with no definition of its key in the document; a mention with a `label` or a kind other than `user`; and `metadata`, except `metadata.fields` with a frontmatter node under C2-W-011.

Where a field that cannot be spelled makes its whole node read back as another type, as a frontmatter `format` that is no format name does, the report is `structure-unspellable` at that node. A loss is reported at the node that did not read back, not at a wrapper around it.

Where blocks are written into a slot that holds only inline content, such as a caption, a title, a cell or a term, the writer puts a separator between the content of two former blocks, so that no word and no delimiter run is joined across the boundary.
Where the whole content of a block is one node whose own spelling at the block's column reads back as a block of another kind, the wrapper is lost. The loss is reported and never silent.
The loss of such a bare wrapper is the only structural difference the gates forgive for a supplied tree. A wrapper that carries attributes, a label, a destination, a level or a kind is not bare.

A paragraph promoted to a block image is written as its source spelling, the image alone on its line. `role: "image"` is a fact of the tree (C2-A-136), and the written line gives it back when it is parsed.

A line after the first of a code span, a raw span, a literal-text span, a math span, a braced comment or an editorial comment is a line of its leaf. Where that line would open a block (C2-B-014 to C2-B-019), or would be a comment-only line because it starts with `%%` after its spaces and tabs (C2-B-137, C2-B-138), no spelling keeps the value, and the writer refuses it with `field-unspellable`. A lone CR as the last character of a line is refused the same way: the writer ends every line with LF, and a CR directly before an LF is part of the line ending and no content (C2-B-010), so `a` and a CR at the end of the input has no canonical spelling.

Two code spans with nothing between them have no spelling: written together, the two runs read as one span. A parse never gives that pair. For a supplied tree the writer reports `structure-unspellable` for the second span and writes its content into the first.

A math block is written as its display math span alone on its line, with an attached attribute block glued to the span (C2-B-198). The mark `role: "math"` is a fact of the tree (C2-A-184), and the written line gives it back when it is parsed.
One blank line stands between two sibling blocks. This is requirement W1 of the migrate design.

A run of blank lines is written as one blank line, except the three of C2-W-028. Blank lines inside verbatim content, which is the value of a code block, a raw block, a comment block and frontmatter, are data and are written as they are.
No line of the output holds only spaces or tabs: such a line is written empty. A line of a code block, a raw block or a comment block is data and is written as it is.

No space or tab is written at the end of a line outside verbatim content or a delimited table body (C2-W-066), and the output ends with one line ending. A no-break space directly before a soft break or at the end of the content has no spelling, since a backslash and a space at the end of a line are a hard break (C2-I-011): its nearest form writes the character U+00A0, and the writer reports `structure-unspellable` (C2-W-117).

Every block of an item, a description or a footnote body after the marker line is written at the content column, and every continuation line of a paragraph in it is written at that column too. A continuation line of a caption or of a term is written at the column of the first character of its text, behind the mark and its space. The markers of one list stand at one column. This is requirement W3, and it replaces the lazy and the indented continuation styles of the source.
Continuation lines of an ordered item with a task box are indented to the width of its marker and marker padding, as for every other item. The task box does not increase that indent.

When a table with no attribute line follows a list, description list or footnote across a line comment, the writer puts `{footer-rows=0}` above the comment. That line closes the preceding container and leaves the table tree unchanged.

When a named div follows a list, description list or footnote across a line comment and its first class is its only attribute, the writer puts that class in an attribute line above the comment and writes the div with an unnamed opener.
One space follows a list marker. An uppercase marker with a dot takes two (C2-B-040), and the content column moves with it.
A continuation line whose text would read as a list marker is kept text by an escape, not by a smaller indent.
An item, a description or a footnote body whose first block is not a paragraph is written with that block's opener on the marker line (C2-B-057, C2-B-072). This is requirement W8.

Two adjacent lists of the same kind in one container are separated by exactly three blank lines (C2-B-052). The writer does not change a bullet character or a delimiter to separate them, because both are meaning (C2-L-032, C2-B-037). Adjacent ordered lists of different styles are separated in the same way when the first written marker of the second would be a sibling of the first list (C2-B-038, C2-B-039, C2-B-049); otherwise they need no extra blank lines. This is requirement W4.

Where a comment stands between two lists of one kind, the comment is written by its own rule (C2-W-059) and the three blank lines stand between the comment and the second list, except when attribute lines of the second list stand above the comment. In that case the attribute lines and any consecutive line comments follow the preceding list after one blank line, since directly below the last paragraph of the list an attribute line is a lazy line of that paragraph (C2-B-024, blocks Example 264). A line comment can follow a list, a description list or a footnote body as a sibling in two cases. One is C2-W-123. The other is a comment that stands below the attribute lines of the next block: those lines are written above the comment, as the source had them, after that blank line, since the attribute line then closes the list and the comment belongs to the container (C2-B-091). In every other place the comment line belongs to the last item (C2-B-138), a parse never gives that tree, and for a supplied tree the writer reports `structure-unspellable` (C2-W-117).
Two lists are adjacent for C2-W-028 also when every block between them writes nothing.

A loose list is written with one blank line between all of its items. A tight list is written with none, also when an item holds several blocks: the blank line then stands inside the item, before its later block. This is requirement W5.
A quote written with `>` lines carries `> ` on every line of its content and a bare `>` on a blank line inside it.

A div, an admonition or a hard-break block with an empty body is written with one blank line between opener and closer. An empty line block is written with its closer directly below its opener, because a blank line in it is a `line` (C2-A-069).

Every fence, div and comment block is written with its closer, also when the source left it unclosed, except the fence of C2-W-123. A supplied code or raw block whose value has no final line break (C2-A-047) is written with one, and the writer reports `field-unspellable` for `value`. The closer stands at the column of its opener. The closer of a code fence and of a comment block is a bare run of the opener's length (C2-B-110).

A line comment that is a region marker of an include (`#region`, `#endregion`) keeps its line: the writer moves no marker and opens no new line beside one. As in 0.1 (CARVE-P11-073). Since the line ends a paragraph (C2-B-137), a marker among the inline children of a supplied paragraph has no spelling, and the writer reports `structure-unspellable`. A marker that follows another block is a sibling block, and one blank line stands before it (C2-W-017): `a` directly above `%% #endregion` is written with a blank line between, as the tree is the same with or without it.
In a description list no blank line stands between a term and its description or between two entries. A later block of a description follows one blank line, at the content column.

A heading is written with `=`, one per level, and one space. A `#` in the source is rewritten. A level above six, which only a supplied tree holds (C2-A-071), is written with six markers, and the writer reports `field-unspellable` for `level`. A line break inside a heading is kept, and each continuation line is written at the heading's content column, that is the marker width plus one (C2-B-154).
A thematic break is written as `***`.

A code block is written with a backtick fence of the length C2-W-038 states. An info string that holds a backtick has no spelling (C2-B-118): a parse never gives one, and for a supplied tree the writer leaves it out and reports `field-unspellable`.

The fence of a code block and of a raw block is the shortest run of at least three backticks that is longer than every bare backtick run on a line of the value, at any indent (C2-B-109 has no column test). This is requirement W6.

A div is written with the shortest colon run of at least three that is longer than the run of every div inside it. The name of an admonition or a directive is its kind. The name of a plain div is its first class, when that class has the shape of a div name and is not one of the names that C2-B-127 gives another meaning; otherwise the div has no name, and all of its classes stand on the attribute line. A writer with an enabled extension matcher keeps the first class on the attribute line when that matcher would claim a div named by it (C2-X-008). The opener of a div, an admonition or a directive is the run, then one space and the name when there is one, then one space and the quoted title when there is one, then one space and the label in brackets when there is one. A raw block is written as a backtick fence whose run is glued to `=` and the format name, with nothing after it.

A class has the shape of a div name when it holds only ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-` (C2-I-030) and is none of the names of `data/div-names.json`. Any other first class stands on the attribute line, which gives the same tree (C2-B-128).

A title is written with a backslash before each double quote and before each backslash that stands before ASCII punctuation or at its end, since the title reads escapes (C2-I-033, C2-A-073). A title that holds a line break and a label that holds a closing bracket or a line break have no spelling on an opener (C2-B-117, C2-B-119): the writer leaves that field out and reports `field-unspellable` for it. The opener of a code fence is the run, glued to the language word, then one space and the quoted title when there is one, then one space and the label in brackets when there is one: ```` ```php "src/Auth.php" [Composer] ````.
The title of a code block is written in the info string, in double quotes.

A decimal list is written with the numbering form the sidecar records (C2-L-016): the bare dot, or sequential digits from the start value. In the bare form a start value other than 1 stands in a `start` attribute above the list (C2-L-030); in the numbered form the first marker carries it. A start value of more than nine digits cannot be a marker (C2-B-036) and cannot be a `start` attribute (C2-B-219), and a reader refuses it (C2-A-056). A list of repeated `1.` markers is renumbered to sequential digits. A later marker whose number would have more than nine digits is written as `1`: only the first marker carries a value (C2-B-041). With no sidecar fact the bare dot is written (C2-L-030). The bare dot is written only for a list whose delimiter is the period: a decimal list with `)` is written with sequential digits, because a bare `)` is not a marker (C2-B-036, C2-L-031). A bare dot is not written directly behind a bare-dot marker on the marker line, where it would read as text (C2-B-043): there the inner list is written with digits, as in `. 1. a`.

A list whose style is not decimal is written with its letters or numerals in sequence (C2-L-031). Where the first marker so written would read as another style (C2-B-042), which is an alphabetic list that starts at `i` or `I` and a roman list that starts at a one-letter numeral other than `i` or `I`, the list is written from the first value of its style, `a` or `i` in its letter case, under a `start` attribute that carries the real value (C2-B-045). A later single roman letter stays in an open roman list (C2-B-038), and every single letter stays in an open alphabetic list (C2-B-039). Only the first marker carries a value (C2-B-041), so a later marker that the marker grammar cannot hold, a letter past `z` or a numeral of more than nine letters (C2-B-036), is written as the first value of its style, and a first marker of that kind moves its value to the `start` attribute in the same way.
A task item is written with the character in `task.mark` (C2-A-060). The tree holds `x` for an authored `X`, so `[X]` comes back as `[x]`.

The attributes of a block are written as one brace block on one line directly above the block, with no blank line between. Glued blocks and consecutive attribute lines of the source are merged into it (C2-B-093, C2-B-102). This is part of requirement W7.

Inside a brace block the parts are written in the order id, classes, language, keys, classes and keys each in tree order, with one space between two parts and none inside the braces. The language is written as `:tag` (C2-I-029, C2-A-037). A class that the `.name` form cannot hold, such as `a.b`, is written as a quoted `class` key at its place among the classes (C2-I-042).

A key whose value is the empty string is written as the bare key: `{kbd}`, not `{kbd=""}`. A key that starts with `_` is written with an empty quoted value, `{_k=""}`, because a bare key does not start with `_` (C2-I-031).
A value is written unquoted when it has the shape of an unquoted value (C2-I-032), and in double quotes otherwise.
The attributes of a list item and of a table cell are written glued to the marker (C2-B-101).

Frontmatter whose format is `yaml` is written with the bare opener `---`, also when the source named the format. Every other format, `YAML` included, keeps its format name glued to the opener: `---toml`, `---json` (C2-B-164). The form with a space before the name, `--- toml`, is read too (C2-B-164) and is written glued. The body is written as it is.
A caption is written directly below its block, with no blank line (C2-B-146), as `^`, one space and its content. This is part of requirement W7.

A definition is written at column 0 at its place among the children of the document (C2-A-052). A footnote definition is `[^key]:`, one space and its first block on the marker line, with its later blocks at the content column (C2-W-024, C2-W-027). An abbreviation definition is `*[key]:`, one space and the expansion, whose leading spaces and tabs are written after that space. An expansion of a supplied tree that holds a line break has no spelling: its nearest form writes one space in place of each line break, so the definition stays one line, and the writer reports `field-unspellable` (C2-W-117). The writer does not move definitions to the end and does not sort them, because their order is part of the tree (C2-A-080).

A link definition is written as `[label]:`, one space, the destination and, when there is one, one space and the title in double quotes. A parsed tree has no link definition with an empty destination, because such a line is text (C2-B-083). For a supplied one the writer reports `field-unspellable`.

There is no sentinel for an empty body. A parsed item, description or term is never empty: the empty spelling is a marker plus a comment (C2-B-145), and the comment is a node. A footnote body is never empty either, because its marker needs content on its line (C2-B-082). An empty body in a supplied tree has no spelling, and the writer reports `structure-unspellable` for it.

An include writes its decoded `options` in the rank order of `data/include-options.json`: `lines`, `region`, `rows`, `cols`, `shift`, `code`. A range writes its range text, a list of column names writes a quoted comma-separated list with escapes, an integer writes decimal, `auto` writes `auto`, and `code: true` writes `@code` without a value. Original quote and escape spelling comes from the source-layout record (C2-L-055). The entries of `invalid` follow the options, each after one space and as the tree holds it (C2-A-181). An entry that would not read back as the same invalid option, such as `@lines:1-2` with no `lines` before it, has no spelling and is reported (C2-W-117). A path is quoted when its bare form cannot hold it (C2-B-202); a double quote and a backslash in it are escaped with a backslash. A path with a line break is unspellable and reported (C2-W-117). The writer never writes the `children` or the `file` of an expanded include, and reports no loss for them (C2-N-080).

A comment is written in its `form` (C2-A-074): `%% text` for a line comment, with the one space the reader removes again (C2-A-074) and with no space when the value is empty, a `%%%` block for a block comment, whose opener and closer are the shortest run of at least three percent signs that is longer than every bare percent run in its body (C2-B-110), `{% text %}` for a braced comment, and `{%%}` when its value is empty. A comment-only line is written at the column of the leaf or container that holds its node (C2-B-138). A comment that a container holds is written after one blank line when the block before it ends in a paragraph, a heading, a term or a caption, because without the blank line the comment would be a lazy line or a child of that leaf and move into it (C2-B-024, C2-B-138), and when the block before it is a table, because the comment would become a child of the table (C2-A-086); a comment that stands between a figure group and its caption is written between the closer of the group and the caption line, and so is a comment that is the sibling after a code block with a caption (C2-A-082); in every other place it stands directly below the block before it. Where a block of the same item follows the comment, that blank line stands inside the item and does not make the list loose (C2-W-030).
A term is written as `::`, one space and its content. A description is written as `:`, one space and its first block, and its later blocks at the content column.
A table row is written as a pipe, its cells, and a closing pipe. Every row ends with a pipe (C2-B-166).

A cell is written as its prefix glued to the opening pipe, one space, its content and one space before the next pipe. The prefix is the header mark `=` when the cell is a header cell, then the brace block when the cell has alignment or attributes; in that brace block the alignment marks stand first, the horizontal mark and then the vertical mark, and `?` stands in place of the horizontal mark where the cell has a `valign` other than `baseline` and no `align`: `|={>} Price |`, `|={>^} Price |`, `|{?v} 2 |`. A mark is written from the cell's own `align` and `valign` only; an alignment the cell takes from its column is not written on it (C2-B-213). A `valign` of `baseline` has no mark: the writer leaves it out and reports `field-unspellable` (C2-W-117). The space after the prefix is written also where the content is empty, `|= |`; after a header mark with no brace block it is what keeps the mark a mark before text (C2-B-171). A data cell whose text starts with `=` needs no escape: its padding space keeps the `=` off the pipe, `| =SUM(A1) |`.

A span mark is written with the same padding: `| ^ |`, `| < |`. In the head it carries the header mark, `|= ^ |`, so that a row of span marks stays a head row (C2-B-174). A cell whose content is only `^` or `<` and is not a span is written with an escape.
A row is written with exactly the cells it has. The writer adds no empty cell to make the rows equally wide.
A row attribute is written glued to the closing pipe (C2-B-167).

A table is written in the form the sidecar records, pipe or delimited (C2-L-023), when the tree allows it. With no fact it is a pipe table, and a table with no rows is a delimited table (C2-L-036). Where a delimited table is written and no fact names its format, the format is `csv`. A delimited table is written with a `header-rows` attribute, whose value is the number of rows of its head, 0 for a table with rows and no head, where the head is not exactly the first row, the default of the form (C2-B-209), and where the sidecar records `headerRows` with that number (C2-L-057). A table with no rows has an empty head, which is the default, and takes no `header-rows`. A pipe table never takes the attribute: its header cells make its head (C2-B-178). In a delimited table a cell that holds the separator, a double quote or a line break is written in double quotes with each double quote doubled, and so is an empty cell that is the only cell of the last row, which an empty line would drop (C2-B-226); every other cell is written bare. A cell that holds only one space is therefore written as a bare space line inside the delimited table body (C2-W-022).

Continuation rows are written at the places the sidecar records (C2-L-019, C2-L-020). With no fact a row is one line (C2-L-035). A node in a pipe table cell whose value holds a line feed, which only a supplied tree gives, has no spelling there: the writer writes a space in place of each line feed and reports `field-unspellable` (C2-W-117). A delimited table writes a cell that holds a line break in double quotes (C2-W-066).

The option `alignTables` pads the cells of each column to one display width. It is off by default, the tree is the same with it on, and the two gates hold in that mode too. As in 0.1 (CARVE-P11-071). C2-W-118 and C2-W-119 state the padding and the width.

With `alignTables`, each cell of each line of a pipe table is a segment: the cell prefix, one space, the content as the writer spells it on that line, and one space.
