An empty cell is its prefix and one space. A span mark is the content of its own cell. On a continuation line the leading `+` takes the place of the leading pipe and is outside the first segment. The width of a column is the largest display width (C2-W-119) of its segments over every line of the table, continuation lines included. Each segment is padded with spaces after it, before the next pipe, up to that width; no space is added before the content, also for a right or centered cell. A row attribute behind the last pipe, a caption and the lines around the table count toward no width. A table written with `alignTables` and formatted again in that mode keeps its bytes, and `carve fmt --check` in that mode compares the source with the aligned form.

The display width of a segment is the sum of the widths of its extended grapheme clusters, by UAX #29 of Unicode 18.0.0. A cluster has width 2 when any of its code points has the East Asian Width W or F of Unicode 18.0.0 (UAX #11), and width 1 otherwise, an ambiguous-width (A) cluster included. A padding space has width 1. These property values hold whatever Unicode version the host runtime has; the version is the one C2-I-127 pins for every Unicode property of the 0.2 documents.

A `comment` among the rows of a table, or after its last row, is written as a comment-only line at its place (C2-W-059). The trailing line comment of a row reads to the same tree as that line (C2-A-086), so the writer does not write the trailing form: `| 1 | 2 | %% note` is written as `| 1 | 2 |` and, on the next line, `%% note`. A comment that is the last child of the last group is written below the last row and its continuation rows and is followed by the empty continuation row `+ |`, which adds nothing to the row (C2-B-184) and keeps the comment in its group (C2-A-086): the tree of `| a |`, `%% x` and `+ b |` on three lines is written `| a b |`, `%% x` and `+ |`, and `fmt`, which keeps the continuation row of the source (C2-A-094), writes `| a |`, `+ b |`, `%% x` and `+ |`. That last row stands for every continuation row of the source that has only empty fragments, and `fmt` writes none of those again, so its output is formatted to the same bytes (C2-W-003).

A key `aligns`, `valigns`, `widths`, `header-rows`, `footer-rows`, `body-rows`, `body-header-rows` or `body-header-cols` that a table keeps in `attrs` (C2-B-227) is written once, from `attrs`, at its place among the keys (C2-W-048). The writer makes one of these keys from the table fields, as it makes `header-rows` from the groups (C2-W-066), only where `attrs` holds no key of that name. A table of more than one body, or with an empty body, a body that starts with rows of header cells or a `rowHeadColumns`, is written with `body-rows`, the data rows of each body; with `body-header-rows`, the leading rows of header cells of each body, where a body has them; and with `body-header-cols` where a body has `rowHeadColumns`. A body that lacks one of these takes the entry `0` in `body-header-rows` and an empty entry in `body-header-cols` (C2-B-230). The cells of those leading rows are written without header marks: the key makes them header cells, and a leading row of header marks would read as the head (C2-B-178). Where a supplied tree holds both, such as `aligns=x` in `attrs` and an `align` on a column, the two cannot be spelled as two keys of one name (C2-A-035): the writer writes the key from the table fields and reports the key in `attrs` as `field-unspellable` (C2-W-117).

Emphasis is written with `/` and strong with `*`. Where the bare delimiter would not open or close at that position (C2-I-047, C2-I-048), or the content holds the same delimiter in a position that would pair, the braced form is written: `{/usr/local/}`.
An emphasis or strong node with an ancestor or a descendant of its own kind is written in the braced form.
Underline, strike and highlight are written in their braced forms, `{_text_}`, `{~text~}` and `{=text=}`. They have no bare form in 0.2 (C2-I-046).
A link title is written in double quotes. Single quotes are rewritten to that form.
A link with an empty destination is written as `[text]()`, and an image as `![alt]()`. The writer adds no placeholder.

A reference is written with the verbatim text the sidecar records (C2-L-022), including its authored backslashes and without spaces and tabs at the end of a line of it (C2-W-022), when reading that text gives the node the tree holds: the same content, the same `key` and the same form (C2-L-006). Otherwise it is written from the tree: its content, then `[key]` for the form `full` or `[]` for the form `collapsed`, and no label tail for the form `shortcut` (C2-L-040). A key that starts with a caret or an at-sign is written with one space before it inside the label brackets, since a label whose first character is one of them is no reference label (C2-I-078) and the space folds away (C2-I-079).
An attribute block of an inline host is written glued to the host, as one block in the order of C2-W-048. Glued blocks of the source are merged (C2-I-039).

A code span is written with the shortest backtick run that does not occur in its content, and with one space of padding on each side when the content starts or ends with a backtick or with a space that C2-I-016 would remove. A value that starts with a line break and ends with a backtick has no spelling, since the pad before the line break is trailing whitespace (C2-I-002) and only the closing pad would stay, and a span without its closing run is text (C2-I-017). This holds for a literal-text span and a math span too, which are written as a code span with their prefix (C2-W-116). The writer writes the padded form and reports `field-unspellable` (C2-W-117).
A smart-punctuation node is written as its `source` (C2-A-098).

Every other inline node is written in the one spelling its syntax clause gives: a mention as `@name` and a tag as `#name` (C2-I-090), a symbol as `:name:` (C2-I-093), an unqualified inline extension as `:name[content]` (C2-I-094), superscript as `{^text^}` and subscript as `{,text,}` (C2-I-057), an insertion as `{+text+}` and a deletion as `{-text-}`, an editorial comment as `{#text#}` (C2-I-063), an inline footnote as `^[content]` (C2-I-089), a footnote reference as `[^label]` (C2-I-087), a cross-reference as `</#id>` (C2-I-096), an autolink as its target in angle brackets, which for the email form is its `text` (C2-I-073, C2-A-216), a no-break space as a backslash and a space (C2-I-011), a literal-text span as `!` glued to a code span (C2-I-018), raw inline as a code span with `{=format}` glued to it (C2-I-021), and an `abbreviation` as its `key`, the word as typed. A `caption_number` is written as `#`, the mark of C2-B-207; only its number is a resolution result (C2-A-133, C2-A-162) and is not written. An inline node that needs content and has none in a supplied tree, such as an emphasis, a span or a link text with no children where the syntax needs at least one character, has no spelling: the writer leaves it out and reports `structure-unspellable`. A `cell_paragraph` is written as the content of its cell (C2-W-062).
A hard break is written as a backslash at the end of the line.

A div with the class `hardbreaks` is written in the form the sidecar records (C2-L-018) when the tree allows it. With no fact the opener is used when every line break in the div is a hard break and `hardbreaks` is the last of its classes, and the class form otherwise (C2-L-034). The opener adds the class last (C2-A-068), so the opener form on any other div would change the tree. Where the opener is written, the class `hardbreaks` is not written on the attribute line: the opener stands for it. The class form is a div whose classes are written as for any div (C2-W-039): where `hardbreaks` is the first class it is the div name, as `{.x}` above `::: hardbreaks`.

A quote is written in the form the sidecar records, `>` lines or a quote fence (C2-L-017). With no fact it is written with `>` lines (C2-L-033). A quote with no children is written as one line that holds only `>`, or as a quote fence with no body where the sidecar records that form. A sigil div is written with one space between the colon run and its sigil: `::: >`, `::: |`, and the backslash for a hard-break block (C2-B-196).
The writer takes six spellings from the sidecar when the fact is present and the tree allows the form (C2-L-042):
The writer also takes `rawRef` (C2-W-075) and `optionSpelling` (C2-W-058).

The writer reads no other sidecar fact. The heading marker, the thematic break, the fence character and length, the frontmatter opener, the marker columns, the continuation style and the counts of blank lines are written in their canonical form whatever the sidecar records. The other facts of the sidecar are for editors and other tools (C2-L-046).
The tree wins: a fact that contradicts the tree is ignored (C2-L-006).
Both gates hold with and without a sidecar. `fmt` reads the sidecar of its own parse, so C2-W-003 is tested on that path.

The option `normalize` makes `fmt` write as if there were no sidecar: every spelling of C2-W-083 takes its form of the column "Without", a reference is written from its key and not from `rawRef`, and an include option from its value and not from `optionSpelling` (C2-W-084). It keeps the reference form, including `shortcut`. So a quote fence becomes `>` lines, a delimited table a pipe table, written numbers the bare dot, and a continuation row joins its row, unless the tree needs the other form. It is off by default. The tree is the same with and without it (C2-W-002), and a normalized document is stable under `fmt` with the option and without it (C2-W-003). On the command line it is `carve fmt --normalize`, and it combines with `--check` and `--diff`.

The escapes of a text written from the tree rather than from verbatim reference text (C2-W-075) are found by one procedure. The text is written bare and parsed in its context, including the link definitions of the whole document. While the parse holds a construct that the tree does not hold, the opener of the leftmost such construct gets a backslash (C2-W-090), and the text is parsed again. Leftmost is by the offset at which the construct starts, and of two that start at one offset the outer one. A bare `[text]` that would form a shortcut because of a definition receives a backslash when the tree holds that bracket pair as text. In text written by this procedure, a backslash it does not place is a defect, and so is a missing one; C2-W-125 names the few it adds.

An escape is decided by reparsing the candidate line in its context, with the 0.2 parser, and not from a list of characters. The reparse defines the bytes; a writer that reaches the same bytes another way, as from tables, follows this clause (C2-W-010). The lists below name the cases the test has to cover. They are not the rule. This is requirement W2.

The unit of an escape is the opener: where a construct opens on a run of characters, the escape is placed so that the whole run reads as text. The backslash stands before the first ASCII punctuation character of the construct, with two exceptions. In a hyphen run it stands before the second hyphen (C2-W-099), or before the first when the second starts a dash that the tree holds. In a sigil glued to a bracket or a backtick (`![`, `^[`, `!` or `$` before a backtick) it stands before the bracket or the backtick, or before the sigil when the bracket or backtick opens a construct that the tree holds.

The procedure gives one form for each tree. It can hold an escape that a later one makes needless, and it does not go back to take one out. The text `x<a:b>=}` is written `x\<a:b\>=}`: bare, `<a:b>` reads as an autolink, so `<` is escaped; then `>=` reads as the comparison sign (C2-I-117), so `>` is escaped. The escape of `>` alone would have stopped both, and still the form with two is the canonical one. The text `x(/u)(/u)/` is written `x(\/u)(\/u)/`: bare, the third and fourth slash pair, so the third is escaped; then the first and fourth pair, so the first is escaped. An engine may find the same form with fewer parses, as long as the form is the same. For a tree from a parse the procedure keeps the tree. For a supplied tree it may not: the writer compares the parse of its finished form with the tree and reports each node that did not read back as a loss (C2-W-011, C2-W-124).

The procedure of C2-W-088 can end while a node of the tree has not formed, because a character that opens nothing in the bare text keeps it from forming or ends it early. The writer then places a backslash for that node, takes out the backslashes the procedure had placed for the same stretch, and runs the procedure again from there. These are the only cases. One: a bare opening brace that reads on into a later construct of the tree gets the backslash, `x *\{*` for a strong `{`; of several braces it is the one glued before the construct, or else the last one inside the construct before its own attribute block, or else the nearest before it. Two: where the right neighbor decides the direction of a smart quote of the tree, the neighbor gets it, `x/"\]` for a left double quote before `]`. Three: where a sigil stands before the bracket of a footnote reference of the tree, the sigil gets it, `x\^[^[]`. Four: where a hyphen run starts with a dash of the tree and ends in text, the first hyphen behind the dash gets it, `x--\-` for an en dash and a hyphen. Five: where a closer, a lone bracket or a sigil inside a bracket label keeps a link from forming or ends it early, its first character gets the backslash, as the `/}` inside a braced emphasis, a `[` or `]` inside an inline footnote, and the caret of link text `^a` in `[\^a](/u)`. Six: where a text character directly behind a node would lengthen that node, it gets the backslash, as a backtick behind a code span and a name character behind a mention or a tag: the text of a code span `a` followed by a backtick is written with a backslash before that backtick, and a mention `@a` followed by an underscore as `@a\_`. Seven: where the escape of a sigil opener would change the direction of a smart quote of the tree before it, the backslash goes before the bracket of that opener instead: a right single quote before the text `:n[]` is written with the backslash before `[`, not before the colon; where the opener is a run without a bracket, as a comparison sign, its second character takes the backslash, `!\=`. Where more than one case fits an input, the cases are tried in this order and the first that gives the tree is taken. Where none gives the tree alone, the writer keeps the backslash of case six when case six fits, and otherwise that of the first case that fits, and runs the procedure again from there: for the text `x{.c}` and a backtick, the code span `a` and the text of a backtick, the brace stays bare and both text backticks take a backslash. A form with these backslashes is the canonical one, and C2-W-088 does not call them defects.
A paragraph line is tested for reading as a block opener or as an interrupter. The cases:
A delimiter is tested for pairing: a `/` or `*` that would open or close emphasis or strong, and a delimiter inside a braced span that would close a span opened outside it.
A bracket is tested for forming a construct: a pair followed by a link tail, by `[label]` or `[]`, or by a brace block; `![`; `^[`; `[^`; and a bracket pair whose label would resolve as a reference.

A sigil is tested for forming: `@` and `#` before a name after a boundary (C2-I-090), `:name:`, `:name[`, `<` before a URL, an email address or `/#`, a backtick run, `$` before a backtick run, and the runs that smart typography replaces where the tree holds text and not a smart-punctuation node.
An opening brace is tested for forming an attribute block, a braced comment, an editorial comment or a braced opener (C2-I-043).

A backslash in text is written as two when the next character is ASCII punctuation or a space, or when it ends the line (C2-I-010 to C2-I-012). In the alt text of an image a backslash is written as two when the next character is ASCII punctuation or when it ends the alt text, and a bracket that has no partner in the alt text takes a backslash (C2-I-074). A `[` directly followed by `^` opens a footnote label (C2-I-087) and would end the image text early, so the writer escapes the `]` directly after `[^`, and where a later `]` of the alt text has no partner it escapes the `]` that closes the `[^` pair instead, so that the `[` takes the later one: `[^]]` is written `![[^\]]]()` and `[^}]{#]` is written `![[^}\]\{#]]()`. A code span and a braced comment in the alt text are read raw: their brackets take part in no pairing, and the opening run of one that has no closer in the alt text takes a backslash.

In a table cell every pipe is written with a backslash, in text, a destination, a title, a label and a quoted attribute value alike, except a pipe between a backtick run and its closing run, as in a code span, which needs none (C2-B-169, C2-B-224). A value of a row attribute that holds a pipe is written in quotes (C2-W-050) with the pipe bare, since a pipe in a quoted value there does not close the row (C2-B-166).

A text line that holds only underscores, or one hyphen, is written as it is and needs no escape: it is not a thematic break (C2-B-159). A text run of two or more hyphens that would read as dashes is written with every second hyphen escaped, starting with the second, on any line, as in `-\-` and `-\--` (C2-I-111, C2-W-095): that leaves no two bare hyphens side by side and adds no escape that is not needed (C2-W-088). The escape also keeps three hyphens on line 1 from opening frontmatter (C2-B-161). Where the first block of the document would read as another tree on line 1 and reads as itself below a blank line, as a paragraph that holds only an em dash node with the source `---` does (C2-B-161), the output starts with one blank line. Formatting that output again gives the same bytes.

`carve fmt` writes the canonical form of each file, and with `--normalize` the normalized one (C2-W-127). With `--check` it changes nothing and exits with status 1 when a file would change and 0 when none would. For each file that would change, in the order of the files, it writes three lines on standard output, the product of the command (C2-T-014): the path, a colon and the number of the first line that differs, as `a.crv:2`; then `- ` and that line of the file; then `+ ` and the line `fmt` writes there. Where one side has no such line, its line is the prefix alone, `-` or `+`. Lines are compared with their line endings, so a file that differs only in a line ending, a CRLF or a missing final line feed, names the first line whose ending differs, and both of its lines are written without their endings: `a` with no final line feed gives `a.crv:1`, `- a` and `+ a`. With `--diff` it prints a unified diff under the same exit codes. The path of standard input is `<stdin>`.

A command line fails with status 2 for an unknown option or a bad option value, for an input file that is missing or unreadable, for AST JSON that is not valid, and for an HTML input the importer refuses (C2-M-006). The first line on stderr starts with `carve[CATEGORY]:`, where CATEGORY is `usage`, `input-unreadable`, `ast-json-invalid` or `import-input-invalid` for these failures; the table of C2-T-040 holds every category with its status.
The writer is also reachable from AST JSON with no source and no sidecar. It then writes the defaults of C2-W-083.

A parse, a render, a write and a lint run report into one diagnostics record (C2-A-172). Every entry has a code, a severity, a position, a message and a channel (C2-A-173). The position is a byte range in the source, a path into the tree, or both: a finding of the writer on a supplied tree has the path alone.

The channel is `parse`, `render-loss` or `lint`. A code belongs to one channel. The writer's codes `structure-unspellable` and `field-unspellable` are in the render-loss channel, and so are the codes of the HTML importer (C2-M-080).

The severity is one of `hint`, `warning` and `error`, in lower case. The 0.1 engine source writes the first with a capital, `Hint`. The default is `warning`: a rule has that severity unless the catalog names another.

Every code is an entry of one catalog, `data/lint-rules.json`. A code is a contract: it is not renamed and not reused. A single plain message applies to every finding of its code. A row may express that same message as one variant whose `when` is `every finding of this code`; it applies to every finding. When a row has several messages, every variant states a `when` condition, and at least one condition must match every finding; if conditions overlap, the first matching variant in `messages` applies. The `reports` text of a row states what the code reports and the clauses it rests on; for a rule kept from 0.1 it is the trigger of the 0.1 engine with the row's `change`, stated on the 0.2 tokens and tree.

Lint is computed by a lint call from the parsed document: its tokens, tree and source ranges assigned by the parse. A render call does not run lint or return lint-channel entries; `unresolved-reference-link` belongs to a lint call, even when C2-H-085 writes the same unresolved reference as text. A source shape counts only where the parse reads it as the construct a catalog row names. A mark that C2-I-010 reads as an escaped character is not the start or end of a source shape that any catalog row reports. Where a rule reports a shape because it stays text, the shape counts only where the parse reads it as text of a paragraph, heading, cell, term, caption or line of a line block. Lint does not search the body of a comment block, a line or braced comment, a code span or block, raw content, an attribute key or value, a link destination or title, frontmatter, math content, or the marks of a braced opener or closer that formed or that C2-I-060 leaves as text, unless the row expressly names that place. The `reports` text cannot extend a trigger beyond a clause it cites: where they give different results for an input, the clause decides and the row must agree.
Lint never changes the tree and never changes the output of `fmt`.

The option `rules` turns single rules on and off, and `platforms` selects the platform rules. A rule can be suppressed in the source by the control comments of 0.1 (C2-B-215, C2-B-216). A rule that is off by default is turned on by its id. There is no named group of rules.
A rule whose id starts with `deprecated-` reports a spelling that 0.2 removed and that now reads as something else. These rules are on by default through 0.2.x.
Each `deprecated-` rule states its trigger on the 0.2 tokens and tree. The 0.2 engine holds no 0.1 parsing code for them.

A finding that a syntax chapter calls a diagnostic or a warning is reported by the parser, in the parse channel. A finding that a chapter calls lint, and every other rule of this catalog, is reported in the lint channel. A code keeps its one channel in every tool.

`comment-splits-table-row` reports a comment between a table row and its continuation row (C2-B-175), as a comment-only line or as the trailing comment of the row, at the comment. The comment belongs to the row's group after the whole row (C2-A-086), so it does not stay where it was written, and where it ends the last group the writer keeps it there only with an empty continuation row behind it (C2-W-135). The message suggests moving the comment above the row or below its last continuation row. The rule is a hint and changes neither the tree nor `fmt` (C2-W-108).

The range of an entry is the source span of the construct that the catalog row of its code names, in `reports` or `channel_reports`, unless that row states a `range` or names a range in `reports`, or the clause of the rule names another place, as C2-W-137 and C2-M-081 do. A stated catalog range takes precedence over the general extents below. Where that construct is a part of a node, such as an attribute, an option, a destination, a delimiter or a quote, the range is that part and not the node. Where the row states no range, an attribute range is its whole key and value as written, without the enclosing braces; a block opener range is the opening mark only, without indentation or following content. An entry of a run on source carries that range, in the render-loss channel too, and its path, where it has one, names the node that holds the construct. An entry on a supplied tree has the path alone (C2-W-103); where its construct is a field, the path names the field, as `/children/1/href`. A finding about a whole document starts where the document starts.
